title: Ollie, a privacy-focused AI assistant, is shutting down
snippet: As an increasing number of AI assistants flood the market, the founder of Ollie, an assistant that respected its users' privacy, says it will be shutting down in a week.
fullText:
Ollie, a startup whose mission was to deliver an AI assistant that respected its users’ privacy, says that it will be shutting down in a week. Bill Lennon, the company’s co-founder and CEO, took to X on Friday to deliver the news, noting that the app will officially shut down on November 6.

“I’m really proud of what we accomplished,” Lennon said. “We built an incredible personal assistant with a small team, and learned a ton. I’m grateful to our amazing team, our users, our investors, and everyone who supported us on this journey.”  

The text-based AI assistant market has exploded over the past year, as the increasingly powerful models that undergird such applications have made them significantly more useful for daily tasks.

Ollie, which discussed its $7.5 million seed round led by Khosla Ventures with TechCrunch in September, offered a subscription-based model. The assistant was focused on helping families stay connected and organized. The app connected to a user’s email and calendar, while also providing integrated functions to help with appointment bookings, meal planning, and bill payments. The company had also planned to eventually move into household budgeting.

Crucially, Ollie was one of the first mainstream apps that managed to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard that companies can attain via an independent audit. Unfortunately, user privacy has never been a hugely profitable aspect of the tech industry. If anything, many new digital assistants present unique privacy challenges for their users — as companies like Instinct have shown. 

Ultimately, the pressures of the burgeoning AI industry took a toll on the company, Lennon said. “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up,” he added. “With Muse, Instinct, and others entering the space, it became harder to stand out, grow, and raise the capital we needed to succeed.”

Ollie’s customers will receive instructions on how to export data and receive refunds in the coming days, Lennon added.

title: AI law firm Crosby bids on disintegrating, famed firm Weil Gotshal
snippet: Like a real-life episode of "Suits," the demise of famed white-shoe Wall Street law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges has been the talk of the legal industry. And now an AI firm has entered the picture.
fullText:
Like a real-life episode of “Suits,” the demise of famed white-shoe Wall Street law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges has been the talk of the legal industry this week. And now Silicon Valley has entered the picture.

Two-year-old AI-first law firm Crosby has put in a bid to buy some of the assets of Weil Gotshal, including its trademark, its brand, and some unspecified internal data, TechCrunch has confirmed. Separately, it is also working to hire some of the firm’s 1,200 lawyers. The Information was first to report this offer.

The once-prestigious Weil Gotshal confirmed to the New York Times this week that it was preparing to vote on dissolution in the coming days. The wind-down is happening after the firm’s presumed leadership heir apparent turned down the role, a number of its top-producing lawyers left, and a hoped-for merger with its rival, Willkie Farr & Gallagher, was shelved, the Times reported.

Meanwhile, Crosby’s founders believe they are the future of law firms. Rather than selling their internally developed AI tech to existing firms like Harvey or Legora, Crosby is an actual law firm. It uses its AI to provide legal services at, the startup promises, a speed never before possible. 

The startup has raised about $85 million, including a $60 million Series B round in March led by Lux and Index, with participation from its seed-lead Sequoia, Elad Gil, 01 Advisors, and Bain Capital Ventures. Crosby came out of stealth mode in 2025 armed with $5.8 million in seed money. 

While no one has pointed to the rise of legal AI as a contributing factor to Weil Gotshal’s downfall, AI may be key to the legal industry’s future. Terms of the bid weren’t disclosed and there’s no guarantee that Crosby will prevail. But if it does, Weil Gotshal’s legacy could somehow rise from the ashes, transformed by an AI-first firm.

title: Satlyt takes another step toward turning satellites into space data centers
snippet: Satlyt ran a successful test this month bringing it closer to turning spacecraft, starting with satellites, into virtual data centers.
fullText:
Naturally, Rama Afullo’s first reaction was, “Let’s GOOOO,” he said. His company, Satlyt, is building software to turn existing satellites into data processing networks, similar to the orbital data center concept. And he just took another step closer to that.

After 13 months of work, the company had a successful test earlier this month. Working with the University of Houston on a NASA-funded research project, the test showed how the startup’s software can spread out tasks among computers while in orbit based on communication and available compute.

He said the goal is to create software that connects to multiple satellites to share computing assignments. Users of the system “will only need to define permissions, priorities, and operating limits,” while the software will make decisions within those limits, Afullo told TechCrunch. Its software is already on three satellites in orbit and the first step to that vision was this test. While the test used NASA-funded research, the agency has not yet selected it for any particular mission or chosen it to deploy its technology.

Afullo said NASA missions face the same constraints that Satlyt hopes to address — “limited computing resources, intermittent communication, and the need to get useful information back to people.” 

In this test, the company created a simulated network with four computers, four users, and eight services. The software then assessed how to assign and run tasks on those computers, accounting for compute and communication availability. One physical computer aboard a spacecraft ran the experiment, evaluating a simulated network of four computing hosts, then returned the results to Earth. The test proved that Satlyt’s software can generate plans on hardware in orbit, but more testing will be done to see how those computers transfer information amongst each other in practice when multiple physical computers are used. 

“The finding is a trade-off,” he said. One approach worked best, though it required more computing power than the others.

Still, Satlyt which was in the top five of TechCrunch Disrupt Battlefield this year, calls this a win. “It’s a building block toward satellites sharing computing work,” he said.

The Satlyt team, from left to right, engineer Leina Moli, founder and CEO Rama Afullo, engineer Junn Wangari, and CTO Nelson PsenjenImage Credits:Satlyt under a Satlyt license.

NASA already has a technology network designed to move data through space even when communication links face delays. It started using this tech earlier this year and has already tested it on aircraft. 

Afullo, who previously worked at Google and SpaceX, founded Satlyt in 2024 to turn spacecraft into virtual data centers. Its software helps operators run AI and other applications onboard, processing data closer to where it is collected and reducing dependence on downlinks, where satellites send data back to Earth, and ground-based analysis.  

For example, if a spacecraft sees a wildfire on Earth, such software can help it transmit relevant information much faster. “The goal is to get useful answers to people sooner and make better use of limited communication windows,” he said. “This experiment tested one planning component of that broader capability.” 

Satlyt said it still needs to test its own software under various workloads, hardware, and connectivity conditions. They also found an issue in how their software was time-referencing delays, Afullo said — it was stamping it as arrival time (the time it arrived) rather than elapsed delay (how long it took to arrive), which is a different metric. 

It doesn’t mean the experiment failed, however. “The software development, onboard execution, and return of outputs succeeded,” he said. 

But Afullo said much work remains. “We also need usable communication links, permission from participating operators, secure transfers, resource scheduling, and recovery when a connection of computers becomes unavailable.” Satlyt is also researching applications beyond low Earth orbit, including supporting 4K video streaming from the Moon through its NASA-funded work.

“Our next technical steps are broader validation and integration, followed by demonstrations of computing work shared across separate spacecraft,” he said. “Longer term, we want developers to build applications for space without having to rebuild the infrastructure for every mission. That’s what virtual AI data centers in space mean to us.”

title: DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents
snippet: DoorDash said that it is open to working with third-party agent makers.
fullText:
Image Credits:Pavlo Gonchar/SOPA Images/LightRocket / Getty Images	

	

						

6:54 AM PDT · October 30, 2026

											

			

There’s a big uproar about AI agents taking over commerce and orders, but that might not be the case just yet. Delivery company DoorDash revealed during its third-quarter earnings call that it has only seen “several hundred” orders from third-party agents like Muse, Instinct, Fo, and others. For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily.

“I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional,”  DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst’s questions about the topic. “What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents,” he said.  

Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash’s app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents.

DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent it launched in September, a CLI agent introduced in July, and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched in June, which allows users to place orders through prompts and photos. The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering.

The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors.

title: The Wild World of Third-Party AI Apps for Ring Security, and Whether You Need Them
snippet: Ring cameras offer broad capabilities, but third-party AI tools give HOAs, landlords and others even more ways to use them.
fullText:
Ring’s powerful cameras are backed by a complex AI app store you may not know about.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

I’ve spent plenty of time talking about Ring’s latest features, including cutting-edge uses of AI and capabilities including facial recognition, which have led to lawsuits by some worried about their privacy. But behind the scenes, Ring has been busy supporting a sizable platform of third-party AI apps for its security cameras and video doorbells, with capabilities that go far beyond those of traditional security cams. That could present an opportunity or a potential privacy issue, so I took a closer look.

Ring’s lesser-known app store is packed with unique AI capabilities.Ring

Basically, this software leverages Ring’s object recognition ability to use it for a wider range of monitoring possibilities. I’m trying out some of these apps to see just how they work, but if you or people in your neighborhood use Ring devices, you should know what they’re capable of. These mini apps range from casual fun to Flock-like levels of surveillance. Most require a Ring subscription and an additional monthly fee, typically a few dollars. Here are popular examples of those apps, how they work, if they’re legal and what they could be doing in your neighborhood.

Keeping an eye on trash and dumpsters

Some apps help your Ring cam spot trash or criminals.Ring

For those annoyed by illegal trash dumping or other waste violations, the DumpWatch app promises to watch for trash miscreants using Ring’s AI for about $8 per month. The app records footage whenever it detects large amounts of waste being left in the camera’s field of view and creates a timestamped PDF that can be used to submit a complaint or file a police report.

			

More from CNET

Note that some examples DumpWatch uses show trash bins left on the sidewalk, a common occurrence on collection days, or extra trash placed beside bins, which may be allowed by local waste companies. It’s not guaranteed to capture only illegal activity.

Watching lawns, shrubs and toys for HOA violations

Ring’s apps can also fuel HOA searches for violations.Ring

Yes, these little apps can also serve as tools for homeowners associations if your neighborhood has strict rules about what’s permitted. One example is the $3 per month LawnWatch app, which is trained to monitor properties for HOA violations such as leaving toys cluttering a lawn, dog owners not cleaning up poop and so on. A somewhat more benevolent app, Greenlapse, tracks grass and plant growth over time, and is primarily designed to monitor your own landscaping projects.

This is one application that I have legal doubts about. If a nosy neighbor is trying to spot HOA violations in other people’s yards, not just their own, that probably violates privacy laws and could land them in legal trouble. I’d say it’s safer to use it on your own property to proactively avoid complaints — and avoid any “Karen” allegations.

Monitoring rental guests and tenants

Ring also lets landlords watch tenants — but it’s important to follow the rules. Ring

Ring’s app store includes a slew of monitoring apps made specifically to track tenants and short-term rental guests, collecting info for landlords to use. One example is the $5-per-month ZoneGauge app, which continuously tracks how many people are in a space, letting owners know when someone is throwing a party, for instance.

Another option is the GuardCat app. It’s $8 per month and it summarizes guest check-outs, cleaner visits, “house rule violations” and more based on what Ring security cameras pick up using AI detection.

A quick reminder here: Companies such as Airbnb have banned indoor security cameras entirely. Apps like these shouldn’t be used indoors at all.

Analyzing pet health and wildlife

Ring’s veterinary services could be an alternative to pet camera subscriptions, but I’m dubious about some of the claims.Ring

Using AI to monitor pets for unusual behavior that could signal health problems is nothing new. We’ve reviewed quite a few pet cameras and smart tracking collars that do something similar. But apps such as Pet Vet AI can use Ring cams as an alternative for $10 per month. Here, the app analyzes pet snapshots for issues such as limping, throwing up food, sleeping in unusual spots and more, then summarizes any problems for pet owners. The app says it works with birds, reptiles and fish, too, but I’ve never seen pet AI advanced enough to get any worthwhile analysis from the non-mammals in our homes.

On the lighter side, the YardWild app uses Ring’s night vision capabilities to identify wildlife that enters your property. It intentionally ignores birds and people to protect privacy and reduce unnecessary alerts.

Watching when workers sign in and how they behave

Ring also provides AI analysis and reports for workers, although I advise caution.Ring

Ring’s mini apps extend beyond the home and into many aspects of the workplace, too. Apps such as ProofClock and TimeStack are designed for construction, freight and similar industries to monitor when teams arrive at a location and how long they work, even when the Ring camera owner isn’t present. Some of these apps can also generate uptime and service-level agreement reports, although I’m dubious about tying Ring AI, which isn’t always reliable, so closely to payroll.

Identifying birds

Bird AI is fun, but some smart bird feeders offer this for free.Ring

We’ve tested plenty of bird feeder cameras that can identify bird species with varying degrees of success. But if you’d like to point a Ring camera at a feeder or birdbath, an app such as What’s That Bird.AI can do something similar for $5 per month. It captures screenshots of nearby birds and attempts to identify them so you can see which species are stopping by.

There’s a small problem here: Feeders from Birdbuddy and similar brands give you bird recognition for free, so if you don’t mind buying a dedicated bird watching camera, there’s no need to pay a subscription at all. 

Do these apps work with any Ring device?

No. Each app has its own requirements, displayed on their download pages. Some will work with nearly any Ring device that uses a camera. Others require a wired-in Ring device or a more recent Ring camera from the past year or so, or both.

Do these apps collect personal data about users?

One thing I like about Ring’s app store is its “App privacy” section, which lists the types of information each app collects. That can include motion events, your email address, access to your Ring camera’s live view and more. Developers can also indicate whether they use the data to train AI models.

Are these apps legal to use?

Generally speaking, yes, since they’re made for use on private property and in places where there’s a low expectation of privacy. These AI features can detect strangers, but I haven’t seen any that use facial recognition or other technology that could run afoul of privacy laws.

Keep in mind that tools like these aren’t perfect and shouldn’t be the sole basis for filing a complaint or taking other action. They’re also expensive for what they do — such as charging $5 per month just to tell you when your mail arrives — so I don’t think they’re worth the cost for the average user. One exception may be pet AI, which could replace more expensive pet camera services. Either way, it’s important to know your options — and which apps your neighbors may be using.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: Apple acquires Ascend․io, an agentic AI engineering startup
snippet: Apple recently struck a deal to acquire Ascend.io, a company focused on agentic data engineering technology. Under the Digital Markets Act, Apple must now publicly report acquisitions above a certain size. This has given us new insight into the company’s acquisition strategy, including glimpses at its future goals. more…
fullText:
Apple recently struck a deal to acquire Ascend.io, a company focused on agentic data engineering technology.

Under the Digital Markets Act, Apple must now publicly report acquisitions above a certain size. This has given us new insight into the company’s acquisition strategy, including glimpses at its future goals.

The latest update to the EU’s “List of Acquisitions” website reveals a deal between Apple and Ascension Labs, Inc., perhaps better known as Ascend.io.

This is a typical acquihire situation, with Apple’s update saying it “will have the right to make employment offers to and hire certain employees” of Ascension Labs. The deal also includes a “non-exclusive license to Ascend’s intellectual property rights.” Apple will also be able to “be assigned certain patents” owned by the company.

Ascend.io describes itself as “the first Agentic Data Engineering platform,” with AI agents that “automatically handle all the tedious stuff” associated with data engineering. The company was founded in 2015.

Ascend.io’s website has also been updated with the following note:

For the past ten years we pursued a singular mission: Make Data Engineering Delightful. We introduced the industry’s first declarative data pipeline technology. We launched a unified platform that brought all of ingest, transform, and orchestration together. We invented DataAware automation. And most recently we pioneered Agentic Data Engineering — where agents work alongside teams across the entire data engineering lifecycle. Each chapter was different, but the goal the same: make life better for data engineers.

Earlier this month, Apple also struck a deal with an AI startup that lets musicians rework recorded music.

title: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test

fullText:
During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company’s still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions.

But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player.

“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call.

Success is not guaranteed. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.)

“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”

— Derek Mulvey

But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse.

Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. He continued:

So, our view is that that is going to become a big driver of demand. And I think it’s unclear how quickly the whole — you know, the whole US market and the whole automotive market — starts to shift to really wanting this, and this being a major purchase criterion. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us.

But Scaringe was cagey about other details. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.”

Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin.

Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. It also warned that adding two processors and costly lidar sensors to some R2 models could eat into the profits it hoped to make by building the vehicle in large numbers.

The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong.

To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.

title: Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth
snippet: Google's AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Google says it tried out other space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts as well. The test is part of Google's Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google launched the satellite into orbit earlier this … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Skip to main content

The Project Suncatcher satellite generated a haiku about being in space.

The Project Suncatcher satellite generated a haiku about being in space.

by  Emma Roth

Oct 30, 2026, 6:21 PM UTC

Image: Google

Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Google’s AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space:

Blue marble below

Data streams in silent grace

Starlight feeds my core. ✨

Google says it tried out other space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts as well. The test is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google launched the satellite into orbit earlier this month.

“Next, we will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit,” Google says. “Verifying our TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space paves the way for our next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027.”

title: Zest’s new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text
snippet: Can't agree on where to eat? Zest's AI concierge can combine everyone's tastes, put restaurant options to a vote, and make the reservation.
fullText:
Zest, the restaurant discovery app that launched earlier this year, is already thinking about a future where mobile apps are no longer the primary interface. On Thursday, the startup introduced a new feature: a personal AI-powered “restaurant concierge” that lives in your text messages, similar to other popular AI agents like Instinct or Poke.

The launch reflects a broader shift in how startups are thinking about AI, as conversational AI agents take on tasks that had previously required users to launch stand-alone mobile apps. For Zest, that means bringing its restaurant recommendations into texts, then allowing users to immediately take the next step of booking a table.

“The agent is the product now,” explains Zest founder and CEO Mario Gomez-Hall. “You text it, and it answers from your own history and your friends’. It doesn’t need weeks of conversation to learn you because it starts from where you’ve actually been,” he said.

Image Credits:Zest

Originally founded in November 2024, with $1.8 million in pre-seed backing from Alexis Ohanian at 776 and Steve Jang at Kindred Ventures, the app’s unique feature is that it links up with users’ credit cards to track where they’re actually eating out to get a sense of their tastes and interests. With this data on hand, Zest can make tailored suggestions of what places you might like to try next, whether that’s in your own city or suggestions of places to try when you’re traveling.

The credit card data used by Zest’s app is imported via the financial services company Plaid, which is used by banks and other fintech and budgeting apps. Zest says it focuses only on those transactions in the food and drink categories when making its personalized map and lists.

The startup’s latest idea is to tackle the same problem — where should I go to eat? — from a new angle. It will now make its suggestions from inside a text message thread and can turn to AI to do things like check availability and make the reservation for you through connected services like OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms. 

Image Credits:Zest

To work, users will text the Zest concierge at (212) 470-6067. What’s even better is that Zest can be dropped into a group chat, where it can blend everyone’s tastes to find places the whole group will love. Here, it can also settle indecision with an in-thread voting feature and then can book a table for the group without leaving the conversation. 

Users can ask Zest for recommendations based on a number of factors, like cuisine, craving, occasion, dietary restrictions, or neighborhood, and can ask questions about the restaurants, like how busy the place may be, or whether it offers Wi-Fi, and more. Plus, you can ask Zest to send you the menu to help you make a decision. 

In TechCrunch’s tests, the AI worked fairly well, offering a list of suggestions for new places matched to our tastes that also fit particular conditions, like time of day, party size, location, and other factors. While finding an open table is something other apps have offered for years, there’s a convenience factor in being able to just text back and forth about the various options and have it tell you the available booking times.

The company began testing the concierge last month, but decided to hold the launch until it could add the booking capabilities; over time, the startup is considering moving Zest beyond restaurants to offer recommendations for businesses, shopping, and more. 

By shifting to texts, Zest hopes the company can scale beyond its initial thousands of users and generate revenue.

“Booking and ordering are the first revenue lines. Zest books your table through OpenTable or Resy today, with food ordering coming, and there are transactions there to participate in,” said Gomez-Hall. “The reason that gets interesting is that Zest learns your taste faster than a general assistant does, because it starts from where you’ve actually been instead of asking you questions. That’s worth something well beyond dinner,” he added.

title: What Are Open-Weight AI Models?
snippet: Open-weight models let you run an AI chatbot on your own computer, even offline. Here’s how they work and what that means for your privacy.
fullText:
You might use a chatbot without thinking about who controls the model behind it. Then an update changes how it answers, or you want help with something private you’d rather keep on your computer.

An open-weight model lets you download the pretrained AI and run it yourself. You’ll need software to use it and a computer that can handle it, but you get to keep a working copy. While chatbots get most of the attention, image and video generators can also have open-weight options.

Downloading an AI model doesn’t necessarily give you unrestricted permission or reveal everything that went into making it, though. Sure, you get more autonomy in how you use AI, but the word “open” still leaves a lot unsaid. Here’s what open-weight models are, what you can do with them and what to consider before trying one for yourself.

			

More from CNET

What are open-weight models and how do they work?

In a chatbot, the AI model is the software that generates the answers. During training, the model learns patterns by adjusting billions of numerical values called neural network weights. When you ask a question, the model uses your prompt and those learned patterns to predict what text should come next, building its answer one piece at a time. 

Developers of closed models, including those behind ChatGPT and Claude, keep their weights private. An open-weight model makes its trained weights publicly available. That means you can download them and run your own copy using compatible software. 

“Whenever you open-weight a model, all the weights are all over the place on the internet, like on Hugging Face and other servers,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at AI company Mistral, tells CNET. “So it’s virtually impossible to cut access to this model.”

With a free model and app, you can chat locally without a subscription or usage fees. More importantly, a fully local setup also keeps your prompts and files off an AI provider’s servers.

Don’t worry if you’re not tech-savvy, because you won’t have to write code or open a terminal to do it. Desktop apps like LM Studio, Ollama and Jan let you download and run open-weight models with a simple install, giving you a ChatGPT-like interface right on your Mac or PC. You still need a computer that can handle your chosen model. Once everything is installed, you can keep chatting offline.

If you know how, you can also adapt the model through further training, where permitted by its license. You don’t have to train an entirely new model from scratch.

Open-weight vs. open-source

People often use these terms interchangeably, but they don’t mean quite the same thing. An open-weight model can also be open-source, but publishing the weights alone doesn’t qualify under the Open Source Initiative’s definition.

Developers must share the code used to train and run it. They must also provide enough information about the training data for a skilled person to build a model that works much the same way. The terms must allow people to use, study, change and share it.

Under the OSI definition, developers don’t have to share the data they used to train a model. The Free Software Foundation says that should be part of the deal, with users free to use and change the data themselves.

Some open-weight licenses limit business use, meaning a model might be free to download but off-limits for an app you want to sell. That kind of restriction would disqualify it under the OSI definition. An open-source license can still require you to keep the same terms when you share a version you’ve changed.

James Martin/CNET

Which models have open weights?

Chinese models currently lead independent AI testing company Artificial Analysis’s intelligence rankings for open-weight models. You may already know about DeepSeek, but there is also Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 family, which offer downloadable weights.

Some US alternatives come from the companies behind familiar chatbots. OpenAI offers gpt-oss models separately from ChatGPT, while Google has Gemma models. Meta has Muse Glimmer and added Muse Spark Open alongside its Llama models, and Nvidia has Nemotron. 

You don’t have to stick with the chatbot giants, either. A US-based startup, Reflection, released Beam, whose weights are now available to download. Another US startup, Thinking Machines Lab, offers its model Inkling.

Europe has a contender in France’s Mistral AI. Its downloadable models include Mistral Large 3 and the smaller Ministral 3 family. The newer Mistral Large 4, dubbed Le Chonk, is available now with downloadable weights.

Not every model mentioned here will run on a laptop. Some larger models need server hardware, while smaller versions can run on personal computers or even smaller devices, like phones.

What are the limits?

An open-weight model can still hallucinate when it’s running offline on your laptop. It can also carry biases from its training. Developers may publish weights while keeping training data private, leaving outsiders unable to fully check what went into them.

Performance varies by model and task, so openness alone won’t tell you whether it will beat a closed alternative. 

The freedom to change a model also means people can weaken or remove its safeguards. 

“Guardrails are necessary to open-weighting a model,” Stock says. When I ask how to keep them safe if people can remove those protections after downloading a model, Stock says, “With a lot of work, you can partially overcome the guardrails,” comparing the effort involved to do so to fine-tuning a model yourself.

Once people have downloaded copies, the original developer has limited control over what happens next. A company can cut off someone misusing its online service, and releasing a safer replacement won’t update everyone’s download. 

Yet those same downloads allow independent researchers to examine models more closely and identify faults. Researchers can test changes themselves, rather than depend on the developer to investigate a complaint.

Microsoft and other companies cited that benefit in an open letter defending open weights after reports of potential US restrictions on Chinese models. They argued that keeping these tools available helps security teams defend against attackers using AI.

“When you open-weight a model, you’re essentially enabling the entire ecosystem to progress together,” Stock tells CNET.

Google/CNET

Would an open-weight model be useful to you?

Open-weight models can draft emails, summarize documents, analyze local files and help with coding just like cloud models. However, when you run one locally, its speed and ability to handle long documents depend on both the model and your computer’s memory and processing power.

Larger models usually run more smoothly on computers with plenty of memory or a powerful GPU, like a Mac with 16GB or 36GB RAM, though smaller models may work on an 8GB Mac. 

If you already own the necessary hardware, it’s worth considering installing an open-weight model. But if you have to buy a new computer to run them, weigh that cost against a $20-per-month subscription for a cloud model.

You can also use some open-weight models through their developers’ own websites that run them for you, like DeepSeek and Kimi. That’s less work than downloading and running the model yourself, but your prompts go to the provider.

If you want occasional help writing an email and don’t mind using an online service, a hosted chatbot may suit you just fine. ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude all have free plans, so avoiding a subscription doesn’t automatically require running your own AI.

Open weights give you the option to take more control yourself, not to mention keeping sensitive documents on your device. An assistant that keeps working when you don’t have access to the internet sounds great. So does being able to keep a model you like even after its developer retires the online one. 

“You don’t want to live in a world in which someone can cut off access to your model,” Stock says. 

The future also looks promising with open-weight models being installed on smaller devices. Google’s Gemma models include smaller versions for phones and laptops. Mistral has a similar range of models, including specialized ones intended for particular uses and devices.

“We also have models specialized in audio, for instance,” Stock says, “and those can fit literally on the smartwatch.”

title: Salesforce’s M&A spree continues with a reported $375M deal for defense tech startup Rune
snippet: The AI logistics startup will bolster the CRM giant's Missionforce defense platform.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

4:21 PM PDT · October 30, 2026

Image Credits:David Paul Morris/Bloomberg / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Salesforce has agreed to acquire Rune Technologies, a startup that builds AI software to help the U.S. military predict supply needs and manage logistics from the field, for $375 million in cash and stock, Resilience Media reported.

The acquisition underscores Salesforce’s push into defense tech through Missionforce, its business unit serving national security and defense agencies. Since Missionforce launched last year, its business has grown 80% year over year, driven in part by a new 10-year, $5.6 billion contract with the U.S. Army, the company said in a blog post. By integrating Rune’s frontline logistics data, Missionforce will extend beyond back-office administrative planning to support battlefield operations.

Since its founding in 2024, Rune has raised a total of $30 million from investors, including Andreessen Horowitz, Point72 Ventures, and IQT, a CIA-backed nonprofit venture firm formerly known as In-Q-Tel. The startup was last valued at $127 million when it raised a Series A led by Human Capital last year, according to PitchBook.

Salesforce has been on an acquisition spree this year. In addition to Rune, the CRM giant agreed to buy AI agent platform Fin (formerly Intercom) for $3.6 billion, bought Qualified for $1.2 billion, and signed an agreement to buy Listen Labs after the startup walked away from a $125 million Series C term sheet at a $1.5 billion valuation, as TechCrunch reported.

Salesforce didn’t respond to a request for comment.

title: ‘Largest Crypto Hack in History’: Binance Loses More Than $6B
snippet: It’s a bad week to own crypto.
fullText:
The popular cryptocurrency exchange Binance was hit by hackers this week. The company confirmed on Thursday that attackers gained access to its servers and stole $6.3 billion, with analysts calling it one of the biggest thefts in cryptocurrency history.

Binance said hackers likely used an employee’s laptop to gain access to their servers. The company says it “will cover all losses” for affected traders using its secured reserves and funds. Binance is working with the FBI and US Secret Service on the investigation, Reuters reports. The company has temporarily paused all withdrawals.

Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. We have found no evidence of any wallet private… pic.twitter.com/5REncAI77y

— Binance (@binance) October 30, 2026

Crypto prices fell across the board upon the news of the Binance breach. Cryptocurrency isn’t regulated like other stock markets or banks. Crypto markets are constantly open, and traders “mine” currency using complex computations that use a lot of energy. (If that sounds familiar, it’s because a lot of crypto operations were the blueprint for AI data centers.) Binance is not insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the government agency that protects your bank deposits (up to a certain amount) if your bank fails.

			

More from CNET

Binance told CNET that of the $6.34 billion the company is committed to covering traders’ losses, $5 billion is being held in exact token assets, with plans to purchase the rest through other market channels. “We are doing this to match the format of the remaining token assets and address any asset shortfalls,” a spokesperson said. So if you lost money in the form of bitcoin, you would ideally be reimbursed in bitcoin, not another cryptocurrency. “This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity and OTC settlement also takes time.”

Cybersecurity breaches are increasingly escalating, thanks to AI powering both defenders and attackers. Polymarket, another crypto trading platform, temporarily paused trading on Thursday morning due to a third-party vendor issue, which was also referred to law enforcement, according to the company.

But the Binance hack may be the “largest hack in history,” according to blockchain research firm TRM. Blockchain analyses from TRM and Chainalysis attribute the hack to a North Korean group called TraderTraitor, but Binance and law enforcement officials have not confirmed that. The FBI told CNET the agency “is aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps.”

title: Samsung’s advanced sleep apnea detection is coming to these Galaxy wearables
snippet: Samsung announced a new, advanced version of its AI-powered sleep apnea detection, and which devices it will appear on in November. more…
fullText:
Samsung announced a new, advanced version of its AI-powered sleep apnea detection, and which devices it will appear on in November.

Sleep apnea detection was first introduced to Galaxy devices in 2024, after Samsung gained approval from the FDA in the US. The tool was offered as a baseline detection feature, so users who might be suffering from frequent breathing interruptions during sleep would be aware and seek further medical help.

Samsung says its new and improved version uses an AI algorithm to analyze breathing disturbances per hour (via GSMArena). It goes beyond detection and breaks those disturbances down into more granular detail – closer to something a dedicated sleep study would be equipped to do.

Users will need to record at least five hours of sleep twice within 10 days for the sleep apnea detection tool to properly get results on their Galaxy Watch or Ring.

	

Samsung is still adamant that this tool does not replace professional diagnosis; it’s simply better at making the user aware of their sleep habits.

Enhanced sleep apnea detection is scheduled for Galaxy devices

	

Samsung says the new sleep apnea detection feature will roll out in November, starting in Korea, after the tool was approved by the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety. It’s FDA-approved in the US, as well, so it should follow shortly.

So far, Samsung has detailed these wearables:

Galaxy Watch Ultra 2

Galaxy Watch 9

Galaxy Ring

After the initial rollout, the Galaxy Watch 7 and Watch 8 will get an update as long as they’re running Wear OS 7.0 or later.

There are no plans to dismantle the current sleep apnea detection tool available on the Galaxy Watch 4 and later.

title: GM’s $220M Payout Shows How Cars Can Secretly Sell Your Driving Data
snippet: The automaker must now obtain express consent before collecting or sharing driver data.
fullText:
GM has settled a multi-state suit over selling customer data without consent.

																			Bloomberg/Getty Images
												
			
				

General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to 35 states and the District of Columbia to settle a major privacy lawsuit over the company’s sale of driver data from its Smart Driver program, which dealerships offered to drivers from 2016 to 2024.

In 2024, The New York Times published a damning investigation into the program, revealing that, in some cases, data on drivers’ habits could be used by insurance companies to set rates. Some drivers saw significant premium increases after GM sold their driving history, and one owner was told a 22% premium increase resulted from driving information supplied by a data broker, according to a press release from the New York attorney general’s office. 

The data collection was described as “spying,” and GM quickly ended the program that year. In 2025, GM settled with the Federal Trade Commission over Smart Driver and OnStar location data, agreeing to a five-year ban on selling driver data.

			

More from CNET

Attorneys general in many of the states involved in the $220 million settlement posted announcements about it, including Anthony G. Brown of Maryland.

“Without asking permission, General Motors sold its customers’ driving and location data, which, in some cases, was used by insurance companies to set drivers’ rates,” Brown said in a release. “Because of our settlement, GM can no longer prioritize profit over Marylanders’ privacy.” 

 The settlement requires GM to obtain affirmative express consent from consumers before collecting or disclosing consumer driving and location data. 

In an email to CNET, a GM spokesperson shared a statement saying the company ended its Smart Driver product in 2024 and said it has strengthened its privacy practices since then.

“Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” the spokesperson said.

The company also told CNET that it has simplified and updated its US privacy statement, created a Privacy Center for consumers and has been “enhancing internal controls for connected vehicle data.”

Not the end of the road for auto privacy concerns

Automobiles have evolved into computers on wheels over the last few decades, collecting vast amounts of data on drivers, including contacts and song lists, location data and diagnostic information. For GM, the issue was less about collecting data than about breaking its promise to customers that it wouldn’t sell it.

There may be more action to come on illegal or unethical data-collection practices in the auto industry. 

“GM was the biggest case and, in some ways, presented the most egregious set of facts. But collecting and selling driving data is an industry norm, not an aberration,” said Peter Cassat, technology partner at CM Law and a former general counsel for Cox Automotive and New Country Motor Group.

“The difference now is that regulators have a template, and every state attorney general has seen a $220 million settlement, so I think we can expect more enforcement actions and settlements,” Cassat said.

The settlement, and the orders in place that GM must abide by, are a good start toward promoting best practices toward privacy in the auto industry, Cassat said.

“Vehicle providers should ask for driver consent feature by feature in plain English,” he said, not simply prompt buyers to check a box.

Protecting your privacy behind the wheel

In addition to whatever paperwork you sign when you buy, lease or rent a car, everyday vehicle use can present some data hygiene problems. Privacy issues can ramp up depending on the level of access you grant your smartphone, and how you’re using the car’s location or connectivity features.

Beyond the touchscreen on your dashboard, modern vehicles run background systems that transmit data straight to the manufacturer, and drivers have little to no control over what gets collected or who buys it.

Protecting your data can be “really tricky,” said Clyde Williamson, a senior security architect at the AI and data security company Protegrity who has spoken out about auto privacy.

“Modern cars can carry many of the same privacy risks as our smartphones, potentially without the same level of attention to security from the manufacturer,” Williamson said. 

Williamson said that while people have started to raise privacy concerns about other smart devices like televisions, automobiles aren’t getting the same scrutiny. And there aren’t a lot of avenues you can go to shield your data in cars without losing key conveniences.

“Unfortunately, there isn’t a lot consumers can do,” he said. “Opt out wherever possible and don’t agree to unnecessary data sharing. Review your own Customer Disclosure Report to see whether driving data appears. And if your car has a modem that can be disabled, consider disabling it.”

title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom
snippet: Big Tech is pouring billions into AI infrastructure, but mounting debt, negative cash flow, and growing investor skepticism are raising questions about the sustainability of the AI spending boom.
fullText:
Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. 

Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. 

Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. 

The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.

A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.

Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it.

Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. 

Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. 

Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank.

It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.  

Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. 

These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m reading about Netflix’s bloody week, playing with Apple Music’s fun new 404 page, mourning Arc’s untimely demise, and devouring Maggie O’Farrell’s new novel, Land.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Anthropic is going public, and thanks to its S-1, we now have access to some of the mouthwatering numbers behind the IPO. In the first half of the year, the company reported $16.3 billion in revenue, up from $1.2 billion for the same period of 2025. If you’ve been following the AI phenomenon at all, you’ll know why: Anthropic’s Claude Code kicked off the AI coding boom in early 2026, causing every company from Google to OpenAI to largely pivot to the enterprise. By the summer we were talking about “token-maxxing” as Claude Fable 5.1 ate billions of tokens every day.

	

With a rumored valuation approaching $1.5 trillion, Anthropic’s IPO, when it does happen, will be the largest of all time, eclipsing SpaceXAI’s by billions of dollars. The interesting thing about the numbers, at least to me, is how much cash is on hand: of the $141 billion raised so far, it has over $112 billion remaining.

However, Anthropic has committed to spending hundreds of billions of dollars with Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and SpaceX for cloud infrastructure, and expects to be compute-constrained over the next year. All of the major hyperscalers, including Google, have are prioritizing their own AI workloads over competitors’, meaning that Anthropic will be on the hunt for newer and potentially less reliable providers, with data centers largely powered by natural gas to keep costs down.

The data in this prospectus are truly outrageous. Anthropic did not exist until 2021 and was largely seen as an ideological research outfit until fairly recently. The notion that it would be one of the hottest stocks of ever was laughable, but here we are.

Conversely, a viral post by Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok last week is making the argument that except for tech, AI is not moving the needle.

In a number of compelling charts, Slok outlines the fact that while the Magnificent 7 are propping up the US economy, the rest of the country’s largest businesses — the S&P 493, as he calls them — are not seeing rising profits or meaningful productivity gains. 

“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence,” it begins, “the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth.”

Perhaps most concerning is where AI spend is concentrated: 80% of the top 1% of all AI spenders in the US are VC-backed companies, reinforcing the idea that frontier models are still the darlings of Silicon Valley more than Main Street.

Ultimately, both things can be true: the AI labs are minting money, but most other businesses haven’t seen the returns.

Welcome to Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with C. Scott Brown, a video creator at Android Authority and on his own channel.

Who are you?

C. Scott Brown

What do you do for work?

I’m a video creator at Android Authority and on my solo channel, C. Scott Brown (clever name, I know).

What do you do for fun?

I enjoy cycling and hiking quite a bit. I spend a lot of time with my partner watching movies, too, as we’re both big film buffs.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

Technology has always been a huge part of my life. I really love it. I love when a piece of technology makes my life better/easier, even if only in a small way. I genuinely believe that technology is what moves humanity forward.

What are three apps you can’t live without and why?

The Homey app is so important to me because my entire smart home runs through my Homey Pro, and I don’t even know what my life would look like without it. I’m also addicted to Reddit, and the Relay app is my way of accessing it, so I open it about 400 times a day. Finally, the Tautulli app keeps me hooked into what’s going on with my Plex server, so I check that a lot each day, too.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

I just got done reviewing the Fitbit Edge. I really like the Edge, but while reviewing it, I had to set my Pixel Watch 5 aside for the week. Now that the Edge review is done, I am very, very happy to have my Pixel Watch 5 back!

How does AI fit into your life right now?

I use AI to solve many practical problems in my life. Being a video creator involves a lot of small, mind-numbing tasks, and AI helps me do them faster or, in some cases, remove them entirely from my plate. However, I will never use AI to take over any creative aspects of my job. That’s the fun stuff!

What’s a book you recently read and loved?

The YouTube Formula by Derral Eves. I’m still learning so much about YouTube and how to improve my videos, and this book has been very helpful. I just wish it was written a bit better (sorry, Derral).

What’s an album (or two) you recently listened to and loved?

My two favorite albums of 2026 so far are Get Mean by Boy Harsher and Fantasia by Slift. I love the minimalist simplicity of Boy Harsher’s music. They’ve locked into a vibe and just beat it into the ground. They’re like the AC/DC of synthwave. Meanwhile, Slift is such an amazing band, and it’s so refreshing to hear loud rock music that isn’t overproduced, radio-friendly, or trying to fit into a modern scene. Fantasia is just guitars cranked up to 11, screaming vocals, pounding drums, and everything else I’ve ever loved about loud music.

What’s a TV show you recently watched and loved?

I mean, the only answer in 2026 is Widow’s Bay. It’s literally perfect. Perfect cast, perfect storylines, funny when it needs to be, just enough scares, terrific drama…there’s nothing to dislike about it.

What’s a movie you recently watched and loved?

Everyone Is Lying to You for Money was a banger. It was preaching to the choir for me because I’ve always known crypto was a giant sham, but even if we set that aside, the film was immensely enjoyable and way funnier than I expected.

What’s a game you recently played and loved?

Dungeons of Hinterberg was one of my recent discoveries. It was like Persona meets Zelda with a millennial going through an existential crisis. It sounds awful when I write it out like that, but I thought it was terrific!

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Drink a cup of tea. Or three or four cups. It is the simplest and most effective way to make me happy.

title: Can AI data centers be mass-produced like cars? This startup aims to find out
snippet: Runware is building a factory to turn out prefabricated AI data centers on an assembly line. The real test will be whether it can deliver at that scale.
fullText:
AI infrastructure company Runware is making news again, just months after unveiling the Sonic Inference Pod, a modular data center built in a factory and shipped to customers ready to install. Now the company has bigger plans. It told TechCrunch it wants to build a factory that assembles these pods on a production line, as if they were cars.

The idea isn’t entirely new. Companies like Crusoe and Schneider Electric also sell prefabricated pods, but Runware says it can ship its pods faster. 

Flaviu Radulescu, co-founder and CEO of Runware, told TechCrunch that the company plans to scale production at its Romania-based factory to 30 megawatts of data center capacity per day by 2028, or nearly 1 gigawatt per month. That’s a whole lot of capacity: At that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year, about 10 gigawatts. But it also reflects an industrywide push to deploy data centers faster and more efficiently. 

Nvidia announced, for example, the Vera Rubin AI factories and the DSX POD earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one. 

Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year. 

Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said. 

The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.” 

Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion, which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December.

“Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.”

Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said.

Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google.

The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.”

Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said.

“Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added.

title: Nvidia weighs playing the cosigner for Nscale’s AI data center in West Virginia
snippet: When investors get nervous about AI spending, it helps to have the chipmaker that sells the chips offer to cosign the loan.
fullText:
Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information reported Thursday. Bloomberg later corroborated the report. Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the project’s first building alone, according to Nscale’s IPO filing. In essence, the chipmaker would be co-signing a customer’s loans, a sign of how hard the AI industry is working to keep its buildout plans afloat as investors grow jittery about the amounts of money involved.

The proposed arrangement would help Nscale secure financing for the electricity and construction costs of its West Virginia campus. Under what’s known as a residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the facility, and help find a buyer and new tenant, according to The Information.

Nvidia’s earlier support for cloud providers has mostly covered leases and chip purchases, not construction.

The stakes are high for Nscale, which is seeking to go public at a valuation of up to $35 billion despite growing concerns about its ability to deliver on ambitious data center projects.

Anthropic’s contract with Nscale covers the first 460-megawatt building at Nscale’s West Virginia campus, which is expected to use Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips. The companies are also discussing a second deal worth roughly $45 billion for another building.

Nscale has struggled to get its projects off the ground. The company had about 25,000 advanced AI chips running in August, a fraction of the nearly 500,000 it plans to deploy. Its West Virginia campus has run into trouble of its own. Runoff from the construction site has flooded nearby homes more than once. In September, after months of negotiations, the project won state certification. 

This month, Microsoft pulled out of a planned Nscale site in England after grid power for it was pushed into the 2030s.

Nvidia has been a major financial backer of the sector, extending roughly $170 billion in investments and credit support to neoclouds and large customers, according to The Information. That includes $1 billion in convertible financing committed to Nscale in September.

Neoclouds, which rent out AI computing power without a cash-rich core business behind them, have come under pressure from investors. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN had each fallen more than 30% in October as of last week, CNBC reported.

The proposed guarantee would deepen Nvidia’s financial ties to Nscale while helping secure a major customer for its chips. Anthropic, one of the largest buyers of AI computing power, has spread its infrastructure spending across multiple chipmakers. One investor told The Information that Anthropic’s involvement likely explains Nvidia’s interest in keeping Nscale’s project on track.

The discussions also come as Anthropic faces questions about how it will finance its own rapid expansion. The company filed to go public this week, but Blackstone has warned investors that Anthropic may receive a below-investment-grade credit rating after its IPO. A junk rating would raise Anthropic’s borrowing costs and could push it to keep relying on stronger partners to back its debt.

title: Vivo’s X500 series launches globally with MediaTek chips and insane cameras
snippet: Following its initial debut in China, Vivo is officially taking its flagship lineup global. The X500 series brings three new models to the international stage, including the Vivo X500, X500 Pro, and the range-topping X500 Pro Max. more…
fullText:
Following its initial debut in China, Vivo is officially taking its flagship lineup global. The X500 series brings three new models to the international stage, including the Vivo X500, X500 Pro, and the range-topping X500 Pro Max.

What’s interesting is that the Chinese OEM has just jumped straight past the X400 to the X500, for what reason, we’re not entirely sure. This is a direct follow-on from the X300 lineup, which was released earlier this year and has been such a promising lineup.

Under the hood, both the X500 Pro and Pro Max are powerhouses, becoming the first smartphones to feature MediaTek’s new 2nm Dimensity 9600 Pro chipset. The standard X500 is powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 9600M. Display-wise, both Pro models sport 2K 144Hz BOE Q11 LTPO AMOLED displays—6.36-inch on the Pro and 6.85-inch on the Pro Max—reaching up to 4,500 nits peak brightness. The vanilla X500 sits in the middle with a 6.59-inch 144Hz AMOLED screen.

Battery capacities have taken a massive leap forward across the board thanks to high-density silicon-carbon technology: an 8,000 mAh cell inside the Pro Max, 6,510 mAh in the Pro, and 7,500 mAh in the standard X500. All three models support 90W wired FlashCharge and 40W wireless charging, carry dual IP68 & IP69 water and dust resistance, and ship running OriginOS 7 based on Android 17.

	

But as expected, the cameras are the (pun intended…) main focus here.

Co-engineered with Zeiss, the X500 Pro and Pro Max center around a custom 50MP 24mm-equivalent main sensor (Sony LYTIA L910, 1/1.28-inch) featuring an f/1.57 aperture, Zeiss T* coating, and 17 EV of dynamic range. The Pro Max features a “gimbal-grade” 3-degree OIS setup, while the Pro steps back slightly to 1.5 degrees.

For zoom, the X500 Pro Max packs an 85mm-equivalent 200MP periscope telephoto (Samsung ISOCELL HP0, 1/1.4-inch) backed by CIPA 7.0 pro-grade stabilization. The X500 Pro uses a custom 85mm-equivalent 64MP telephoto (Sony LYTIA 610, 1/2.0-inch) with the same stabilization rating. Both Pro variants share a 15mm-equivalent 50MP ISOCELL JN5 ultrawide lens and support an optional 400mm-equivalent ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2 Ultra add-on lens. The company has banked on Pro photography kits in recent years, and this is yet another device shipping with an option.

Meanwhile, the base vivo X500 features a 23mm 50MP LYTIA 828 main camera, a 72mm 64MP telephoto, and a 50MP ISOCELL JN1 ultrawide shooter.

Video performance gets a serious upgrade, too. The X500 Pro and Pro Max offer 4K 240fps cinematic slow motion, 10-bit video capture with 422 encoding, and ACES (Academy Color Encoding System) support, while the Pro Max tops out with 8K 30fps recording and 4K 120fps Pro AF Tracking Video.

As for aesthetics, the standard Vivo X500 comes in White, Gray, Black, and Pink. The X500 Pro and X500 Pro Max are offered in White, Gray, Black, and a standout Sunset Orange finish. The White, Gray, and Orange finishes feature a subtle micro-dot shimmer, while the Black option features a pyramid-like light-shifting texture.
