As for why to get the phone? This one’s easy; it’s a foldable. From Apple. First, foldables are whimsical in a way that slab phones will never be. They are toys for grown-ups!  Developers are also clearly having fun building for the new format, so there are lots of new apps to play with. Plus, it’s a great way to watch movies, particularly with that Duo Folio case with a kickstand. 

Image Credits:Apple

Second, it’s a foldable from Apple. The company has taken its time to get it right, which comes through in the details, from the barely visible crease to the consistent aspect ratio between screens, allowing content to scale proportionally. It’s also a foldable in Apple’s software ecosystem, which matters for those who move between Apple devices and services and who use and pay for apps that are designed for iOS specifically.

But here’s a small confession: in day-to-day life, I didn’t unfold the Duo as much as I thought I would. (To be clear: I absolutely did unfold it! I just thought I would do it more!)

There are two reasons for this. One: unfolding the device in public invites conversation, and it feels sort of like a flex; I’m not always in a place where I have time to chat. I expect this problem to diminish in time as the novelty wears off. 

That said, I still had roughly half a dozen conversations with strangers while I was on vacation, from fellow shoppers to servers to business owners. I even handed them the device at times (when they couldn’t easily run off with it!) and let them fold and unfold it. One person wanted to see the Kid Cue feature in particular, which displays playful Snoopy animations on the phone’s outer display to get children to look toward the camera when you take their picture. They were genuinely delighted by this.

Image Credits:Apple

Anecdotally, the consensus was that the unfolded screen was something of a marvel to most: “You can’t see the hinge!” “Is that a screen protector or is it just like that?” (The inner screen has a matte, nano-texture finish, reducing glare. Once explained, it was also praised as “pretty cool.” )

“What if you get sand in it?,” a former Samsung Galaxy Fold owner asked. Their older Android foldable had been ruined after a trip to the beach where sand got into the hinge, causing damage to the screen. (This was not uncommon at the time.) The Duo is rated IP68, the “6” signifying higher dust resistance, making it dust-tight. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 was rated IP48, by comparison. I’m not expecting it will have the same issues, though I do hope a reviewer takes it to the beach soon! 

I am certain that at least one of the handful of strangers I spoke to had never actually seen a phone that folded before. The fact that Apple has now made one means this concept will no longer be niche; it will be known to the mainstream. 

The other reason I didn’t unfold it as much as I thought is that doing so feels like the start of a more intentional screen time session. When I do unfold the phone now, it’s because I’m truly engaging with what I’m doing on the phone, like watching a show on Netflix or dragging two apps side-by-side in split-screen mode for multitasking. (I love reading news in Inoreader and having X open off to the side to see what people are saying about the news, but that’s a use case that won’t apply to everyone!) 

Image Credits:Apple

The split-screen feature is easy to use, too – with the app open, you swipe up from the bottom, then drag it to the left or right edge. Target boxes on each side help you visualize where it can move to, which is helpful. (You can also long-press on an app icon to open a split view, but I don’t do this as much.) 

Image Credits:screenshot Apple News and X by TechCrunch

But as something of a “mini” phone in terms of screen size when closed, I’m somehow less drawn to what I think of as time-wasting apps like TikTok, Instagram, or casual games. 

I’ve been thinking about this, and I don’t believe it’s just the lack of screen real estate when the phone is folded, or the fact that vertical apps haven’t been designed for the Duo’s unfolded landscape screen. Those concerns make sense from a practical, usability standpoint, of course, but there’s something more to this behavioral change, I believe. 

For years, phones have been getting bigger, taller, thinner, and more comfortable to hold. Consequently, they easily sucked us into their digital worlds. With the Duo, the design seems to interrupt the way smartphones effortlessly pull us in, begging us to open apps and scroll endlessly. 

Rather, the Duo feels like a device you open and use when you have reason to do so, not something you reflexively turn to when you’re bored or have a few minutes to spare. Because the best app use cases are when the phone is unfolded, and unfolding is something you do with careful consideration (and careful hands!), device use becomes more thoughtful. 

This is not a bad thing. It also aligns with the embrace of retro tech already underway, where knobs and dials and buttons make engaging with technology feel more deliberate.

And for that reason, despite its faults, the Duo won me over. It’s a phone that’s compelling and fun — a phone I enjoyed picking up, but also found easier to put down.

title: Apple reveals pricing for Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM
snippet: When Apple announced the new M5 Max and M5 Ultra configurations of the Mac Studio in August, it said a configuration with 512GB of RAM would be available in October. Today, the company officially revealed the pricing of that option. more…
fullText:
When Apple announced the new M5 Max and M5 Ultra configurations of the Mac Studio in August, it said a configuration with 512GB of RAM would be available in October. Today, the company officially revealed the pricing of that option. 

If you head to the Mac Studio configurator on Apple’s website, you’ll see the new 512GB upgrade option. As previously announced, the 512GB option is only available with the top-tier M5 Ultra chip that has a 36-core CPU and 80‑core GPU. 

	

It’s a $15,500 upgrade over the base configuration of that processor, which has 96GB of unified memory. 

To put it another way: you’ll pay $22,299 for the Mac Studio with the top-tier M5 Ultra, 512GB of unified memory, and 1TB of storage. You can spec it up all the way to 16TB of storage, which brings the total price to $29,799.00. 

If you order a Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, it’ll arrive in late November to early December.

title: Last-minute Halloween costumes for tech nerds
snippet: No Halloween costume? Just be a deceptively cute AI agent icon, a PHP vulnerability, or sleepy time Bryan Johnson.
fullText:
It happens to the best of us — you’ve completely dropped the ball on figuring out a Halloween costume. Naturally, you’ve decided to solve this problem by turning to… TechCrunch? Yeah, sure, why not. I’ve got some ideas.

Here are some last-minute techy Halloween costumes. Effort levels vary.

Recursive self-improvement

AI leaders like Dario Amodei and Sam Altman have expressed their fears that AI is developing too quickly, but if AI models become capable of “recursive self-improvement,” they’ll be able to advance on their own without human intervention, rendering any efforts to “pace the frontier” futile. 

I’m not sure how to visually represent the idea of an AI building itself, but you could really lean into the “self-improvement” part and forget the “recursive” aspect — it’s a last-minute Halloween costume. You don’t need to try that hard.

Dress as the version of yourself you imagine becoming every year when you make New Year’s resolutions. Carry around a self-help or productivity book like “Atomic Habits” or anything by Malcolm Gladwell, a yoga mat, and a huge bottle of water. Leave in the middle of the party to “go to therapy” when you actually just want to go home. Brag to people about how good your Oura Ring’s sleep score is. 

You are the embodiment of someone trying to better themselves. You are recursive self-improvement.

Image Credits:aldomurillo / Getty Images

A deceptively cute AI agent 

Meta and OpenAI both recently launched AI assistants with creepily cute avatars. It’s almost Elizabeth Holmes-esque — they look innocent, so you underestimate their potential to cause disaster. (While we’re talking about her, you’re only allowed to do the black turtleneck Holmes costume if you’re a natural blonde, or if you have a blonde wig.)

What you’re going to do is make yourself look big and fluffy. Maybe you have a poofy puffer jacket, or maybe you can find some colorful feather boas to wrap yourself in. Add a distinctive hat, glasses, or other accessory to make yourself look more like a ChatGPT dot. If you have a colorful shirt and matching bottoms, that also works.

Throughout the night, ask people if you can obtain read/write access to their Gmail.

Image Credits:OpenAI

Whether you call them “pervert glasses” or not, we should all be able to agree that it would be really spooky if someone just started recording you without your consent — perfectly in keeping with the Halloween spirit. 

Just grab a pair of glasses — or buy a cheap pair somewhere convenient — and attach a big red or white circle to one lens, mimicking the red recording light. If you want to make the costume extra creepy (or, if you can’t make a big circle sticker), you can just wear normal glasses and say that you’re “guy recording with the light covered up.” Please, just don’t actually record people without their consent while you wear this costume.

Image Credits:David Paul Morris/Bloomberg

Mark Zuckerberg wearing a vaguely unsettling T-shirt

While we’re at it, Mark Zuckerberg’s fashion has been pretty recognizable lately. He’s been wearing a lot of slightly oversized, boxy black T-shirts. 

It may be hard to replicate the black-text-on-black-shirt style he gravitates toward, but you could attach a piece of paper to yourself that says “Building is my love language.” 

If you feel confident in your Latin pronunciation, you could go for something actually scary, like the time he wore a shirt that said “Aut Zuck aut nihil,” which means “Either Zuck or nothing.” It’s a little ominous.

Image Credits:Minh Connors/Bloomberg / Getty Images

An AI usage limit notification

For some people, there’s nothing scarier than running out of Claude tokens. 

Grab a piece of cardboard, print out screenshots of notifications telling you that you’ve reached your usage limit, and go spook some vibe-coders. I’ve illustrated this idea using an edited stock photo. You don’t have to dress like you work at Hot Topic — that’s just the model in the image.

Image Credits:4×6 / Getty Images

A PHP vulnerability

The scary PHP-ocalypse is fresh in our memory — it was only last week that AI unearthed critical PHP flaws that could’ve been catastrophic for the internet. The fear that web developers felt is still palpable, making it a good Halloween costume: You are a PHP vulnerability.

Here’s what you’re going to do. Buy a T-shirt and a sharpie, and write PHP on it. Keep it simple. 

What about the vulnerability part? You’re going to have to commit to the bit. All night, you’re going to talk to your friends about your feelings. Actually bare your emotions. Talk about how your recent loss of a loved one made you remember how fragile life can be. If making yourself vulnerable kills the vibe, just pretend it was part of the Halloween costume and that you’re really cool and fun and never feel sad ever.

Image Credits:Tatsiana Volkava / Getty Images

Bryan Johnson

The costume explains itself. 

Bryan Johnson, a second time

Couples costume alert!

Maybe you have more than one Halloween party to go to this weekend, but you want your various costumes to stick to a specific theme. Once you’ve got your sleepy time getup sorted, it’s time to prep your second costume portraying the controversial biohacker: GLP-Bryan.

Johnson wrote on X earlier this year: “I frequently lay on top of Kate with all of my bodyweight. The deep pressure calms her nervous system, quiets racing thoughts, and releases oxytocin which lowers cortisol. We call it GLP-Bryan.”

Naturally, people were confused, so he shared an image to demonstrate.

title: AMVR’s new head strap is my favorite way to keep cool with a Meta Quest 3 or 3S
snippet: The upgraded AMVR BS1 head strap includes better ergonomics, a built-in fan, magnetic rechargeable batteries, and a new breathable mesh top support for ultimate comfort. more…
fullText:
The upgraded AMVR BS1 head strap includes better ergonomics, a built-in fan, magnetic rechargeable batteries, and a new breathable mesh top support for ultimate comfort.

I don’t know how companies like AMVR and BoboVR keep doing it, but AMVR’s latest head strap is now the most comfortable cooling head strap I’ve ever used for the Meta Quest 3 and Quest 3S. If you’re still using the included cloth head strap or haven’t used a “cooling head strap” before, here’s how it works.

The AMVR BS1 uses a breathable forehead pad attached via magnets to the support bar. Inside that support bar is an adjustable-speed fan, which you can easily adjust using the recessed wheel on the right side of the head strap. This fan keeps sweat down and helps prevent lens fog, two problems that can be a constant annoyance.

The fan is powered by the magnetically detachable, rechargeable 8,800mAh battery pack that mounts on the back of the head strap, helping to even out the weight distribution across the headset. That battery pack will also charge your Quest while playing and adds around 4 hours of additional play time. You can always purchase more packs to keep things going for longer, if you need to.

	

AMVR BS1 at Amazon (10% off)

Lots of padding can be found all around the headset, and the mesh support on top accepts any weight that remains. Every bit of padding is easily removable and washable, so you can keep things clean and tidy (especially if you share your headset with others). You can also get extra pads if you’d rather do it that way.

The back of the head strap cradles your skull with a mix of half supple padding and half grippy silicone. You’ll be double happy there, as the pad on the top part further cushions any headset weight, while the silicone keeps the headset from slipping forward and shifting weight onto your cheeks.

If you don’t need a fan, the BoboVR M3 Pro+ is currently $17 less than the AMVR BS1. I find the BoboVR M3 Pro+’s hybrid design to be slightly more comfortable, but the lack of a fan is a big negative for this particular BoboVR strap.

Once you’ve chosen a head strap, grab an AMVR FC4M face pad to add another layer of comfort to the headset. Like the AMVR BS1’s forehead pad, this face pad attaches to the Quest 3 (NOT the Quest 3S) via magnets and is made of breathable, easy-to-clean material. It’s perfect for staying cool year-round and makes the Quest so, so much more comfortable.

title: Google says Gemini 4 Argon ranks well behind Claude and GPT-6 for Android coding
snippet: Google has updated its Android Bench list for showing how good AI models are at Android coding assistance, with Gemini 4 Argon ranking way behind that of the latest Claude and GPT models. more…
fullText:
Google has updated its Android Bench list for showing how good AI models are at Android coding assistance, with Gemini 4 Argon ranking way behind that of the latest Claude and GPT models.

The Android Bench was introduced early this year as a way for Android developers to get a quick way to see what AI models were best suited to Android coding assistance based on a test from Google. That test took into account aspects of AI use that are specific to Android coding and best practices in Android development. As Google has continued its tests and ranking new models, it has also included the average cost as a part of the benchmark so that developers can make the best decision for their needs.

With the October 26 update, Google has added the reasoning level used for each model, as well as adding results for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, as well as Google’s own Gemini 4 Argon.

Currently topping the chart is Claude Sonnet 5.5, with a pass rate of 40% and a completion rate of 80.9%. Claude Opus 5.5, added to the list in early October, comes in second place. 

	

OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol might be the most interesting addition here, coming in at a pass rate of 29.3% and completion rate of 82.8%, but a cost of just $99.50 compared to Claude’s $1,574.90 cost for its first place finish. 

But it’s Google’s own Gemini 4 Argon that makes a rather underwhelming debut, sitting well behind other frontier models in fifth place. It lags behind Claude Fable 5.1 at a mere 21.3% pass rate, 81.8% completion rate, and an average cost of $267.70. 

In a report shortly after Google’s announcement of Gemini 4 Argon, some internal voices claimed that the model “struggles to handle certain coding tasks,” though Google stood by its capabilities.

title: Pokemon Happy Meals Land Nov. 10: Gotta Catch ‘Em All
snippet: You’ll get two Pokemon cards and one toy with each Happy Meal.
fullText:
Calling all Pokemon trainers: Are you hungry? On Nov. 10, Pokemon Happy Meals are returning to participating McDonald’s restaurants. Each Happy Meal will include one of 15 collectible Pokemon toys and two of 15 collectible Pokemon cards.

The Pokemon-themed Happy Meal comes with the standard menu options. You (or your child, or both of you) choose between the Hamburger meal and the four- or six-piece Chicken McNuggets meal, each including a kid-sized fry order, a side of apple slices and a beverage. 

Customers can also scan the QR code on their Happy Meal box to access a digital game featuring the 15 Pokemon Happy Meal toys hidden throughout a virtual classroom and playground.

			

More from CNET

The toys are Bulbasaur, Charmander, Eevee, Espurr, Minccino, Munchlax, Pikachu, Piplup, Rowlet, Sobble, Sprigatito, Squirtle, Torchic, Umbreon and Weedle. The figurines of each character are shaped like a Happy Meal box and squared off, with the Golden Arches as handles.

In addition to the 15 toys, there are 15 different Happy Meal boxes, one for each Pokemon. Don’t let Torchic overhear this, but it looks uncomfortably like a McNugget.

The promotion launches Nov. 10, but if you’re intent on landing one of the meals, don’t wait. Whenever Pokemon cards and toys are involved, there’s almost always a rush and items sell out quickly. McDonald’s tells me the promotion will continue while supplies last, but that could be a very short window.

In August 2025, McDonald’s Japan ran a similar Pokemon Happy Meal promotion and was swamped by scalpers buying up the meals for the included Pokemon cards (and then wasting the food). The company ended up restricting customers to a maximum purchase of three Happy Meals per group. Once that limit was created, only Pokemon toys, not cards, were handed out with the meals, our sibling site IGN reported.

I’ve reached out to McDonald’s to ask if similar purchase limits will be enforced in the US, and will update this story with any news.

title: Samsung Slices at Apple’s iPhone Duo With Its Z Fold 8 Ad
snippet: Samsung’s advertisement features a sliced green apple that rolls right along through the entire Galaxy Z Fold line.
fullText:
Samsung’s new Galaxy Z Fold 8 advertisement makes a direct jab at Apple’s iPhone Duo for its late arrival into the foldable phone market. In an Instagram video, Samsung’s “Slice” ad shows off an apple (the fruit, not the company) that’s chopped into pieces before one slice rolls along past the Galaxy Z Fold lineup, spanning from 2019 to 2026’s Z Fold 8.

It’s not unusual for phone-makers to bash Apple for bringing features and hardware ideas to the iPhone long after they’ve been available on Android devices. Samsung’s $1,900 passport-style Z Fold 8, which debuted in July, has a similar shape to the $1,999 iPhone Duo that debuted in September.

Samsung has also had years to optimize its One UI 9.0 software overlay for foldable phones, with plenty of options that take advantage of the phone’s larger and smaller displays. While the Duo does run Apple’s iOS 27, my colleague Abrar Al-Heeti noted in her review that third-party apps and services are still being optimized for different screens. The Duo is breaking new ground on iOS as Apple’s first foldable phone, but that also gives rivals like Samsung the opportunity to poke a little fun at Apple in their advertising.

		

			

Samsung’s ad ends by touting that the Z Fold 8 is thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo, which Samsung was able to achieve in part by using a new display tech called Flex Titanium and higher-capacity silicon-carbon battery tech.

While it’s fair to say that the iPhone Duo is late to the party, the company has a history of catching up quickly with its competitors. Apple began including wireless charging with 2017’s iPhone 8, years after other Android rivals. Now, Apple has helped develop the Qi2 wireless charging standard with faster speeds and magnets, and last spring the iPhone 17 Pro won CNET’s Lab Test of fastest wireless charging.

But until Apple’s new foldable phone is firmly established, I wouldn’t be surprised to see other foldable phone-makers like Google or Motorola creatively slice up Apple for waiting until 2026.

title: Samsung reportedly slashes production plans for millions of Galaxy phones
snippet: As RAMageddon rages on, brands are making tough choices including price hikes and refocused lineups. According to a new report, Samsung plans to cut production for millions of entry-level and mid-range Galaxy phones. more…
fullText:
As RAMageddon rages on, brands are making tough choices including price hikes and refocused lineups. According to a new report, Samsung plans to cut production for millions of entry-level and mid-range Galaxy phones.

ETNews reports that Samsung is cutting production of Galaxy A smartphones by “approximately 20%.” The cuts are being made to reallocate those resources for Samsung’s flagship products, as those pricier products are more likely to make a profit in current market conditions. For mid-range devices, inflated costs of memory and chipsets now make up around half of the overall cost of production.

This 20% cut to Galaxy A devices is said to account for roughly 10 million units, with further cuts planned going into 2027 (translated):

Component orders for the fourth quarter have decreased by about 20% compared to the production plan at the beginning of the year. On an annual basis, this represents a decrease of about 10 million units. The situation is critical as Samsung Electronics’ Mobile Communications (MX) division is suffering a loss this year… The stance is to cut Galaxy A series production by more than 10% next year as well.

While Samsung does make less on its Galaxy A series, the company’s entry-level and mid-range devices make up a huge share of Samsung’s overall sales. The best-selling Samsung phones are almost always entry-level or mid-range Galaxy A devices, though the Galaxy S26 series finally broke that record earlier this year.

title: iOS 27.2 adds two FaceTime features, including a personal favorite
snippet: iOS 27.2 adds new features to Messages, Podcasts, Photos, and more—including some easy-to-miss upgrades to FaceTime. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 adds new features to Messages, Podcasts, Photos, and more—including some easy-to-miss upgrades to FaceTime. Here’s what’s new.

#1: Dual Capture now works on all video calls, even with groups

Dual Capture was added to FaceTime in iOS 27 and quickly became one of my favorite features. Rather than having to choose between showing your face or the rear camera view, Dual Capture lets you show both at once.

iOS 27.2 expands Dual Capture to work on all video calls, even with groups. Previously the feature was limited to one-on-one calls.

If you have an iPhone 17 or newer, all you have to do on a video call is hit the ‘Flip’ button, and by default both the front and back camera will be activated.

It’s a huge upgrade to the FaceTime experience, and especially great if, like in my case, you have young kids running around and want to let grandparents see them and you at the same time.

The only drawback: everyone in the call needs to have iOS 27, iPadOS 27, or macOS 27 installed.

#2: You can add third-party sign language interpreter or live captioner

iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime more accessible by adding support for third-party sign language interpreters and live captioning.

Inside the three-dot icon, you’ll find a ‘Sign Language’ button that lets you pick an installed VRS (Video Relay Service) app for direct access to an interpreter. The app will appear as a participant tile in the call with a “Waiting for Interpreter” status, then your interpreter’s name will display after they join.

For third-party live captioning, Apple has a step-by-step support document here that outlines the process. You can also optionally stick with the existing built-in Live Captions feature to have your iPhone add automatic captions. It’s available from Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ FaceTime ⇾ Live Captions.

Bonus: Edge Light on iPhone Duo

If you have an iPhone Duo, iOS 27.2 also introduced a new Edge Light feature that works across multiple video calling apps, including FaceTime.

Edge Light works just like on the Mac, adding a ring of light around the iPhone Duo display to better illuminate your face on calls. It’s a built-in alternative to using a physical ring light.

To enable the feature, open Control Center while on a FaceTime call then hit ‘FaceTime Controls’ and tap ‘Edge Light.’ Once enabled, you can adjust settings like the intensity and color temperature.

title: Apple seems to have the right approach to the first touchscreen Mac
snippet: Steve Jobs famously dismissed the idea of a touchscreen Mac back in 2010 when he said that it “gives great demo” but turns out to be “ergonomically terrible” in real-life use. It was inevitable that eyebrows would be raised when the company did a U-turn on this by launching the first touchscreen Mac. But while I have no interest myself, I do think the company’s counterargument some 16 years later makes sense … more…
fullText:
Steve Jobs famously dismissed the idea of a touchscreen Mac back in 2010 when he said that it “gives great demo” but turns out to be “ergonomically terrible” in real-life use.

It was inevitable that eyebrows would be raised when the company did a U-turn on this by launching the first touchscreen Mac. But while I have no interest myself, I do think the company’s counterargument some 16 years later makes sense …

Steve Jobs had this to say back in 2010:

We thought about this years ago. We’ve done tons of user testing on this and it turns out it doesn’t work. Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical. It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue – and after an extended period of time your arm wants to fall off. It doesn’t work, it’s ergonomically terrible. Touch surfaces want to be horizontal […] that’s why we’ve perfected our multi-touch trackpads over the years.

Current CEO John Ternus addressed this change of heart directly. Specifically, he said that touch was intended to be a supplementary way of interacting with the machine rather than a primary one.

The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.

He suggested that it isn’t the headline feature of the new model.

All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.

I’m not interested in a touchscreen Mac

I’m a Mac guy through and through, right from the original Macintosh back in 1984. I’m also a massive trackpad fan, using the Magic Trackpad on my desk setup rather than a mouse. To me, it’s just the perfect way to control a Mac.

There was a period when I quite frequently used a 12.9-inch iPad with Magic Keyboard as a mobile alternative. Like the new MacBook Pro, that setup offered the choice of using the trackpad built into the keyboard or the touchscreen.

What I noticed about my own usage in this laptop-like configuration is that I almost exclusively used the trackpad. The only time I used the touchscreen was for scrolling, especially when I wanted to scroll a significant way down a page. That absolutely tracks with Ternus’ perspective of trackpad first, touchscreen sometimes.

However, when an M1 MacBook Air replaced my iPad with a Magic Keyboard, I didn’t miss the touchscreen at all.

But I can see Apple’s argument

One of the many things that’s changed over the years, in large part because of Apple’s launch of the iPhone way back in 2007, is that almost an entire generation has grown up with a touch interface. For them, the idea of a laptop without a touchscreen seems somewhat archaic.

However, I do very much suspect that even this generation will still use the trackpad as the primary control mechanism for the very reasons Steve outlined 16 years ago. 

	

The nightmare scenario for Mac users was Apple compromising the interface in order to support touch. None of us wanted to lose the high resolution UI elements and see them replaced with giant cartoon-like equivalents. None of us wanted to lose the precise control we get from a trackpad. Thankfully, that hasn’t happened. 

So no, I won’t be buying one personally, but I can see why Apple added the feature, and I do think the company has the right attitude to it.

Do you agree, or have a different view? Please share your own take in the comments.

fullText:

fullText:
Tech is in a weird place right now. There are plenty of exciting developments in AI, tons of new hardware, and rapidly growing ideas, but it’s all surrounded by the effect today’s tech is having on society. So, what tech is making you happy right now?

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

This article spawned from my time recently with new tech including Googlebook, the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, and the Mac Mini that I recently purchased.

Let me explain.

	

In the 10+ years I’ve been working in this industry, Googlebook is the first big launch that left me unable to find the upsides. Even after reviewing the otherwise excellent HP Googlebook 14, I’m still struggling to find anything to be optimistic about. And that largely boils down to the timing, as we discussed in last week’s Weekender issue. Googlebook is not only a platform that’s less capable than its competitors, but also wants to demand more from customers for it, all in a time where our resources as customers are more strained than ever. That same train of thought also comes into the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max that I reviewed earlier this week. It’s a great smartphone, one I think I’ll keep using for a while yet, but it’s also obscenely expensive, not really to the fault of Oppo directly. That’s just the tech industry we’re dealing with right now – heck, it’s the economy as a whole we’re dealing with right now.

So, that Mac Mini I bought. That came out of a limited-time deal where the M4 Mac Mini was $650. I’m still a Windows guy at the end of the day, but as PC components only become harder to find and, frankly, to afford, a $650 Mac Mini was by far the most logical way for me to eke more out of my gaming PC that’s already overdue for some component replacements. 

All of that is to say, the tech industry right now is full of a lot of tougher choices when it comes to the bottom line. As a reviewer, that’s been a tough conversation to balance, and it has me thinking not just about how we’ll interact with new devices going forward, but also where to find the optimism in the tech I’m using.

Here are some recent examples of tech that have brought me a smile:

The Oppo Enco X4 earbuds that I used alongside the Find X10 Pro Max are the harder-to-buy sibling to the stellar OnePlus Buds Pro 3, and they’re just utterly wonderful to use with such an excellent sound profile. 

As I’ve been working up my review of the Fitbit Edge, I’m reminded just how much I’ve come to adore the Fitbit Air for its simple and refreshing take on a wearable – I look forward to going back to it soon. 

There’s delight in the simplest ideas; the Statik Powerstand cable I went hands-on with this week immediately sparked a bit of joy from the moment I picked it up, knowing I’d just found a new staple for my bag. 

So, that’s my question to you.

What tech is making you happy right now? Is it a new gadget you picked up, or just the simple fact that your existing device is still up and running? Regardless of your outlook on the tech industry as a whole right now, it’s a stressful time out there, so let’s all focus on the positives for a minute…

title: Apple cuts App Store commission in Taiwan following regulatory discussions [U]
snippet: Apple today announced that it is lowering its standard App Store commission in Taiwan, following discussions with the country’s Fair Trade Commission. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple today announced that it is lowering its standard App Store commission in Taiwan, following discussions with the country’s Fair Trade Commission. Here are the details.

New rules take effect October 31

Over the past year or so, Apple has faced mounting regulatory pressure on several of its App Store practices and rules worldwide, particularly those related to app distribution, payment processing, commission fees, and alternative options for developers.

In Japan and Brazil, in response to local competition rules and investigations, the company introduced alternative app marketplaces, third-party payment options, and revised commission structures.

In the European Union, Apple recently overhauled its App Store fees and business terms to address concerns raised by the European Commission following a lengthy back-and-forth over its compliance with the Digital Markets Act.

Just last week, an Australian federal judge ordered Apple to allow alternative app distribution and payment methods following its years-long legal battle with Epic Games. Apple plans to appeal.

And yesterday, South Korean regulators fined Apple approximately $15.5 million and ordered changes to its App Store policies over payment restrictions, app review practices, and discriminatory commissions.

Now, Taiwan is joining that list, though the changes announced today are considerably narrower. Apple today informed developers that, starting this Saturday, October 31, its standard commission on paid apps and in-app purchases will drop from 30% to 26% in the Taiwanese iOS and iPadOS App Store.

Apple said the change follows discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission, and added that “signing the updated terms by October 31 is not required to receive the benefit of these commission rate changes starting that date.”

The company also updated its Apple Developer Program License Agreement to reflect the new terms, with translated versions expected to be available within the next month.

To read Apple’s full announcement, follow this link.

Update: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We’re making updates to the Taiwan storefront of the App Store following constructive discussions with the Taiwan Fair Trade Commission. These changes reflect our ongoing commitment to providing developers with a thriving marketplace and ensuring the App Store remains the safest, most trusted platform for users. We will continue to equip developers with the tools, resources, and support they need to build, grow, and scale successful businesses on the App Store.”

title: iOS 27.2 just upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new
snippet: Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And now iOS 27.2 has introduced four more. 

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

you can now edit captions for your photos and videos

comments can be edited too

there’s a feature to prevent adding duplicate photos to an album

the app can display a reminder before albums expire, so participants can save photos before they’re gone

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

#2: SynthID watermarking to identify AI-modified photos

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated. 

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

title: Samsung just released a new foldable that you probably wouldn’t buy even if you could
snippet: Samsung has big plans for its foldable lineup in 2027, but also one more release for 2026. The Galaxy W27 just went official as the company’s latest foldable, but you probably wouldn’t want to buy this one even if you could. more…
fullText:
Samsung has big plans for its foldable lineup in 2027, but also one more release for 2026. The Galaxy W27 just went official as the company’s latest foldable, but you probably wouldn’t want to buy this one even if you could.

The Galaxy W27 continues Samsung’s pattern of releasing a China-exclusive variant of its flagship, book-style foldable. This year, it’s based on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and includes all of the same specs – 8-inch inner display, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 200MP main camera, and everything else.

So what’s special about this one?

It mostly comes down to the fit and finish. Samsung has given the Galaxy W27 some slick golden accents and two striking color variants. One is a dark red, the other a dark blue. This model also comes with 16GB of RAM as standard, regardless of if you pick the 512GB or 1TB storage options. It’s also optimized for Tiantong satellite comms, SamMobile points out. 

	

But this special edition comes at a cost. It starts at CNY 18,999, around $2,800 USD. The 1TB upgrade lands at CNY 21,999, around $3,300 USD. So, even if you could buy this model, you’d likely be better off going with the standard Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra – even the maxed-out 1TB model sells for less at $2,699. Samsung does include a case and even a charging brick in the box with the Galaxy W27, though.

title: MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR vs MacBook Pro: Here’s every difference
snippet: Apple unveiled its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR this week (pre-order here), which joins the lineup alongside the existing MacBook Pro using the same M5 Pro and Max chips. Here’s an in-depth comparison of the two models. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR this week (pre-order here), which joins the lineup alongside the existing MacBook Pro using the same M5 Pro and Max chips. Here’s an in-depth comparison of the two models.

Design, size, and weight: PROLED XDR is thinner, lighter

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has an all-new industrial design. It’s the first design overhaul for the MacBook Pro since 2021.

You still get a 14.2-inch regardless of whether you choose PROLED XDR or not. On the 16-inch model, PROLED XDR is 16.3 inches, slightly larger than the standard 16.2-inch.

Apple’s new design is a bit sleeker and significantly lighter-weight. It also brings back the glowing Apple logo on the lid that was an iconic element in previous generations. Additionally, the PROLED XDR has a newly designed hinge that provides greater stability.

Here’s a breakdown of how each model compares in size and weight:

PROLED XDR 14-inch

MacBook Pro 14-inch

PROLED XDR 16-inch

MacBook Pro 16-inch

Weight

3.0 pounds

3.5 pounds

4.0 pounds

4.7 pounds

Height

0.59 inch

0.61 inch

0.63 inch

0.66 inch

Width

12.24 inches

12.31 inches

14.0 inches

14.01 inches

Depth

8.52 inches

8.71 inches

9.62 inches

9.77 inches

As the numbers show, the overall size difference is fairly minor, but the reduced weight should be obvious to anyone who upgrades.

Display: Touchscreen PROLED XDR with Dynamic Island vs Mini-LED with notch

The new MacBook Pro’s display technology is so important, Apple put it in the branding. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR features a tandem OLED that Apple says is “the world’s best laptop display.”

Again, it’s available in 14.2-inch or 16.3-inch sizes that are nearly identical to the standard MacBook Pro.

The PROLED XDR display is touch-enabled, with macOS 27 introducing a variety of optimizations for touch input. So if you want a touchscreen on your Mac, that’s a big advantage.

Tandem OLED means you’ll get deeper blacks, true-to-life color, and also a new max peak brightness of 2,000 nits (up from 1,600). And Adobe RGB is now supported, along with a host of industry-standard reference modes.

There’s also a Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro. It replaces the notch and serves as the home to software features like Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Performance and memory: M5 Pro and M5 Max chips

Apple is using the exact same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips in its two MacBook Pros, so performance should in theory be the same across models.

That said, real-world testing will reveal whether the new MacBook Pro design has an impact on sustained performance—for better or worse.

Memory options are also identical with the PROLED XDR model and standard MacBook Pro. That means:

M5 Pro models start at 24GB of RAM, with options for 48GB and 64GB

M5 Max models start at 36GB of RAM, with options for 48GB, 64GB, and 128GB

Storage: New 16TB option

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR largely retains the same storage options as the standard MacBook Pro, with one exception.

M5 Pro models start at 1TB, with options for 2TB and 4TB

M5 Max models start at 2TB, with options for 4TB, 8TB, and 16TB

The only change here is that there’s now a high-end 16TB option when you choose M5 Max. Previously, 8TB was the most storage available in any MacBook Pro.

Battery and charging: Identical in every way

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR offers identical battery life and fast charging features as the standard MacBook Pro. That means:

14-inch: up to 22 hours with M5 Pro, or 20 hours with M5 Max

16-inch: up to 24 hours with M5 Pro, or 22 hours with M5 Max

All MacBook Pro models can fast charge up to 50 percent battery in 30 minutes.

Camera: Advanced Video Stabilization

Apple’s MacBook Pro models all feature the same 12MP Center Stage camera with support for Desk View, 1080p HD video recording, and an advanced image signal processor with computational video.

However, because of touchscreen support, the PROLED XDR model adds one new feature: Advanced Video Stabilization.

Essentially, this exists so that if you’re touching your display during a video call, it won’t have an impact on your camera feed.

Speakers: All-new woofer design and closed-lid upgrades

The MacBook Pro PROLED XDR features largely the same speaker system as the standard model, but with a pair of key upgrades. Per Apple Newsroom:

The industry-leading six-speaker audio system in the new MacBook Pro features an all-new woofer design that provides 50 percent deeper bass and all-new tweeters that shape sound dispersion for remarkable clarity…And for the first time, dedicated audio tuning for closed-lid use delivers exceptional sound quality when MacBook Pro is connected to an external display, so users can enjoy a premium audio experience however they work.

Ports: All the same across models, with one small upgrade

Apple clearly learned from past mistakes of removing ports from pro users. With the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, you get all the same ports as on the standard MacBook Pro. Ports include:

SDXC card slot

HDMI port

3.5 mm headphone jack

MagSafe 3 port

Three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports with support for:

Charging

DisplayPort

Thunderbolt 5 (up to 120Gb/s)

USB 4 (up to 120Gb/s)

One upgrade that will benefit some users is that Genlock is now supported by the Thunderbolt 5 ports as well.

Pricing: PROLED XDR adds $400 premium

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. That’s a $400 premium over the standard MacBook Pro.

Apple’s standard MacBook Pro starts at $2,499 for the 14-inch size and $2,999 for the larger 16-inch.

MacBook Pro comparison: wrap up

	

Overall, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR offers a lot of upgrades over the standard model, but with the same basic performance and battery life. If you want a better display, touch support, a Dynamic Island, and various other smaller improvements, PROLED XDR is the way to go.

You can pre-order MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display here for launch-day delivery.

Are you planning to upgrade your Mac soon, and if so, which model will you choose? Let us know in the comments.

fullText:
“Its James Talarico. Can you please please please please pretty pretty please rush in even just $1?”

“Who’s working to elect James Talarico? Marxists.”

“Wow! Wow! Wow! Mark Kelly just made a HUGE announcement!”

“We asked Ben Verlander, MLB analyst and former Tigers prospect, to record a quick video about the election this Tuesday, November 3rd.”

“See which of your friends or family members have voted in the past and remind them to vote this year.”

If any of these messages sound familiar, it’s likely because they’re part of the massive stream of text messages flooding your phone leading up to the US midterm elections on Tuesday. The scale of the issue is not entirely clear, but call-blocking company Robokiller found that 15 billion political texts were sent in 2022, thanks in part to a Supreme Court decision the year prior that made it easier to send some mass calls and texts without consent. Alex Quilici, CEO of spam protection service YouMail, has an even higher estimate of 25 billion to 30 billion political texts this year, but caveats it’s an informal approximation. The volume is about the same to 10 percent higher than in 2024, he says.

There’s some good news and some bad news about these messages, says PIRG consumer watchdog director Teresa Murray. “The bad news is that political calls and political texts are exempt from the do-not-call-list rules,” Murray says. “The good news is that the election is next Tuesday, and hopefully within a few days after that, we’ll know what the results are and there won’t be any need to have any texts, or calls, or emails anymore after that.”

There are still some things consumers can try to stem the flow of these messages blowing up their phones — but it likely won’t significantly reduce it before Tuesday.

“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts … there are going to be some scams in there”

The simplest thing you can do is send “stop” or block and report the messages as spam, which will notify your service provider of a likely spam number. That probably won’t result in any immediate change, Murray says, but if enough people report the same number in a certain period of time, the provider might begin to block it or label it as spam. You can also file a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission or your state attorney general if you believe a number is using an autodialer without your consent — something that even the people behind political texts are not supposed to do. Whatever you do, Murray says, do not click any links you receive from numbers you don’t know.

“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts that are going out to support this candidate, or vote against that candidate, or vote for this issue, or whatever, there are going to be some scams in there,” Murray says. “If you want to donate money at this point, I would recommend going directly to the website for that political candidate, or for that PAC, and donating it that way.”

How did all of these campaigns get your number in the first place? If you’ve donated to a political candidate or issue group, that might seem obvious. But campaigns are also likely getting your information — including details about whether you might be likely to contribute to or vote for their candidate or issue — through data brokers that have nothing to do with politics. Data brokers collect and sell information from both public and private sources, such as public voter rolls, your online behavior observed by advertising web trackers, and loyalty programs. By collating all of this information, campaigns can try to infer your behavior, though they also might end up with outdated info, like old addresses that lead you to getting texts about a state you no longer live in (or even erroneous info that invites them for states you never lived in).

“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do?’”

“Errors in the processing of this information and the identification of individuals are very prevalent,” says Sara Geoghegan, consumer privacy program director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “Sometimes multiple people use the same device. Sometimes people have similar names. Sometimes people move. And this is such an unregulated ecosystem that there aren’t really rules in place to make sure that this is being effective and accurate, let alone free from bias, discrimination, and verified for privacy impact before processing this information.

“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do, and how many numbers do they need to block, and what are the toggle and privacy settings that they should toggle on?’” Geoghegan says. Meanwhile, “the companies that are trading in our most sensitive information are the ones who should stop harmful surveillance and the use of harmful technologies to have us better engage civically with our society, and not the other way around,” she says.

“I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”

Geoghegan worries that the harm of being bombarded with unwanted political texts isn’t just that people get annoyed, but that they stop engaging civically as a result. “Having this surveillance apparatus that invades people’s privacy and really annoys them actually pushes people away from this,” she says. “I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”

Unfortunately, you might get on some political text lists whether you engage in the civic process or not because of data brokers. Murray says the best long-term solution to minimize these spam messages is to limit how frequently you give out your phone number in general, like in an online shopping portal. If you need to give a number, you might consider using a VoIP number like a free Google Voice number, so at least you can silo those messages into another app you don’t need to frequently check or get notifications from.

Murray says she rarely gives out her personal number and limits where she gives out her Google Voice number, too. But even she has seen an uptick in political texts over the past couple of weeks. That’s likely in part because some groups may try to dial numbers in order in a certain area code, or her number could still be floating around on lists from long ago. “You can’t really do anything about the people or the businesses or the political entities that you have already shared your number with in the past,” Murray says. “But I would encourage people to just draw a line in the sand.”

Murray and Geoghegan encourage consumers to take the actions available to them to help limit the unwanted texts they receive, but they say the real solutions to the broader issue will likely come from Congress or regulators. Geoghegan says greater enforcement of existing laws could limit robocalls and texts, and Murray says concerned voters could contact their representatives about putting more pressure on the FCC to address the problems.

“Don’t get just frustrated with what you can’t change in four days, but you may be able to make a difference for the future,” Murray says. “By all means, reply to a text and say, ‘Stop.’ … But just don’t make it your life’s quest because it’s probably a fool’s errand.”

title: Amazon’s latest Echo smart displays and speakers reinforce Google Home’s lost lead
snippet: Amazon just launched a new lineup of Echo smart speakers and a new smart display, all while Google Home’s lineup remains pretty quiet. more…
fullText:
Amazon just launched a new lineup of Echo smart speakers and a new smart display, all while Google Home’s lineup remains pretty quiet.

Amazon has five new devices launching – two smart displays, a “Photo Frame,” and two speakers.

Starting with the speakers, the latest Echo Dot has “a built-in smart home hub” and upgraded audio and starts shipping today for $100. Meanwhile, Echo Studio builds on that foundation with even-better audio and, optionally, a built-in camera. Those start at $220.

Echo Dot at Amazon (shipping now)

Echo Studio at Amazon (shipping now)

On the smart display side, there’s the Echo Time, which is like an Echo Dot but with a small circular display built-in. Amazon touts “hundreds of clock faces” and “Omnisense” which can track your sleep just like Google’s second-gen Nest Hub, and it starts at $200. 

	

Echo Show 16, meanwhile, is a big 16-inch smart display meant to live on your wall with support for smart home controls, the ability to show a family calendar, and full Fire TV built-in as well. It starts at $500 and, like everything else mentioned so far, is built around Amazon’s AI-enhanced Alexa.

Echo Time at Amazon (shipping now)

Echo Show 16 at Amazon (pre-order for $100 off, shipping December 16)

Rounding out the lineup is the Alexa Photo Frame, a simpler smart display that has Alexa built-in but focuses on showing photos from your Amazon Photos library. It has a 10-inch anti-glare display and a design that looks like a normal photo frame and starts at $200.

Alexa Photo Frame at Amazon (shipping now)

9to5Google’s Take

Google Home really is just so wildly behind isn’t it.

In looking at Amazon’s lineup, I can’t help but feel like Google is just wasting potential here. A smart speaker that doubles as a Nest Cam would be awesome. The same goes for a giant Nest Hub that doubles as a Google TV. 

	

And, seriously, how does Google not sell (or at least partner with someone) a Google Photos digital photo frame. Google Photos is a wildly successful platform and that would sell like hotcakes. Big “how am I not in that movie” energy.

I’ve said it before, but Google Home had such a lead in the smart speaker and smart display market, especially with Google’s ecosystem tie-ins, but Amazon is currently running laps around it with products that Google should be selling. Throw in that even Apple has a smart display now where Google hasn’t even teased a new Nest Hub, and it just feels all kinds of bad to be in Google’s camp right now.

What do you think?

title: Chrome 156 for Googlebook rolling out with 14 updates across sites, shortcuts, more
snippet: Google is rolling out Chrome 156 for Googlebooks with a slew of improvements and bug fixes. This follows the last browser update two weeks ago. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out Chrome 156 for Googlebooks with a slew of improvements and bug fixes. This follows the last browser update two weeks ago.

In terms of “New Features,” there’s “Hover Tooltips in the AI Mode Menu: Items in the address bar’s AI Mode menu now show tooltips on mouse hover.”

The remaining 13 updates today are classified as “Improvements.” On the keyboard shortcuts front:

Alt+Tab: Alt+Tab now switches windows on Fullscreen sites and apps when keyboard lock is on, as it does on ChromeOS, Mac and Windows. Users no longer need to hold Esc to exit before switching tabs.

Alt+Shift+Enter Shortcut: Alt+Shift+Enter now opens the typed query in a new background tab and keeps you on the current page.

Up/Down Arrows in Multi-Line Address Bar Text: Up/Down arrows now move the cursor between lines for easier editing when typed text wraps to multiple lines. Suggestions are hidden.

Specific website improvements include:

	

Google Docs: Enabled copying of large selections and tables in Google Docs. 

Facebook Live Video: Performance improvement of Facebook Live streams.

Stability fixes: Stability improvements were made across 1Password and other extensions, third party apps, and Chrome tab functionality.

Site Icons: Site and Google icons appear correctly when clicking into the address bar from a webpage or search results page. Stale site icons are removed when the URL bar is cleared.

There are some meaningful usability fixes:

Close Third-Party Sign-In Prompts: The close (X) button will close third-party sign-in prompts correctly. 

File Downloads: Added “Save As” dialog support to choose download save locations, and fixed a naming issue with duplicate file downloads so they open correctly in apps.

Right-Click on Incognito New Tab Page: Context menu now opens when right-clicking links on the Incognito new tab page.

Finally, the AI Mode updates continue with:

AI Mode Animation Timing: The AI Mode animation waits for the expansion to complete before playing and plays more consistently.

“Add to your search”: The menu for adding tabs and files to an AI Mode search now has an “Add to your search” header.

“View your AI Mode history”: The address bar now correctly displays “Ask anything” hint text and blinking cursor.

We’re seeing Chrome 156 for Googlebook OS widely rolling out via the Play Store today. It comes a week after the stable release started on desktop and mobile (not fully available for Android phones and tablets yet).

title: iOS 27.2 has two CarPlay improvements, here’s what’s new
snippet: iOS 27.2 arrived this week with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 arrived this week with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users.

#1: Apple Podcasts adds sections for New Episodes and Continue Playing

Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’

Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.

Like you would expect, ‘New Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.

This overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your shows and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a big fan of the change.

#2: Siri AI upgrades

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

Per Apple’s release notes:

Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week

Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List

It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

Bonus: Apple Music’s new app icon and design tweaks

	

It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app.

These changes are related to the total rebrand Apple Music unveiled just last week.

title: The Galaxy Ring got a new update just in time for a $75-off sale
snippet: It’s a 0.68MB Galaxy Ring update and a $75 sale. What’s not to like? more…
fullText:
It’s a 0.68MB Galaxy Ring update and a $75 sale. What’s not to like?

Every few months, Samsung delivers a small update to its smallest fitness-tracking product. October 2026 marks the latest tiny Galaxy Ring update, which landed as version Q50XWWU2AZIA for South Korean customers this week (via SamMobile).

Samsung Galaxy Ring on sale at Amazon

As is, unfortunately, the case with most of these tiny updates (and there have been several at this size), no one really knows what’s included since Samsung doesn’t elaborate on the changelog. As you can see from the translated version below, the entirety of the changes seem to be for “stability.” Almost certainly, this just means bug fixes, which is fine by me.

Galaxy Ring updates have been sparse since its release two years ago. In our review, we said it was “in the ring, but not the champ,” and that’s largely been okay since Samsung doesn’t charge a monthly fee for health data. By comparison, the popular Oura ring line will cost you $6.99 per month, which would equate to about $170 over a two-year period.

	

Amazon is also running a $75-off sale on the Samsung Galaxy Ring right now, making it $324.99. By comparison, the latest Oura Ring is $499 and still requires a subscription. The next big Galaxy Ring update will be to add sleep apnea detection, a major feature that will give it a unique win over the competition. We’re expecting the Galaxy Ring 2 to appear sometime early next year, almost certainly with a much higher price tag.

If you’re okay with a used ring, Amazon has several styles and sizes available from as low as $200, which includes free returns if there’s something wrong when you receive it. These rings are quite durable, with titanium construction and week-long battery life, plus a nifty included charging case that works similarly to earbuds.

title: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite
snippet: iOS 27.2 launched this week with many new features for iPhone users, including a Messages addition that was previously announced for iOS 27 but later got pushed back: Suggestions. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 launched this week with many new features for iPhone users, including a Messages addition that was previously announced for iOS 27 but later got pushed back: Suggestions.

Messages ‘Suggestions’ return in iOS 27.2 after being pulled from iOS 27 beta

Throughout the iOS 27 beta this summer, one of my favorite AI features was a Messages addition that didn’t feel like AI at all: Suggestions.

Here’s what they do, per Apple:

Messages offers one-tap suggestions based on the context of users’ conversations, making it easier than ever to get things done, such as creating a reminder or a note. For example, if someone asks for photos, Messages can also help users find the right ones, recognizing keywords, locations, and people in their library to find the best options.

Suggestions appear as small, convenient action buttons beneath messages they’re relevant to.

As seen in the image below, if someone asks you to do something, you might see a suggestion to add to Reminders or Notes. Or if an event is mentioned, suggestions lets you easily add it to your calendar.

Suggestions worked well for me in the iOS 27 beta, but shortly before the public launch last month, Apple delayed the feature into a “future software update.”

Now in iOS 27.2, suggestions have officially returned, launching for all users. And one way they’ve changed might explain why they were pulled in the first place.

As I mentioned, suggestions performed as expected for me during the summer. But if I had one complaint, it was that they sometimes appeared when a message’s context didn’t merit them. At times I saw suggestions to add things to Notes, Reminders, or Calendar when there wasn’t a clear justification for these recommendations.

But in iOS 27.2, I’ve seen far fewer suggestions appearing in my Messages conversations. When I see them, it’s always obvious why they’re being offered. Clearly the feature benefited from a little extra fine tuning.

If you want even more control over the types of Suggestions that appear, you can manually configure categories under Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions.

title: Motorola Signature 27 specs detailed in new video, including Tandem OLED display
snippet: Ahead of its launch next week, a new video offers a closer look at the Motorola Signature 27 as well as confirming some key specs. more…
fullText:
Ahead of its launch next week, a new video offers a closer look at the Motorola Signature 27 as well as confirming some key specs.

A video hands-on from Danny Winget on YouTube offers a closer look at Motorola’s upcoming flagship, and only makes its arrival all the more enticing. 

There are several key specs mentioned in the video, with the most interesting being the “Extreme AMOLED Duo” display which makes use of Tandem OLED technology. Tandem OLED isn’t a new idea, with the tech stacking multiple layers of diodes on top of each other to improve contrast and brightness. Tandem OLED can be found on Apple’s new “PROLED” MacBook Pro, as well as 2024’s Honor Magic 6 RSR. But Motorola’s use of it in the Signature 27 is certainly nice to see, especially given the other spec shared. 12,000 nits of brightness. That rather insane figure is apparently the peak brightness on this new flagship.

Hardware shots of the phone also show the textured backs on the two color variants as well as the curved glass around the display.

	

Other specs shared in the video include:

6.8-inch Extreme AMOLED Duo display, 120Hz, LTPO, Tandem OLED, 12,000 nits max brightness

Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

16GB RAM

Up to 1TB UFS 4.1 storage

Android 17 with 7 years of OS updates

Cameras: 50MP Lytia 910 main, 200MP periscope telephoto, 50MP ultrawide, “dedicated action sensor” for motion capture improvements

The battery capacity isn’t revealed, but Winget says that it is “sizable.” Similarly, the vapor chamber is described as “40% larger” but a point of comparison wasn’t given. 

It’s all shaping up for a powerful flagship in every sense of the word. Motorola has confirmed that Signature 27 will launch on November 5, and I don’t know about you, but I’m only getting more excited about it.

title: RAMageddon is ready to rage on through 2030
snippet: SK Hynix, one of the major companies behind memory production, says that it’s sold out through 2029, leaving RAMageddon ready to rage on for at least the next three years. more…
fullText:
SK Hynix, one of the major companies behind memory production, says that it’s sold out through 2029, leaving RAMageddon ready to rage on for at least the next three years.

On its latest earnings call today, SK Hynix confirmed that production of both DRAM and HBM (high-bandwidth memory) are effectively sold out not just for this year, not just for next year, but through 2029. That puts RAMageddon, the global shortage of memory, lasting at least another three years before we see any relief.

SK Hynix’s CFO explains (via The Motley Fool, Seeking Alpha):

…memory supply cannot keep pace with this level of demand growth, thus, we expect it to be difficult to fully meet customers’ volume requirements in the near term, given the complexities involved in implementing leading-edge processes and the lead times required to construct new production facilities. A situation where supply cannot keep up with demand is expected to persist for some time, a constraint projected to continue through 2030.

Micron, one of the other companies responsible for memory production, previously said to expect 2027 to be “even tighter” compared to 2026. 

	

The SK Hynix call also details how the company is making long-term agreements which already account for “more than 50% of our total capacity for 2027 and 2028.”

SK Hynix isn’t the biggest name in DRAM/HBM production, with Samsung accounting for a larger share, but everyone else is dealing with the same constraints. PCMag points out that SK Hynix is working to build out more production capacity, as everyone else is too, but it takes time to build out the complex infrastructure.

Buckle up folks, this isn’t ending anytime soon. 🫠

title: HomeKit Weekly: SwitchBot’s K11+ Pro packs strong suction and Apple Home support into a tiny robo vacuum
snippet: The robot vacuums designed for large open floor plans often have big batteries but take up a ton of space. The SwitchBot K11+ Pro goes the other direction: a tiny vacuum, a small dock, and Matter support so it works with Apple Home. more…
fullText:
The robot vacuums designed for large open floor plans often have big batteries but take up a ton of space. The SwitchBot K11+ Pro goes the other direction: a tiny vacuum, a small dock, and Matter support so it works with Apple Home.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The SwitchBot K11+ Pro is 9.76 inches across and 3.62 inches tall, and weighs about 5 pounds. That size is the whole point. It can work its way between chair legs, get closer to corners and walls, and slide under beds, couches, and cabinets that larger robots bump into and give up on. If you have a couch that sits lower to the ground, you know what this means

Navigation for the SwitchBot K11+ Pro is done by LiDAR for mapping and route planning, plus a close-range sensor for spotting furniture legs and following wall edges. It stores up to five maps, so you can carry it upstairs and it’ll know where it is, too. Inside the SwitchBot app, you get room and zone cleaning, schedules, no-go zones, and virtual walls. I use the SwitchBot app almost daily and really like it a lot. It’s super easy to use and navigate.

A dock that isn’t as big as a trash can

To me, the small dock is more critical than a small vacuum. Self-emptying docks are great until you realize most of them are the size of a small trash can. The Switch K11+ Pro’s station is around 9.4 by 7.1 inches. It also has a wood-patterned lid, so it looks less like an appliance sitting in your living room or laundry room. Inside the dock is a disposable dust bag that should last up to 3 months, depending on usage.

SwitchBot rates the K11+ Pro at up to 12,000Pa of suction, which is double the original K11+. I’ve got the original K11+, and while it’s great, it’s better suited to a bedroom than to a main living area. One thing to keep in mind: that’s a peak number from Max mode. Day-to-day, the Quiet, Standard, and Strong modes run much lower, and the robot automatically bumps up to Max when it hits carpet. On the other end of the power spectrum, Quiet Mode runs at about 45dB, which makes it a lot more realistic to run while you’re working from home or after the kids are in bed. My wife prefers quiet mode at all times, where I want more power at all times. With my other SwitchBot vacuums, the difference between Max and Quiet mode is that the latter can run while watching TV, whereas the former cannot.

For pet owners, it uses an all-rubber main brush and a two-arm side brush, both designed to keep hair from wrapping around them. If you’ve ever had to sit on the floor with scissors cutting dog or cat hair out of a roller, you’ll appreciate this feature.

How it works with Apple Home

The K11+ Pro supports Matter over Wi-Fi, so it pairs directly with Apple Home, and you can start a cleaning with Siri. SwitchBot lists Apple Home support for section cleaning, so you’re not stuck with an all-or-nothing on/off switch. Once it’s in Apple Home, it’s also available to your automations. Start cleaning when everyone leaves the house, and finish it before anyone gets back, etc. One thing to keep in mind is that the mapping and advanced functionality are managed in the SwitchBot app. So you’ll need to do a lot of your initial setup in it, but then you can rely on Apple Home day-to-day.

Wrap up

Big robots are built for big houses, but smaller homes will fit perfectly with it. The K11+ Pro is small enough to reach under the furniture, the dock is small enough to hide, and Matter means it works well with Apple Home. We have a larger unit in the main part of my house, but I am considering swapping to this one simply for its smaller footprint and manageable power. If you vacuum while no one is at home, you won’t mind that it has to recharge and empty itself a few times.

The SwitchBot K11+ Pro is available now in Black and White on Amazon and SwitchBot’s website.

And you’re in control of what goes on the screen. Choose the shortcuts you want for each app, arrange them the way you like, and Super Mouse automatically brings up the right ones as you switch between apps […]

Double-tap, and Super Mouse becomes a multi-touch trackpad. Switch to trackpad mode and use familiar finger gestures to scroll, swipe, and zoom.

title: Major Even Realities G2 smart glasses update adds Conversate ‘Pro Mode,’ Knowledge Base
snippet: Even Realities today announced that a new software version will be rolling out to the G2 smart glasses, complete with a personal knowledge base that, thankfully, only remembers what you tell it. more…
fullText:
Even Realities today announced that a new software version will be rolling out to the G2 smart glasses, complete with a personal knowledge base that, thankfully, only remembers what you tell it.

When the G2 smart glasses launched, Even Realities packed them with features aimed at professionals, as well as tech geeks who appreciate retro mixing with the modern. But features like Conversate can be valuable to anyone in the right situation.

Even Realities says Conversate is getting an overhauled “Pro Mode” that pulls data from something it’s calling Knowledge Base – a feature that remembers the information and data you select. These feature refreshes are included in the Even Realities G2 version 2.4.0 update, which also upgrades the company’s AI interface to Even AI 2.0.

In order, it works like this:

	

Files and audio recorded in Conversate mode on the Even Realities G2 glasses, along with any manually uploaded files, sync to a secure Google Cloud Platform server in the EU.

Knowledge Base updates your information to disseminate.

Even AI 2.0 and active Conversate sessions pull context from the Knowledge Base.

Even Realities allows users to select up to 10 Conversate records to upload to that context tree during the initial setup. More can be added as they’re recorded. It also seems that new Conversate sessions need to be selected for upload and won’t be added to that database automatically, unless the user toggles automated uploads on.

Whatever data is there, Conversate Pro Mode will surface during relevant sessions. For instance, if you’re a sports journalist and have a backlog of recorded meetings in Conversate, new instances will provide context based on what you already know. It’s a more trustworthy approach than letting an AI model surface information it thinks is relevant. Even AI won’t stop doing that, but the Knowledge Base might be a more palatable source for some.

The biggest part of this update comes down to Even AI 2.0. Even Realities says it’s a “major upgrade” to how users interact with the G2 glasses as a whole. In reality, it comes down to quality-of-life changes that should make the smart glasses easier to use.

The G2 glasses are now able to activate Even AI with the touch sensor. When you hold it down, the recording starts, but stops when you release. And instead of requiring a new wake word for a follow-up, users can enable multi-turn conversations. Opening Even Hubs apps and changing certain settings right from the AI chat are supported, too.

Even Realities says Knowledge Base and Conversate Pro Mode will both launch today in beta. Because it’s still an early feature, it will be limited for users based on a monthly usage allowance. There’s no mention of pricing after beta in Even Realities’ press release.

Oh, and there’s a new tortoiseshell color option.

snippet: iPadOS 27.2 arrived this week as the latest noteworthy iPad software update, here are two new features it includes. more…
fullText:
iPadOS 27.2 arrived this week as the latest noteworthy iPad software update, here are two new features it includes.

#1: Siri AI contextual popup and more improvements

Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri, and I’m using it all the time on my iPad—often with a CMD + Space keyboard shortcut since Siri and Spotlight are now integrated.

In iPadOS 27.2, Apple added another convenient way to interact with Siri that first debuted on the Mac in macOS Golden Gate.

When you select text in iPadOS 27.2 via a trackpad or mouse, there’s a new Siri contextual popup that appears to the left of your selection. If you hover over the Siri icon with your cursor, it instantly expands to offer an ‘Ask Siri’ text field.

This makes it quick and easy to ask Siri about whatever you’ve highlighted. And if you’re in the writing process, the Siri popup even has suggestions like ‘Proofread,’ ‘Rewrite,’ and ‘How does this sound?’ so you can get help with just a click.

Siri AI also includes several new upgrades that make it more capable. Per Apple’s release notes:

Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week

Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List

#2: Profiles in Apple TV app

iPads make great video devices whether you’re an adult or a kid. And if you share an iPad with a partner or child, the Apple TV app has a welcome new addition: user profiles.

iPadOS 27.2 brings over the same profiles feature that tvOS already offered on Apple TV 4K.

When you open the Apple TV app on iPad, you’ll see a new profile selection screen at startup. From here, you can choose who’s watching and the TV app will automatically update its queue, playback history, and content recommendations based on your selection.

If you’re a parent, profiles will take content restrictions into account. So when your child’s profile is active, they’ll only see films and TV shows that match the age settings you’ve previously set.

And if you don’t want to use profiles, it’s easy to disable them from showing on startup with a quick tap.
