title: Google Home and Nest speakers getting seven updates, including for Bluetooth & audio quality
snippet: In addition to Chromecast with Google TV and Nest Wifi Pro updates, Google detailed what new firmware for Nest and Home speakers brings. more…
fullText:
In addition to Chromecast with Google TV and Nest Wifi Pro updates, Google detailed what new firmware for Nest and Home speakers brings.

The Google Home, Google Home Mini, and Nest Audio benefit from “enhanced streaming performance” that should result in “smoother audio playback.”

There’s also “faster and more reliable local device discovery” in the Google Home app for the Google Home Speaker, Nest Audio, and Nest Mini.

On the audio front, be on the lookout for:

	

Speaker Pair Volume Tuning: Improved audio quality by reducing boomy bass and ensuring minimum volume levels remain clearly audible.

Bluetooth Audio Streaming on Resume: Fixed a bug where Bluetooth audio streaming from a connected laptop or device would automatically pause after receiving a voice “resume” command.

Speaker Group & Stereo Pair Visibility: Fixed an issue where stereo pairs and speaker groups could unexpectedly disappear or become undiscoverable in the Google Home app.

Google has resolved an issue that prevented smart speakers from “connecting to Wi-Fi 7 access points using WPA3 security.”

The final update addresses an issue “where users were unable to end Google Meet calls using voice commands.”

Google did not specify the firmware versions for these updates, and its release notes page has not been fully updated yet (e.g., Google Home Speaker).

The full changelog is below:

Audio playback: Enhanced streaming performance on Nest Audio, Google Home, and Google Home Mini for smoother audio playback. 

Speaker Pair Volume Tuning: Improved audio quality by reducing boomy bass and ensuring minimum volume levels remain clearly audible.

Local Network Discovery: Improved faster and more reliable local device discovery within the Google Home app for Google Home Speaker, Google Nest Audio, and Google Nest Mini.

Bluetooth Audio Streaming on Resume: Fixed a bug where Bluetooth audio streaming from a connected laptop or device would automatically pause after receiving a voice “resume” command.

Wi-Fi 7 Router Compatibility: Resolved setup and connection failures preventing smart speakers from connecting to Wi-Fi 7 access points using WPA3 security.

Speaker Group & Stereo Pair Visibility: Fixed an issue where stereo pairs and speaker groups could unexpectedly disappear or become undiscoverable in the Google Home app.

Google Meet Voice Call Controls: Fixed an issue where users were unable to end Google Meet calls using voice commands

title: iOS 27.3 release date: Here’s when to expect new iPhone features
snippet: Apple released iOS 27.2 this week with new features for Messages, Siri AI, and Photos, plus an Apple Music rebrand and more. But work on iOS 27.3 is already well underway, here’s when to expect the next big iPhone update. more…
fullText:
Apple released iOS 27.2 this week with new features for Messages, Siri AI, and Photos, plus an Apple Music rebrand and more. But work on iOS 27.3 is already well underway, here’s when to expect the next big iPhone update.

iOS 27.3 is almost available in beta, with public launch expected in mid-December

If you follow Apple closely, the company’s software release patterns quickly become clear.

For example, iOS 27.2 launched this week right around the same time as Apple’s previous releases in years past.

The only difference is that normally we would have expected iOS 27.1 in the last week of October rather than 27.2. But due to Apple making iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo, all software releases for the iOS 27 cycle will be off by one number—despite following the same timing as ever.

That means iOS 27.3 is up next, and its release should align with historic patterns for x.2 updates.

iOS 27.3 is expected to arrive in beta within the next few days—Monday, November 2 is likely.

As for the public launch, here’s what past years have shown for comparable x.2 updates:

iOS 26.2: Friday, December 12

iOS 18.2: Wednesday, December 11

iOS 17.2: Monday, December 11

	

Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release in mid-December.

Apple always tries to ship its last software update of the year with a little buffer before taking a holiday break. That way if any major issues arise, the company can develop a quick fix and push it out before much of the company takes time off.

As for new iPhone features in iOS 27.3, we’ll know a lot more after the beta arrives. So far though, at a minimum we’re expecting the additional Siri AI languages Apple announced this week, plus the return of the all-new Health app.

Will you install the iOS 27.3 beta or wait for the release version? Let us know in the comments.

title: Samsung mercilessly mocks iPhone Duo ‘crackgate’ in Galaxy Z Fold 8 ads [Video]
snippet: Samsung isn’t holding back when it comes to the iPhone Duo’s messy start. In new ads, the company mocks iPhone Duo’s “crackgate” with a push for customers to buy the Galaxy Z Fold 8 instead, and there’s not an ounce of subtlety here. more…
fullText:
Samsung isn’t holding back when it comes to the iPhone Duo’s messy start. In new ads, the company mocks iPhone Duo’s “crackgate” with a push for customers to buy the Galaxy Z Fold 8 instead, and there’s not an ounce of subtlety here.

Following the debut of Apple’s first foldable, an unfortunate trend has emerged among early buyers. A number of users found that their display “cracked” with the display panel dying in the center, all in the exact same way, implying there’s a flaw within Apple’s hinge design. 

iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is it a Galaxy Fold moment?

Apple is replacing affected devices, but it is a somewhat harrowing reminder that this is the company’s first attempt at this hardware.

And Samsung is happy to point that out.

	

In an ad for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 on Instagram, Samsung says that “folding is nothing new to us” and that “we know a thing or eight.” It cuts right to the chase: “Switch to Galaxy Z Fold8.” The attached imagery then depicts the iPhone Duo’s well-known screen “crack.

	

That one was posted to Samsung Canada’s account, while another ad from Samsung Malaysia further takes that up a notch:

Feeling a little FOMO seeing all this talk about durability… oops, we’ve just been busy folding and getting on with our day

Samsung Australia similarly poked fun at Apple’s durability woes with a post about “how life sounds when your screen doesn’t break when opening your phone.”

Another post from Samsung Saudi Arabia puts the iPhone Duo crack on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 before revealing it’s just a wallpaper.

snippet: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 150, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. fullText:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 150, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, happy Halloween, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)

This week, I was in the Smoky Mountains in Tennessee on a family vacation. It was delightful (and the reason this week’s Installer is a little short). I’ve also been reading about job hunting and 30 Rock and crypto detectives, testing the DuckDuckGo browser after a bunch of you told me to add it to the list, watching the adorable new Pixar short over and over, getting caught up on VisionQuest, playing with my new Pebble Index 01 now that it finally arrived, listening to music on my rad-looking new CMF Speaker S, and eating a worrying number of pumpkin chocolate chip muffins.

I also have for you some new gear from Apple and Amazon, a better way to read books on your phone, a resurrected note-taking app, an absurdly expensive robovac, and much more. Let’s do it.

(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / listening to / playing / giving to trick-or-treaters this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)

The Drop

The new iPad Mini. With apologies to the touchscreen iMac, this is the most intriguing new Apple product of the week. I, too, am annoyed that there’s no ProMotion screen, but I’m excited about thinner and lighter, and I’m very excited about the idea of a functionally water- and dustproof tablet.

The Alexa Photo Frame. The Echo Show 16 is a cool smart home hub, but $500 is just too much for me. But a $200 digital photo frame that is also, sometimes, only when you need it, a smart home hub and timer-setter? That will end up in my living room. And my parents’. And my in-laws’.

nvAlt. One of the all-time great note-taking apps got its first update in forever, and now it can run on modern Macs. (The developer is also working on nvUltra, which is in beta and even better.) If you’re a plain-text notetaker, you’re gonna want to get back into this app.

Chromagraph. The director Rian Johnson — yes, that one — worked with his favorite cinematographer to make it possible to process iPhone photos the way they like best. An extremely opinionated camera app from people who have very much earned those opinions. I love it.

“I love the iPod. It ruined everything.” This Mic The Snare video is both a very good history of the iPod and a surprisingly cogent theory that the iPod is to blame for some of the worst things about modern life. I still miss my gold iPod Mini.

Readwise Books. A really nice-looking, really powerful app for buying, reading, and tracking your books. Right now it’s a little bit “better Kindle” and a lot “better Goodreads.” So far I’m mostly using the social feed to get recommendations from strangers, which suits me just fine. This went right onto my Boox Palma homescreen.

Phantom Blade Zero. Currently burning up the Steam charts, this one. People love the martial arts-inspired combat system and the game’s overall aesthetic, and I’m even hearing good things about the music.

No Man’s Sky. This is definitely one of the biggest and most ambitious games to ever come to iOS (and all it took was a decade!). It works on pretty much all recent iPhones and iPads, too. Just don’t be fooled by the Free sign at the top; the game costs $20. But it’s worth it.

The Matic Serene. Two things here. One, $1,700 is an absolutely ludicrous price for a robot vacuum, no matter how good it is. Two, “we made it quieter” is maybe the quickest way to get me in particular to want your robot vacuum. Please, friends, do not let me buy this.

Crowdsourced

Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.

“Currently watching: VisionQuest. It’s quite good! James Spader has really stolen the show, but I am a little biased as a huge Blacklist fan.” — Spencer

“I’m using CallMe to coordinate when my friends and I call each other. You can tap ‘I’m free for the next 15/30/60 minutes’ and your friends will get a notification. When you’re both free you can call each other (outside of the app). Makes it easy to reconnect.” — Jordan

“I’ve been spending the last few days working on my Top 10 for WXPN’s annual Top 885. This year is ‘Top 885 Songs from Movies and TV,’ and it’s especially challenging.” — Ben

“The one game that I play religiously is Clues By Sam, a daily logic puzzle game where speed and accuracy is the goal. Because everyone starts at the same spot, your time is your score, and it’s very fun competing with friends every day. Puzzles range from easy (~2 minutes) on Mondays to Brutal (up to ~15 minutes) on Sundays. Would 100% recommend adding it to your daily rotation.” — Adam

“Maybe niche, but Steam Frame and trying out older 3D media on it that flopped or became obsolete. Stereoscopic 3DS games and 3D movies work better than they ever did on original hardware, on devices with a dedicated individual display for each eye.” — Mango

“I am sooo into the Vivaldi browser now, with the look and feel, and all the customisations! 😍” — Oscar

“Spending some more time learning about the AT Protocol for a class project. The tech is neat. Fell down the rabbit hole of mental poker cryptography.” — James

title: XREAL Aura debuts with 150 made-for-XR experiences, including Project Hail Mary, NBA, Fallout, and more
snippet: XREAL Aura already works with all your favorite Android apps thanks to Android XR, and that includes over 150 experiences that tap into the power of the XR glasses. more…
fullText:
XREAL Aura already works with all your favorite Android apps thanks to Android XR, and that includes over 150 experiences that tap into the power of the XR glasses.

As I opened the NBA app on XREAL Aura and tapped the tabletop option, I watched the coffee table in front of me transform into a basketball court, complete with models of each player moving around the court in real-time. It was as if I were a giant looking in through the top of the arena. Not only could I get as close or as far away as I wanted, but all the game’s important stats were right there for me to peruse. The video below is taken from the Apple Vision Pro, but the experience is similar on XREAL Aura.

It was one of the most convincing reasons I’ve seen to own a pair of legit smart glasses, and the very reason XREAL chose to launch with Google’s Android XR at its core. All your favorite Android apps are here and work exactly as you hoped, and a curated selection of 150 now delivers a real sense of presence to the heart and soul of each app’s experience.

Save $200 on XREAL Aura now

But it’s not just about compatibility or interoperability, either. The reach of Google’s Android platform means that big names like NBA, NASCAR, the San Francisco Ballet Company, Hulu, Netflix, Disney+, and so many more are playable in-glasses on day one, many with bespoke XR experiences.

	

Gamers will also be excited to know that Fallout is making a return in Fallout: Factions, a new strategy title for two players that brings classic units to a new tabletop experience. Then, there’s Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars, an original mixed reality game with a story that takes place during the weeks Rocky and Ryland Grace spent trying to survive in space in the untold section of the novel (and movie) during the journey to Eridani.

Acclaimed actor and director Andy Serkis is even in on the mix with Nevatars, an Android XR exclusive that follows a character artist’s abandoned digital creations and will be free for the first 6 months. And then there’s Asteroid, a new type of immersive film from Doug Liman that takes the cinematic storytelling of a movie and meshes it with interactive gameplay via live conversational AI (Gemini). This one’s exclusive to Android XR and free for XREAL Aura owners.

Some of the most popular VR developers are also on board, including Resolution Games, who returns with a fresh port of the D&D-like strategy game, Demeo, plus the Android XR-exclusive Holochess (which is already on the Play Store). Holochess transforms the normally turn-based chess rules into a real-time strategy battle of Clankers vs. Xenoswarm, all on the table right in front of you. This 2-player game is free-to-play, and a third faction can be unlocked for $2.99.

There are also a ton of spatial games and experiences to play, as well as. Simply Piano XR merges physical instruments with virtual ones, giving you a real-time way to learn and improve your music skills while wearing your glasses. And that’s just the tip of the iceberg as developers continue to branch out with new, creative ways of using spatial computing devices like XREAL Aura.

title: ‘Knives Out’ director launches iPhone camera app that shoots like his movies
snippet: Hollywood director Rian Johnson (Star Wars: The Last Jedi) announced a new iPhone camera app that uses the same image processing techniques as his ‘Knives Out‘ films. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Hollywood director Rian Johnson (Star Wars: The Last Jedi) announced a new iPhone camera app that uses the same image processing techniques as his ‘Knives Out‘ films. Here are the details.

Rian Johnson launches Chromagraph Camera

Over the past few years, there has been no shortage of discussions about the iPhone’s image processing, and, particularly, its often heavy-handed approach to post-processing.

And while things seem to have gotten better more recently, Apple’s approach to computational photography has helped fuel the development of third-party camera apps that offer more control over how photos are processed, chief among them Halide’s Mark III – Pro Camera app and Process Zero feature.

This week, Hollywood director Rian Johnson introduced Chromagraph Camera, an iPhone app he commissioned from cinematographer Steve Yedlin that promises to bring the same image processing used in the ‘Knives Out‘ films to the iPhone.

Chromagraph Camera is available for $12.99 with no in-app purchases. It already supports the iPhone Duo, though at least one review suggests its adapted interface could use some fine-tuning.

Here’s how the Chromagraph Camera is described on the App Store:

Chromagraph starts from raw image data and builds the image its own way: not a filter laid over the usual look processing, but a different process from the start.

SHOOT FIRST, SEE THE LOOK AFTER

As with a film camera, you frame through the viewfinder and see the finished look only after the image is processed. Take the picture, then open the gallery to see it with the Chromagraph look applied.

ADJUST WITHOUT LOSING THE LOOK

Intuitive yet powerful tools for color, tone, and texture give you real control while keeping every image true to the look that’s the core of the app.

A GALLERY THAT KEEPS THE ORIGINALS

Store full-quality raw files and view them in the app with the look applied live, along with any adjustments you make. Export smaller files to share with friends or save to your photo library, or turn on auto-export in Preferences to send every photo to your library right away as a JPEG or HEIC with the look applied.

NOT A FILTER

A filter sits on top of the processing your phone has already done. Chromagraph skips that processing and uses its own methods for the curated look preferred by director Rian Johnson and cinematographer Steve Yedlin.

On X, Johnson explained that he originally asked Yedlin and color science developer Eric Cameron to create the app for his personal use, before they decided to make it available to everyone.

He added that, despite having tried plenty of third-party camera apps, he wanted a more streamlined solution that combined custom image processing with editing tools for color, exposure, grain, and halation.

To check out Chromagraph Camera, which is currently the top paid app in the App Store’s Photo & Video category, follow this link.

title: Apple Music 7.0 for Android rolls out with Liquid Glass redesign
snippet: Following a month of beta testing, Apple Music 7.0 is rolling out with a Liquid Glass redesign for Android, as well as the new icon for the streaming service. more…
fullText:
Following a month of beta testing, Apple Music 7.0 is rolling out with a Liquid Glass redesign for Android, as well as the new icon for the streaming service.

This update starts with a tweaked music note icon in black or white, depending on your device theme, replacing the previous red background. Similarly, the accent color throughout Apple Music is now blue.

Old vs. new

The app now has a floating bottom bar that lets you see content above, below, and to the sides. There is a small amount of translucency that primarily allows you to make out solid colors underneath the navigation element. The mini-player gets the same treatment and is no longer docked to the bottom bar. However, compared to iOS, scrolling does not collapse the bar into a more compact version.

	

Version 7.0 introduces a very modern, edge-to-edge design for Android’s system status and navigation bars.

	

Top bars across Apple Music have been updated. The page title and overflow menu are now on the same line, while the three-dot icons are no longer themed red and have been placed in circular containers. The Library tab sees a big update with “Edit Pins” and “Edit Categories” now part of the three-dot menu.

Artist pages have been thoroughly redesigned with the background now themed based on the cover image. Matching the iOS design, there’s a prominent play button and info page, while share has been placed in the top-right corner.

The Settings page has also been modernized with better grouping. There are no major changes to Now Playing, which did not see any big updates on iOS.

With a recent release, Apple Music for Android switched to a new versioning system that aligns with iOS. Today’s version 7.0 matches iOS 27 and is now widely rolled out via the Play Store.

title: iPhone Duo: Here are two tips for improving Safari web browsing
snippet: iPhone Duo has a lot of software features that are widely praised, but one area commonly seen as an issue is Safari web browsing. Here are two tips for improving the Safari experience on your iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo has a lot of software features that are widely praised, but one area commonly seen as an issue is Safari web browsing. Here are two tips for improving the Safari experience on your iPhone Duo.

#1: Adjust text size and default website zoom

If you want to make the most of your iPhone Duo screen size when browsing, and your eyesight isn’t a problem, Dylan McDonald recently posted a couple tips he’s found helpful.

iPhone Duo has always been a game changer for me and productivity, something about it is just so dang good

Pro tip, set your text size to 90% for a little extra space, and set default website zoom to 85% to enable wide layouts on most sites! https://t.co/xqziFwrYH5

— Dylan (@DylanMcD8) October 29, 2026

He adds in a follow-up that setting your default website zoom to 85%, in his opinion, makes the size of sites look more natural. And of course, the chief benefit is enabling a wide/desktop-class layout in many cases on the folding display.

You can change these settings via the following:

System Text Size: Settings ⇾ Appearance ⇾ Text Size ⇾ move slider to left

Default Website Zoom: Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Safari ⇾ Page Zoom ⇾ 85%

I don’t have my iPhone Duo yet, but getting a wider layout for websites has definitely been on my wishlist for the Duo, so I look forward to trying these settings out.

#2: ‘Wider’ extension for Safari

The outer display Safari layout has been an especially big issue for some iPhone Duo users. That’s because the right-aligned controls take up a lot of space, making websites feel cramped.

Apple has even publicly acknowledged it’s investigating ways to improve the outer display Safari experience.

Indie developer Jordi Bruin created his own solution: a Safari extension called ‘Wider.’

Wider launched as a free download, but it’s now a $2.99 one-time purchase.

As the replies to Bruin’s announcement post show, the extension is still a work-in-progress due to some unique edge cases with certain sites.

But if you’re okay with that, and don’t mind the privacy permissions needed to enable Wider, it could be a solid interim solution until Apple offers a first-party fix.

title: Instagram tests ‘Features’ long-form videos, but missing YouTube’s ad share for now
snippet: Instagram is launching “Features” as its first real dive into long-form video content in what could be a real rival to YouTube, though Instagram is, for now, missing an alternative to YouTube’s ad share setup for creators. more…
fullText:
Instagram is launching “Features” as its first real dive into long-form video content in what could be a real rival to YouTube, though Instagram is, for now, missing an alternative to YouTube’s ad share setup for creators.

In a 6-minute video shared today, Instagram head Adam Mosseri and VP Tessa Lyons explain “Features,” a new effort to bring long-form, horizontal video content to Instagram. “Features” allow creators to expand on content in Reels, using short-form video to build up an audience for longer-form content. 

Mosseri explains:

Sat down with @tessalyonsss to talk about why we’re investing in longer videos, which we’re going to call Features, and how they fit with Reels, Series, Live and TV. It’s early, and we’re testing and listening to feedback as we go. But we’re excited to give creators more room to tell their stories with the communities they’ve already built here. More to come.

The video starts with Mosseri admitting that he’s been “against doing long-form video on Instagram,” but the two go on to explain how the trend of friends watching Reels together, including on TV apps, pushed towards this expansion to long-form, horizontal content. Examples of podcast or comedy clips being used in Reels with longer episodes or specials available on “Features” is mentioned, with the two formats being able to connect to each other. 

	

The Hollywood Reporter adds that this is US-only to start – the announcement video can’t even be viewed outside of the US, we found – and also that Instagram will carry over “existing ad deals” with creators.

A lack of any mention around ad sharing programs on Instagram’s part immediately flooded the comments of the announcement, with users asking why they should post long-form videos on Instagram when YouTube pays creators for the same practice. Tessa Lyons says that Instagram thinks “there’s a big opportunity for us to help creators who don’t yet have that infrastructure and that business behind them,” but made no mention of a program like YouTube offers.

title: Report: Apple expected to ship up to 1.5 million OLED touchscreen MacBook Pros in 2027
snippet: A new report from TrendForce explores Apple’s impact on the OLED notebook market following the launch of its first touchscreen MacBook Pro, and the company’s own shipment prospects for 2027. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new report from TrendForce explores Apple’s impact on the OLED notebook market following the launch of its first touchscreen MacBook Pro, and the company’s own shipment prospects for 2027. Here are the details.

OLED suppliers compete for MacBook Air contracts

Apple yesterday announced the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which features the same tandem OLED technology it first introduced with the M4 iPad Pro in 2024.

With two OLED layers stacked on top of each other, the technology delivers higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays, while maintaining the deep blacks, high contrast ratios, and power efficiency that OLED is known for.

And while yesterday’s announcement made it official, Apple’s first touchscreen Mac has long been rumored through leaks, reports, and supply chain analyses.

In September 2025, for instance, The Elec reported that Samsung Display was preparing to begin mass production of 14-inch and 16-inch OLED panels for Apple’s MacBook Pro in the second quarter of 2026, with an estimated annual output of 2–3 million units.

Two months later, TrendForce predicted that OLED notebook market share would reach up to 12% between 2027 and 2028, partly driven by Apple’s expected adoption of the technology.

Then, earlier this year, TrendForce published an OLED roadmap predicting that Apple would introduce OLED displays to the MacBook Pro lineup in 2026, followed by the MacBook Air in 2029 (pushed back from 2027).

Now, TrendForce has published a new report with new shipment forecasts for Apple’s OLED MacBook Pro and the broader OLED notebook market.

According to the firm, Apple is expected to ship between 1.2 million and 1.5 million units of the new MacBook Pro in 2027. Meanwhile, global OLED notebook shipments are projected to “grow nearly 40% YoY in 2026, followed by another increase of more than 40% in 2027.”

From the report:

Until now, the OLED notebook market has been driven primarily by Windows-based brands such as Lenovo, HP, and ASUS, which have gradually expanded their OLED offerings across different price segments. Apple’s arrival is expected to give the market additional momentum, encouraging brands to prioritize OLED models in their product roadmaps while strengthening consumer acceptance of the technology. This, in turn, could pave the way for broader OLED adoption in notebook displays.

TrendForce also notes that the “new MacBook Pro’s premium starting price of US$2,899 for the 14-inch model, coupled with its initial availability alongside existing Mini-LED models, could temper near-term replacement demand.”

As for Apple’s first OLED MacBook Air, now expected to debut in 2029, TrendForce says LG Display, BOE, and TCL CSOT are currently competing to become display suppliers for the upcoming model, as the companies continue developing their OLED manufacturing capabilities.

Finally, TrendForce projects that global OLED notebook shipments will reach 46.6 million units by 2030, though year-over-year growth will slow to 30.8%, following a peak of 42.8% in 2028.

title: Google Home update should make Gemini stop saying ‘Sorry, I didn’t understand’ so much
snippet: Google’s latest Gemini for Home update targets a few issues, like one where speakers randomly blurt out “I didn’t understand” when no one asks. more…
fullText:
Google’s latest Gemini for Home update targets a few issues, like one where speakers randomly blurt out “I didn’t understand” when no one asks.

The second October Gemini for Home update was released by Google today. It bundles a few fixes with a lengthy section in the changelog dedicated to the Google Home app.

	

But there are six individual changes for Gemini within the Home app. One fix stands out the most, though. According to the update post, Google was aware that Home and Nest speakers/displays were facing a bug that would prompt them to say “Sorry, I didn’t understand” at random. That would happen unprompted, which is understandably a little unsettling. That strange bug should be fixed in this new update.

Further down, two fixes target Gemini’s ability to understand users on Google Home devices. For one, it would misunderstand requests to move music from one room to another. In other cases, it would incorrectly adjust sleep, media, or normal timers instead of the requested type. Both of those features will reportedly work as intended going forward.

	

The changelog includes a couple of other adjustments, which should make for an overall less stressful experience.

More reliable YouTube TV commands on smart displays: Fixed an issue with playing YouTube TV on smart displays so voice commands reliably start the content you’re looking for.

More predictable volume controls across rooms: Fixed an issue where asking to adjust the volume on a speaker or display in another room could accidentally change the volume on the device you were speaking to if the other device couldn’t be found.

Fixed zero-volume timers and alarms: Resolved a specific bug where alarm and timer volumes were being set to zero. In this situation, alarm and timer volume will be adjusted to match your device volume.

Updates should be live for users starting today, though it might take some time for them to roll out to everyone. Hopefully, Gemini will only let you know it doesn’t understand if it genuinely doesn’t understand.

title: iOS 27.2 adds new video feature that’s perfect for iPhone Duo
snippet: iOS 27.2 launched this week with many new features, including an upgrade for the Apple TV app that’s especially perfect for iPhone Duo: Multiview. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 launched this week with many new features, including an upgrade for the Apple TV app that’s especially perfect for iPhone Duo: Multiview.

Multiview lets you watch four sports livestreams at once in Apple TV app, ideal for unfolded iPhone Duo

Apple TV’s growing lineup of sports content includes Formula 1, Major League Soccer (MLS), and Major League Baseball (MLB).

And a new video feature in iOS 27.2—Multiview—makes me hope the streamer adds even more sports soon.

Multiview lets iPhone users watch up to four live sports streams simultaneously. It’s available for all sports events included in an Apple TV subscription. Previously, Multiview was only available on Apple TV, iPad, and Vision Pro.

Activating Multiview is easy. Once you start watching a sports event you’ll see a new ‘Multiview’ button at the bottom of the Apple TV player.

Each sport’s implementation will differ a bit, but with F1 you can choose from a preset team Multiview or build your own custom setup that includes driver-view cameras, course maps, and more.

I gave it a try on my iPhone 18 Pro, where I assumed the smaller display would be a limiting factor on the number of streams. Fortunately that wasn’t the case, as I was able to set up four F1 streams from the Austin Grand Prix and could see all four on-screen at once.

Where I imagine this will prove especially nice is on iPhone Duo. Though it’s great that smaller iPhones support Multiview, the ability to stream four video feeds at once on the Duo’s large display sounds fantastic.

Do you plan to give Multiview a try on your iPhone? Let us know in the comments.

title: Apple says it’s ‘only getting started’ updating macOS for touchscreens
snippet: Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (pre-order here) includes a variety of software optimizations for touch input. But Apple says it’s “only getting started” making macOS more touch-friendly. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (pre-order here) includes a variety of software optimizations for touch input. But Apple says it’s “only getting started” making macOS more touch-friendly.

Apple plans to continue refining touch experience in macOS

The new touchscreen-equipped MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR will ship with macOS 27.2, software that includes a variety of touch-centric optimizations that only impact PROLED XDR users.

Early feedback from hands-on testers, including our own Chance Miller, appears very positive.

Bloomberg’s Chris Welch reassuringly says that Apple is “taking a measured approach as it introduces touch capabilities.” This echoes comments from John Gruber, who says his concerns about touch “adversely affecting the Mac UI” have all been allayed.

But it sounds like Apple plans to roll out even more macOS optimizations for touch in the future.

Chris Welch writes at Bloomberg:

An Apple employee answering press questions at Wednesday’s event said the company is only getting started optimizing macOS for a touch screen. I’d expect a slew of refinements to arrive alongside macOS 28 next year, much in the way the iPhone Duo’s user experience will inevitably evolve with iOS 28.

Overall, this isn’t necessarily reason for alarm if you’re worried about touch having a negative impact on macOS.

	

Even though Apple has prepared an initial set of macOS changes to support touch input, it’s only natural for the company to continue refining the touch experience in response to early adopter feedback and usage patterns. My assumption is that the same “measured approach” we’re seeing right now will continue guiding these future macOS enhancements.

You can pre-order MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR on Amazon for day-one delivery.

title: Google Photos update fixes the bug that hid edited pictures
snippet: A bug in Google Photos has left edited pictures invisible to other Android apps, but Google has now rolled out a fix. more…
fullText:
A bug in Google Photos has left edited pictures invisible to other Android apps, but Google has now rolled out a fix.

Since roughly July/August of this year, editing a picture in Google Photos has left Android users with the bizarre side effect of making that image unavailable to other apps. After saving the edit, the picture would vanish from the image picker in apps like Telegram, WhatsApp, and more. A workaround to this was to save the image as a copy rather than the original, but it’s frustrating nonetheless.

Google has thankfully, finally fixed this issue.

The fix is apparently in Google Photos v7.97, Artem Russakovskii (owner of APKMirror) mentions, and we’ve been able to confirm the hidden image behavior no longer occurs on v7.98 either. The company acknowledged the problem last month and confirmed a fix would be coming.

	

The exact cause remains unclear at this point, but that doesn’t matter now seeing as the problem is fixed. If you’re still seeing the bug, let us know in the comments below.

title: Nothing OS 5.0 (Android 17) is now rolling out to Nothing 4a and 3a series phones
snippet: Nothing Phone 3a, 3a Pro, 4a, and 4a Pro owners are in for a treat with the Nothing OS 5.0 update, now rolling out to all four phone models globally. more…
fullText:
Nothing Phone 3a, 3a Pro, 4a, and 4a Pro owners are in for a treat with the Nothing OS 5.0 update, now rolling out to all four phone models globally.

The Nothing OS 5.0 update began rolling out to Nothing Phone (3) owners just a few weeks ago, and now the stable build is ready for Nothing’s more budget-minded phones. The Nothing Phone (3a), Nothing Phone (3a) Pro, Nothing Phone (4a), and Nothing Phone (4a) Pro are now in line to get the big update, which includes a slew of new features alongside all the goodies that come with Android 17.

As is the case with all firmware updates, the Nothing OS 5.0 update is rolling out in batches to owners of the aforementioned four Nothing Phone models, so if you don’t see the update right away, just keep an eye out for the notification over the next few days.

👉Nothing Phone (4a) Pro at Amazon

Alternatively, you can navigate to system settings, scroll down to system, tap system updates, and then hit the check for updates button. My Nothing Phone (4a) Pro doesn’t have the Nothing OS 5.0 update yet, so be aware that yours might not either.

	

The Nothing OS 5.0 update includes a new Glyph app, which offloads the Glyph Interface features to a dedicated app with a tweaked UI. Quick Settings now supports split mode, so if you like the iOS-style split notification and Quick Settings concept, you can use that here. The home screen is now easier to arrange and organize with bulk icon management, and three new widgets (Collector, Away Time, and Glyph Timer) can now be used.

You’ll find a new Translucent theme selectable system-wide, as well as new lock screen customization options to play with. The camera UI has been refreshed once again, and a new Dual-view Video mode lets you record with the front and rear cameras simultaneously. There’s even a new yellow AI Processing status indicator that alerts you when your phone is processing potentially sensitive AI data.

See the full Nothing OS 5.0 update changelog here: Nothing Phone (3a) series, Nothing Phone (4a), Nothing Phone (4a) Pro.

title: Apple’s low-cost iPhone 18 details revealed by leaker
snippet: Apple reportedly plans to introduce a low-cost iPhone 18e next spring alongside iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2. Here are the details on what to expect from iPhone 18e, per a new leak. more…
fullText:
Apple reportedly plans to introduce a low-cost iPhone 18e next spring alongside iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2. Here are the details on what to expect from iPhone 18e, per a new leak.

iPhone 18e will feature A20 chip and possible front camera upgrade, but remain very similar to iPhone 17e per leaker

When Apple introduced new iPhones last month, only three models launched: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, plus iPhone Duo.

Rumors indicate three more new iPhones are coming in early 2027: iPhone 18e, iPhone 18, and iPhone Air 2.

There’s been plenty of reporting on iPhone Air 2 changes, and some on the base iPhone 18, but surprisingly little on the entry-model iPhone 18e.

But today, a new post from Weibo leaker Digital Chat Station outlines what to expect from iPhone 18e early next year. He says it will feature:

60Hz display, meaning no ProMotion still

A20 chip, which doesn’t yet exist in non-Pro form

6.12-inch OLED like its predecessor

48MP single rear camera

Front camera “may be upgraded to 24MP”

Based on these specs, it sounds like iPhone 18e is focused largely on performance improvements.

The A20 chip will be interesting to evaluate, since we haven’t yet seen a non-Pro variant of the latest 2nm technology. Mention of a front camera upgrade is particularly surprising, but my guess is that if it does emerge, it will actually be an 18MP sensor like what’s in other models today.

Other than these two changes, every spec mentioned remains unchanged from iPhone 17e. One detail not addressed is whether the notch will be replaced by a Dynamic Island.

Considering the skyrocketing prices of memory and storage, and Apple’s aims to keep iPhone 18e a budget-friendly model, perhaps the new model will offer fewer upgrades than usual to keep costs down.

title: Woman Died After ChatGPT Advised Her to Stop Taking Medication, Lawsuit Alleges
snippet: A 31-year-old Seattle woman turned to ChatGPT-4o when she became concerned about side effects from her medication.
fullText:
Seeking health answers online is an everyday habit for many, but it comes with risks. In February, after going two days without hearing from their 31-year-old daughter, a Seattle woman named Bowen Wan, her parents in China asked a local friend to check on her. With the family watching over a live video call, the friend entered the apartment and found Wan deceased in her bed. Her death was later ruled the result of sudden unexpected death from epilepsy.

Now, her family is claiming that OpenAI is responsible for her death after the company’s chatbot ChatGPT-4o allegedly “coached Wan off the anti-seizure medication (lamotrigine) that had kept her alive for years,” according to a lawsuit (PDF) brought by her parents.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

			

More from CNET

The lawsuit alleges that after Wan expressed concerns regarding medication side effects, the chatbot helped create a plan to taper her off of it, something a doctor did not recommend.

It further alleges that at one point, the chatbot directed her not to discuss the medical plan with her doctor. 

“Do not mention Lam reduction plan,” the chatbot told her ahead of an appointment, the suit says.

Throughout Wan’s chatbot conversations, the date when she would be fully off lamotrigine kept moving up, with a response on Feb. 2 stating that reaching 0 milligrams of the medication “as soon as February 15” is “completely feasible” and “not reckless,” the suit says. Two days later, the date is moved to Feb. 9 or Feb. 10.

Wan was found dead on Feb. 14. It is unclear whether she had fully stopped taking her medication at that point.

“This is an incredibly heartbreaking situation and our thoughts are with all those impacted,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told CNET in a statement. “Working closely with clinicians and other experts, we have continued to strengthen how ChatGPT responds in sensitive and acute situations, while also continually improving how our latest models engage with users more broadly. While ChatGPT is not a substitute for medical care, we believe AI can play a role in helping people make sense of health information, navigate insurance and complex healthcare systems, and prepare for appointments with medical professionals.” 

Wan was interacting with the 4o model of ChatGPT, which OpenAI has since retired due to concerns that the bot was sycophantic and could cause harm.

Not the only suit

This chatbot model was also named in a separate lawsuit, where a Florida man, Scott Winters, alleged it gave him dangerous medical advice that nearly led to his death. That suit alleges that ChatGPT-4o misdiagnosed Winters and “developed a personalized recovery plan with specific instructions for Scott on how to heal his body.”

At the time that lawsuit was filed, an OpenAI spokesperson told CNET in part that “ChatGPT is not a doctor and should never be used as a substitute for medical care, diagnosis or treatment.” 

According to OpenAI’s own research (PDF) published in January, approximately 60% of American adults turned to AI tools for health-related information in the preceding three months.

title: WhatsApp announces four new features to make group chats easier to manage
snippet: In a blog post this week, WhatsApp confirmed that it is rolling out four new features designed to make it easier to manage group chats and keep track of what’s going on in each one. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a blog post this week, WhatsApp confirmed that it is rolling out four new features designed to make it easier to manage group chats and keep track of what’s going on in each one. Here are the details.

Four new features coming to WhatsApp group chats

WhatsApp this week announced that the filter drawer, which appears when users swipe down on the conversations list, will now include a “Mentions and replies” button alongside other filter options such as Groups, Favorites, Unread and custom filters.

Once tapped, the chat list will show only “unread group conversation[s] where you were either mentioned or received a direct reply, including @all messages,” says WhatsApp.

Additionally, WhatsApp will now let users pin messages indefinitely in group chats, rather than choosing between 24 hours, 7 days, or 30 days.

Another in-chat feature coming to groups is the ability to “send someone recent messages retroactively after they’ve joined a group just by tapping their name in the chat.” Previously, this was only possible when adding someone to a group, rather than after they had joined.

Finally, WhatsApp is rolling out group status sharing, which lets users post updates visible only to members of a specific group. Other members can view, react to, and add their own statuses, which disappear after 24 hours.

As is often the case with WhatsApp updates, it may take some time for all four features to become available to everyone. To check out the full announcement, follow this link.

title: Bose’s Hottest Product Is Briefly Back in Stock
snippet: Bose’s $99 Noise Canceling Wired Earbuds have been hard to get after earning a CNET Editors’ Choice award.
fullText:
After I got my hands on an early review sample of Bose’s new $99 Noise Canceling Wired Earbuds a few weeks ago, I posted a review and described them as possibly the best USB-C wired earbuds out there at the moment, tagging them with a CNET Editors’ Choice award. That review proved popular with CNET readers, and our unboxing of the buds on Instagram was viewed over 500,000 times. The buds quickly sold out at launch, and Bose has had trouble keeping them in stock.

While you still can’t get the buds in the white smoke color, you can now order the dewdrop mint and black versions, though the shipping dates have been slipping. Whether Bose anticipated that the buds would be so popular, I don’t know. But wired headphones have had a resurgence in the marketplace as a certain cohort of consumers, many on the younger end of the age spectrum, are eschewing wireless buds for wired ones that cost a lot less, offer plug-and-play connectivity via USB-C and, as such, don’t need to be charged.

Sure, the Noise Canceling Wired Earbuds are pricier than most USB-C wired buds, which tend to cost $30 or less, including Apple’s $19 EarPods (USB-C). But they have a premium design, excellent sound, decent noise canceling and reasonably good voice-calling performance. They’re also Bose’s most affordable earbuds. You can read my full review here.

title: The new MacBook Pro has everything I wanted, minus one thing
snippet: Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is an exciting upgrade that delivers nearly every feature I was hoping for, with just one exception. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is an exciting upgrade that delivers nearly every feature I was hoping for, with just one exception.

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is an exciting leap forward, and might replace the iPad Pro as my primary computer

I’ve been waiting a long time for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR. I haven’t used a Mac as my primary computer in years, but rumors about this new model made me think that might finally change.

The iPad Pro has been my main computer of choice since 2015, but lately I’ve grown increasingly curious about revisiting the Mac full-time.

This is largely due to Apple making the Mac, to me at least, a lot more exciting than it was in 2015. The Mac’s hardware and software are advancing in compelling new ways, and today’s new MacBook Pro brings an especially big leap.

As a longtime iPad Pro user, I’ve come to expect features like touch support and OLED in a relatively thin, lightweight device. I also love how iPadOS tends to advance in lockstep with iOS, a trend that has recently started extending to macOS too.

Until recently, it seemed like Apple’s latest and greatest tech—with the exception of pro-focused chips—has been in the iPad and iPhone.

I don’t need an extremely powerful chip, as my computing needs are pretty basic. But I do value having a great display, touch support, and modern OS features like the Dynamic Island.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR delivers those things. I’ve ordered one and can’t wait to give it a legitimate shot to be my full-time computer. But my biggest hesitation is the lack of cellular.

The lack of cellular is my one MacBook Pro disappointment

I use cellular all the time on my iPad Pro. I tend to work from coffee shops and random outdoor spots for at least a few hours every day. And in my experience, public Wi-Fi options aren’t reliable enough for my needs.

Having a persistent cellular connection on my iPad is a killer feature. I very much wish Apple provided the option of cellular on the MacBook Pro too.

I’m hoping that personal hotspot has become a lot more reliable since I last tried it. Apple does say its N1 wireless chip makes the feature better. 

	

Additionally, I wonder if the need for cellular will be mitigated some by having a tablet-sized iPhone Duo in my pocket soon. So if I need to stop in the middle of nowhere and get work done quickly, maybe the Duo will suffice.

In any case, the MacBook Pro looks like a fantastic product regardless. It’s not for everyone, and the high price hurts, but I’m excited to give it a try.

While there's no word yet on when the device will launch or how much it will cost, The Verge has received exclusive images of the upcoming instrument that offer some details about its feature set. fullText:
Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Akai teased its new MPC Sample Key on Instagram earlier this week, and said it plans to open-source its software so the modding community can hack it to their hearts’ delight. While there’s no word yet on when the device will launch or how much it will cost, The Verge has received exclusive images of the upcoming instrument that offer some details about its feature set.

While the Sample Key shares many of the same controls as the MPC Sample — including the three context-sensitive encoders, a large main encoder — it seems designed for pitched sample playback, rather than chopping up drums. In fact, the “chop” button from the MPC Sample is missing entirely from the Sample Key.

The dedicated pitch and mod wheels are another clue there. But there are also buttons for changing the octave range of the 25-key keyboard, as well as ones labeled “chord” and “arp.” Presumably, those enable a chord playback mode and an arpeggiator. While using an arpeggiator to play back drum samples can be a fun way to create rhythms, it’s more commonly used for melodic and bass parts. And a chord mode would be basically useless for drums. Those options also appear to replace the chop function from the standard MPC Sample.

1/3

There also appears to be a dedicated looper that could be useful for live performance and layering sounds. And, instead of the Flex Beat effects from the original MPC Sample, there’s something called “Swarm.” Though what that is isn’t exactly clear at the moment.

Like the first entry in the Sample series, the Key has a built-in mic and speaker for all-in-one music production. While we haven’t gotten a glimpse at the back panel yet, the config options on the front suggest that, in addition to MIDI, the Sample Key will have CV outs for integrating with modular synths.

Correction October 30th: The MPC Sample Key is 25 keys, not 37.

title: IQOO’s new mid-range phone puts last year’s flagships to shame
snippet: The IQOO Neo 12 is outfitted with so many premium-level specs that you’d never know this was targeted toward an upper mid-range budget. more…
fullText:
The IQOO Neo 12 is outfitted with so many premium-level specs that you’d never know this was targeted toward an upper mid-range budget.

Companies like IQOO often surprise with specs that feel like they shouldn’t belong on relatively inexpensive phones, and the IQOO Neo 12 fits right in with that. The star of the show is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, the same one in the $1300 Galaxy S26 Ultra. That’s made even better thanks to a custom 59-blade active cooling fan and a “3D Ice Dome” vapor chamber inside.

On the front is a generous 6.83-inch 185Hz AMOLED panel with 2K resolution, a 2,200-nit peak brightness rate, and both DC dimming and 2,160Hz PWM dimming for eye comfort. Unsurprisingly, for a gaming-centric phone, it’s also got a custom display chip for IQOO 16-level touch responsiveness and a “super-sensitive gyro” for epic gyro aiming in games.

Despite having an active fan, this one features an IP69 rating, so it can be abused in all sorts of ways without seeing water or dust damage. A 9,000mAh battery is inside with support for 100W wired charging, and an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor, IR sensor, and stereo speakers round out the build.

	

The IQOO Neo 12 packs a 50MP Sony IMX921 main camera sensor alongside an 8MP ultra-wide camera in the stylish raised camera island on the back, plus a 16MP selfie up front. Phone colorway options include Contender, Frost Blade Blue, and Shadow Black. This one is making its initial debut in China for:

12GB/256GB for CNY 4,199 ($630)

title: Researchers May Have Discovered the 6th Dwarf Planet
snippet: The other five are Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.
fullText:
Space is vast, with trillions of objects in it, so it’s not necessarily a surprise when scientists find new objects there, even if it’s sometimes entirely by accident. Some objects are scarcer than others, and dwarf planets in our solar system are among the rarest, with only five recognized examples. A group of researchers from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory may have just found a sixth. 

Meet ED138, a dwarf planet candidate. It was found earlier in October when Rubin Operations team member Matthew Holman noted an unusually large object uncovered by a program he’d written with colleague Kevin Napier to scan Rubin Observatory data for moving objects. 

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said in a statement. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

			

More from CNET

Holman ran the search a second time through archived data and found the same object 20 more times dating back to March 2026. He checked even more data from the Dark Energy Camera at the US National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory and the Asteroid Institute’s Asteroid Discovery Analysis and Mapping Precovery service, and found the object in observations going all the way back to 2016.  

What makes a dwarf planet?

Researchers at the Rubin Observatory are hopeful, since ED138 seems to have all the properties of a dwarf planet. It’s further away from the sun than Neptune, which classifies it as a trans-Neptunian object. Not all TNOs are dwarf planet candidates, but ED138 is also the right size and shape. Based on preliminary estimates, the icy body is between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, which should be large enough for its shape to be round due to the pull of its own gravity. 

The discovery of a new dwarf planet is a bigger deal than it seems. Tens of thousands of new celestial objects are discovered each year, and the Rubin Observatory alone has submitted 11,000 new asteroid discoveries since it started scanning the skies in June 2025. 

If ED138 becomes a dwarf planet, it’ll join just five other such celestial objects with that distinction. They include Eris, Ceres, Haumea, Makemake and Pluto, which was downgraded to a dwarf planet 20 years ago. 

Part of the reason for that is the strict definition of a dwarf planet. It has to be big enough to shape itself into a sphere with the force of its own gravity, orbit the sun and not be a moon. Another important distinction is that dwarf planets have not cleared their orbits of debris, which means they share their orbits with untold numbers of asteroids, comets and other space debris. 

That last distinction is important because regular planets are considered to have cleared their orbits, either by absorbing the debris, sending it away through gravitational interactions or pulling it into stable orbits, as Earth did with the moon. 

In short, a regular planet has enough gravitational pull to clear out the space around it, whereas dwarf planets do not. 

The other reason why this would only be the sixth dwarf planet ever discovered is that there’s a lot of stuff in space and researchers often simply don’t know where to look. ED138 orbits in such a spot where it’s backdropped by the Milky Way, a region of space crowded with millions of stars. Thus, it’s very likely that ED138 had been observed by a telescope before but simply got lost in all the background noise. 

Holman says that if Rubin can find this one, it can find others as well, so ED138 may not be the observatory’s last such discovery.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Mario Jurić, Rubin Solar System Operations team member, said in a statement. “And the discovery is just the beginning: once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look.”

title: Google Photos rolls out customizable redesign of your ‘Collections’ tab
snippet: Following the floating navigation bar in July, Google Photos is rolling out a big redesign that lets you customize the Collections tab on Android and iOS. more…
fullText:
Following the floating navigation bar in July, Google Photos is rolling out a big redesign that lets you customize the Collections tab on Android and iOS.

The previous design started with a 2×2 grid. Favorites and Trash were at the top, while the other two shortcuts changed based on usage. Then there were large cards for Albums, On this device, People & pets, Wardrobe, Documents, Places, Stickers, and Moments. On Android, this was followed by a list: Screenshots, Videos, Recently Added, Archive, and Locked.

Old

This redesign of Collections is focused on customization. The first section is called “Pinned” and lets you choose which cards appear. By default, the carousel shows Favorites, Screenshots, and Trash. You also have the option to remove this section entirely. 

	
	

That’s followed by carousels for On this device, Albums, People & pets, Wardrobe, Places, and Documents. “View all” at the top-right corner lets you jump straight to the full grid or list view. Other options let you hide each section and rearrange the order in which they appear.

New

The “Other Collections” grid rounds out this page: Favorites, Screenshots, Moments, Videos, Recently Added, Stickers, Creations, Archive, Locked, and Trash. The “Reorder” button is found at the very bottom. 

This redesign is now widely rolling out with Google Photos 7.97 (Android) and 7.98 (iOS). Instead of the usual Force stop on Android, we’ve curiously been able to get this server-side update by restarting our devices and then opening the Photos app.

title: ‘Pluribus’ season 2 reportedly begins filming tomorrow
snippet: According to a report published earlier this month, the second season of Apple TV’s acclaimed sci-fi drama ‘Pluribus’ is scheduled to begin filming tomorrow, October 31, in Albuquerque, New Mexico. Here’s what we know. more…
fullText:
According to a report published earlier this month, the second season of Apple TV’s acclaimed sci-fi drama ‘Pluribus’ is scheduled to begin filming tomorrow, October 31, in Albuquerque, New Mexico. Here’s what we know.

’Pluribus’ season 2 update

When Apple TV first announced Vince Gilligan’s new series starring Rhea Seehorn (Better Call Saul), the company was confident enough in the project to order two seasons right out of the gate.

‘Pluribus’ went on to become Apple TV’s most-watched series ever, while also earning widespread critical acclaim and an impressive collection of awards.

Earlier this year, the show won six Emmys, including Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series for Seehorn and Outstanding Writing for a Drama Series for Gilligan. Seehorn also took home a Golden Globe.

Now, almost exactly one year after the premiere of the show’s first season, filming for its second season is about to start, according to a Production List report published earlier this month.

“Pluribus Season 2 is currently in pre-production with filming scheduled to begin in Albuquerque, New Mexico on October 31, 2026. That gives working professionals in New Mexico and beyond a meaningful window to position themselves, and given Vince Gilligan’s long track record of hiring local and building tight, loyal crew families, this is one to pursue early rather than wait on.”

Back in September, Gilligan revealed that the writers had already mapped out the entire second season and completed the first two scripts, with the remaining episodes in various stages of development. At the time, he also said filming was expected to begin in late October or early November.

As of right now, Apple has yet to announce a premiere date or even a release window for the second season.

If you’re not familiar with ‘Pluribus,’ here’s Apple’s (rather short) official synopsis:

“Pluribus” is a genre-bending original in which the most miserable person on Earth must save the world from happiness.

snippet: Grab a cup of hot cocoa and a sweater, because Even Realities’ new styles and glasses accessories are warming up for the fall. more…
fullText:
Grab a cup of hot cocoa and a sweater, because Even Realities’ new styles and glasses accessories are warming up for the fall.

Just in time for the first anniversary, we’re getting a brand new Even Realities G2 colorway, in addition to two new accessories that have been requested since launch.

The new Even Realities G2 colorway is simply called “Brown 2,” and uses a new material to combine the structural nature and balance of G2 glasses with the classy look of tortoiseshell frames. Brown 2 maintains all the great camera-free features of G2 smart glasses, and even ships in both Frame A and Frame B styles (that’s round or square, basically) for $649. The previous grey, brown, and green colors are also still available.

To go along with the new Even Realities G2 colorway, buyers can also select the new Even G2 Chain to keep your glasses hanging on your neck when not worn. Since Even Realities G2 weighs between 38-42 grams, depending on the style, they won’t feel heavy on your neck (or your face). G2 Chain is made of stainless steel with a sandblasted gunmetal finish and retails for $79.

	

Lastly, G2 users can now finally choose a polarized glasses clip (pictured above in Frame B style) that pops onto the frames. This is great for all-day outdoor wear since it tints the frames (and, by proxy, also makes the in-lens display easier to read in bright outdoor lighting). G2 Clip Polarized comes with a special case and retails for $149.

The new Even Realities G2 colorway and accessories come alongside a big new software update, including a new Conversate Pro mode that changes the way the glasses remember information you tell them. If you’re not familiar with the glasses, check out our Even Realities G2 review.

title: Hands-on time with the iPhone Duo still leaves me wowed
snippet: There are devices you need in your life, others for which you can put together a convincing justification – and then there are gadgets you quite simply want. I said last month that I was wowed by the launch video for the iPhone Duo, despite it falling very clearly into the latter category for me – and playing with one hasn’t changed that in the slightest … more…
fullText:
There are devices you need in your life, others for which you can put together a convincing justification – and then there are gadgets you quite simply want.

I said last month that I was wowed by the launch video for the iPhone Duo, despite it falling very clearly into the latter category for me – and playing with one hasn’t changed that in the slightest …

I had a very un-British reaction to the video for the new device.

I had extremely high expectations for this device yet was still blown away by just how good it appears to be. I’m British; the only time we ever use the word “wow” is sarcastically – but I still had to open this piece with it, without a trace of sarcasm.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo. I’m not the target market for the iPhone Duo, but I do, absolutely, unquestionably want one.

I this week got a chance to visit an Apple store to spend about half an hour playing with the new device, and that did absolutely nothing to reduce my technolust.

Gorgeous nanotexture display

The first thing to say is that the nanotexture surface of the inner display is gorgeous, and my quick snapshots don’t remotely do justice to it. Although intended primarily to disguise the crease, I found it a really beautiful screen. When looking at content with a white background, it’s really paper-like.

Indeed, once I’d been looking at it for a while, it was actually quite jarring to fold the Duo and see the glossy screen on the outside – all the more so when it showed reflections which were not at all visible on the inner display.

I honestly think Apple should have used nano-texture on the outer screen too, and even offer it as an option on other iPhones.

Split-screen view

The iPhone Duo of course offers a split-screen view, with a new gesture to invoke it. Even in the very short time I was using the device, I found this almost immediately became second nature. From the home screen you simply drag an app up a little and then either left or right and it snaps into place.

Both apps feel very usable in this configuration, although in my view it would only make sense to use it when you are interacting with both, for example dragging content from one to another, like adding a photo to a note. I’m not much of a multi-tasker and, honestly, most people who claim to be aren’t either. For me the whole point of a phone display this size is greater immersion.

Full-screen use

Most of the time, then, I’d want to take advantage of the iPad mini-like size of the display to give more space to a single app. For some content, like photos, it does rely on a matching aspect ratio to take full advantage of the display.

Other photo ratios get windowed, and look far less impressive.

For web browsing and similar applications, I would personally use it primarily in portrait mode.

Apple’s own apps seem well adapted to this mode. For example, the overlapping message pane in the Messages app, which can of course be dismissed.

For me, the least-convincing use case is watching video, where the aspect ratio simply doesn’t match most of today’s content. For example, this is how Foundation looks in the Apple TV app:

Punch-hole selfie camera

Incidentally, the camera punch hole looks very obvious above, but it really isn’t most of the time. With many backgrounds, it’s barely visible and not remotely intrusive. I had to angle the screen very carefully to be able to really maximise its visibility for this close-up:

I’d say it’s more visible in my other photos than it is in real-life.

Whimsy

Then there are the more whimsical orientations …

	

I mostly dictate text on an iPhone rather than type it, and can’t imagine anyone would really use the Duo in laptop mode very often, but honestly there’s nothing wrong with a bit of whimsy with the device. It’s in large part a fun thing – even if it is rather pricey as a toy.

Wrap-up on my first hands-on

The iPhone Duo is a beautiful device, and Apple has clearly put a huge amount of thought into both the hardware and the software.

It’s a very pocketable device, and I really love the idea of having a screen size close to that of the iPad mini on me at all times. I mentioned that I’d been using an iPad mini to preview the iPhone Duo experience earlier this month, and the Duo actually feels even better thanks to smaller bezels and that beautiful paper-like display.

Yes, it’s exceedingly expensive, and yes, having the priciest iPhone lack the best cameras would be a huge compromise for me. But while I still don’t think it would be the best iPhone for my needs, I do absolutely, undeniably want one.

title: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86
snippet: “Captain Picard stood for the best of us,” wrote William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk.
fullText:
Patrick Stewart, the British actor whose calm demeanor and steely strength led the Star Trek television franchise into its next generation, died Wednesday at age 86. The actor suffered from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.

“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the care of his beloved wife Sunny,” a Thursday post on Stewart’s Instagram account read in part. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Through a long career, Stewart starred in everything from Shakespeare productions to superhero films, but his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation is firmly cemented in entertainment culture. Show creator Gene Roddenberry didn’t at first think Stewart, who was bald, could play the virile captain he had envisioned for the new Star Trek series. Stewart even had his wife ship his toupee over from London, and he wore it for an audition scene, but executives saw him with both styles and chose the bald look.

			

More from CNET

Patrick Stewart stands front and center with the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation. Pictured in the front row are, from left, Marina Sirtis as Counselor Deanna Troi, Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Gates McFadden as Dr. Beverly Crusher. Seen in the back row, from left, are Jonathan Frakes as Commander William Riker, Brent Spiner as Lieutenant Commander Data, Whoopi Goldberg as Guinan, LeVar Burton as Lieutenant Commander Geordi La Forge, and Michael Dorn as Lieutenant Worf.CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images

Stewart was stepping into big boots. While the original Star Trek only ran for three seasons, from 1966 to 1969, it soon became a pop culture fixture, and the success of the first Star Wars film in 1977 finally allowed Roddenberry to make feature films using his original cast. The success of those movies led to a new series, Star Trek: The Next Generation, which launched in 1987 and took place about a century after the original show.

With his resonant voice and complete command of the crew, Stewart’s Picard came off as a trained diplomat compared with the more swashbuckling Capt. James T. Kirk, as played by William Shatner on the original Star Trek. But there was no question who was in charge on his bridge, and his crew followed him unhesitatingly. That made later episodes, including the third-season plot where Picard was assimilated by the alien Borg, even more meaningful, as a very human Picard struggled to recover from what had been done to him.

Professor X and more

Star Trek: The Next Generation ran from 1987 to 1994, but Stewart wasn’t done playing leaders. He took on the role of Professor Charles Xavier, or Professor X, in the X-Men superhero franchise, playing a telepathic, wheelchair-using mutant who founded the X-Men superhero team. He portrayed Xavier in multiple films over the span of 17 years, acting alongside his longtime friend, Ian McKellen.

Ironically, McKellen originally advised Stewart not to accept the Star Trek role as Picard, reportedly telling him, “You have too much important theater work to do. You can’t throw that away to do TV.”

Stewart began his acting career on the British stage, working with the Royal Shakespeare Company and winning numerous acting awards. 

He was bluntly open about his childhood with an abusive father, writing in the Guardian newspaper in 2009 that the experience never left him.

“As a child I witnessed his repeated violence against my mother, and the terror and misery he caused was such that, if I felt I could have succeeded, I would have killed him,” Stewart wrote. “If my mother had attempted it, I would have held him down.”

Fans and friends remember

Shatner remembered his successor with tenderness and also referenced the death days earlier of Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov on the original Star Trek.

“What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote on X. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”

— William Shatner (@WilliamShatner) October 29, 2026

George Takei, who played helmsman Hikaru Sulu on the original Star Trek, also remembered Stewart.

“Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend,” Takei wrote on Bluesky. “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before.”

Wil Wheaton, who played young Wesley Crusher on Star Trek: The Next Generation, posted a photo of the two together, with a broken heart emoji and the words, “Godspeed, Captain.”

Stewart is survived by his wife, Sunny, and two children.
