iOS 27.2 and its corresponding updates for the HomePod lineup bring several key new features to Apple’s smart speakers. The most exciting update? The ability to finally use your HomePod as the default sound output for your Mac. This means that the 2nd-generation HomePod and HomePod mini 2 can now function as low-latency wireless speakers for your Mac!

Watch our hands-on video for an in-depth look at how the new wireless speaker functionality works, along with other new features like Sound Glow, Lock Controls, and home theater surround sound support. Be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more in-depth videos.

HomePod as speakers for Mac

It’s long been possible to use a HomePod as a wireless speaker for the Mac, but doing so came with at least one big caveat: wireless latency. While it’s generally fine for movie playback, the latency is immediately noticeable when playing anything in real time. For example, playing instruments in Logic Pro, audio and FaceTime calls, etc. For these particular applications, HomePods have, up until now, been less than ideal speakers for the Mac.

Video walkthrough

Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos

Apple has addressed this issue in the 27.2 update, significantly reducing latency when using a HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) as a wireless speaker for Mac desktops and laptops that support Wi-Fi 6E. This, unfortunately, excludes some early Apple Silicon machines, such as those powered by the M1 family of chips, but it’s good to see this feature made available.

HomePod 2nd Generation set as the Default System Output Device in System Profiler

For the HomePod mini 2, Apple included a different Wi-Fi/Bluetooth architecture based on PCIe and revised audio routing to prioritize low-latency applications. It’s also worth noting that Apple’s Wi-Fi 6E requirement applies to the Mac hardware itself and doesn’t imply that a user needs a 6E-enabled router.

HomePod 1 vs HomePod 2 latency test with Logic Pro

From that, we can gather that the update will allow the HomePod to work similarly to how it currently works with an Apple TV, when set as the default audio source. In other words, instead of relying on traditional AirPlay, it creates an ad hoc point-to-point connection between the Mac and the HomePod for minimal latency. This will make a HomePod a viable speaker-output destination for real-time audio applications.

Notice that the Play sound effects through setting now allows for AirPlay

Apple is so confident of the low-latency connection that it defaults to playing sound effects via AirPlay when a compatible HomePod is selected as the output destination. Obviously, sound effects are the sort of thing that relies on low latency, since their sound has to correspond to what is happening in the environment at that exact time; otherwise, it would be disorienting. If I select my HomePod mini (1st generation), that option is not even available.

The Play sound effects through setting doesn’t allow for AirPlay on older HomePod hardware

Needless to say, this update instantly has me reconsidering my speaker needs for my Mac desktop setup. I recently got rid of my Yamaha HS3s because I’m looking for something with a little more umph. A pair of full-sized 2nd-generation HomePods in a stereo pair would definitely fit the bill, and look much better to boot.

Lock Controls

Have you ever accidentally brushed the touch sensor on the top cap of the HomePod, activating it to play music? Do you have pets who surreptitiously activate your HomePod while you’re not in the room? If so, then the new Lock Controls switch in 27.2 will help.

When Lock Controls is enabled, the touch surface on top of the HomePod is locked, meaning touch, touch-and-hold, and volume adjustments are disabled. You’ll easily recognize when Lock Controls is enabled by the bright red “no” animation that appears.

Even the first-gen HomePod gets some love

Lock Controls will prevent a HomePod from playing audio or taking action when the device’s top cap is touched. However, intercom, alarms, timers, Check in, and FaceTime calls will continue to respond to touch.

Of all the new features in the 27.2 software update, Lock Controls is the only one that appears on all HomePod models, regardless of generation. That means that, yes, even the original OG HomePod lands support for the handy new addition!

Sound Glow

My favorite new feature in the 27.2 update is Sound Glow. This is the feature that displays ambient light that corresponds to the colors and rhythm of the album artwork for the music or podcasts being played.

Sound Glow takes full advantage of the LED Matrix displays beneath the HomePod top cap. The big HomePod features an array of 37 RGB LEDs, while the smaller HomePod mini features an array of 19 RGB LEDs. As a side note, the original HomePod features 19 LEDs across a smaller surface area than the updated version.

To enable Sound Glow, you must update your iOS device and your HomePod to 27.2. Once updated, open the Home app and venture into the settings for the HomePod you wish to adjust. There, you’ll find a Sound Glow switch you can enable. 

Apple notes that you’ll also be able to toggle Sound Glow with your voice, but it will require an Apple Intelligence‑enabled iPhone running the latest software. This could be enabled once Apple enables Siri AI on the HomePod mini 2, and perhaps the 2nd-generation HomePod, but this remains to be seen.

Home theater surround sound

If you plan to purchase an Apple TV 4K (fourth-generation), you’re likely interested in the new home theater surround sound option available with the HomePod mini 2 or the 2nd-generation full-sized HomePod. This feature lets you use four HomePods, two identical matching stereo pairs in front and rear, for a surround sound setup.

I haven’t been able to personally test this yet, because I don’t yet have the newest Apple TV 4K, but I can bet it will sound fantastic, especially when four full-sized Dolby Atmos-enabled HomePods are involved. That being said, this is an expensive proposition.

Here are the pricing details for those looking to set up a four-speaker home theater surround sound option:

Apple TV 4K ($299) + Four HomePod 2 ($349×4) = $1695

Apple TV 4K ($299) + Two HomePod 2 ($349×2) + two HomePod mini 2 ($149×2) = $1295

Apple TV 4K ($299) + Four HomePod mini 2 ($149×4) = $895

By way of comparison, Sonos’ Dolby Atmos-enabled four-speaker Immersive Set with Beam Ultra bundle can be had for less than $1600 and comes with a dedicated subwoofer. I’m not a home audio expert or an audiophile, so I can’t say which one is better, but it’s interesting that both it and the highest-tier HomePod surround setup are so similar in price.

When managing your HomePod speakers via the tvOS interface on the Apple TV 4K, you’ll see new options for Surround Sound and Whole Room Audio under the Home Theater section. The surround sound option is self-explanatory and ideal for movies and television shows, but the Whole Room Audio option is better suited to listening to music, as it provides left- and right-channel placement no matter which direction you face.

9to5Mac’s Take

iOS 27.2 provides noteworthy updates to all HomePod models, including the original HomePod, which now includes the new Lock Controls capability. But the real fun starts with the HomePod mini, with its Sound Glow support, and the HomePod mini 2 and HomePod 2nd-generation, with their support for working as the default speaker for Wi-Fi 6E-enabled Mac hardware. I think a pair of HomePod mini 2’s would look great sitting next to Apple’s just-released M6 iMac.

What do you think? Are you planning to get any of Apple’s new Home-focused hardware, or are you looking to take advantage of the new 27.2 features on hardware you already own? Sound off in the comments with your thoughts on the matter.

title: Apple VP talks new iPad mini: OLED without ProMotion, Acoustic Display, more
snippet: Apple unveiled its “biggest update ever” for the iPad mini this week, introducing a thinner, lighter design and an OLED display. In a pair of interviews, Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering, discussed the new iPad mini’s design, display, and more. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled its “biggest update ever” for the iPad mini this week, introducing a thinner, lighter design and an OLED display.

In a pair of interviews, Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering, discussed the new iPad mini’s design, display, and more.

While the new iPad mini features an OLED display, it doesn’t support ProMotion. Instead, it’s limited to a 60Hz refresh rate. Here’s what Pakula had to say about that decision in an interview with Chris Lawley:

Display experience is about more than just a single spec. One of the things that’s really cool about OLED is it actually has this really fast pixel response time. So it’s more than an order of magnitude faster than the pixel response time for an LCD display.

What that does is it makes everything really smooth. Motion blur is significantly reduced compared to LCD. When you pair that with the other things, the contrast, the brightness, and the color, this is just a killer display.

In addition to being lighter and thinner, the new iPad mini is also IP67-rated for water and dust resistance, a first for an iPad. One key enabler is a new Acoustic Display. Pakula explains how that technology works:

One of the cool things we realized as we started experimenting was that the unique size and form factor of this display actually had a resonant frequency that’s in the audible range.

I think more importantly, it’s in the range of like a traditional woofer that you’d have in a speaker. What we did was we built these custom drivers that actually energize the display and emit sound directly through the enclosure, but that only really works for the mid and low frequencies.

For the higher frequencies, we actually designed these little custom tweeters. There’s one on each end of the product, and they’re actually ported out through these hidden ports between the glass and the aluminum. The result is we have this product that’s water and dust resistant. I think the sound that comes from it is so surprising for a form factor of this size.

Pakula also sat down with Katarina Mogus for an interview, where he discussed how the iPad mini fits into a world where iPhone Duo also exists:

What we love about the iPad mini is it’s really the full iPad experience in the palm of your hand. That gives you access to a million+ apps in the App Store. It’s got incredibly powerful creative accessories like the Apple Pencil Pro. And it’s got the advanced multitasking of iPadOS 27. 

It is really incredibly universal. And honestly, with all these updates, all of those experiences just got so much better.

You can watch both interviews below. The new iPad mini is available to pre-order now, with the first orders arriving on November 6.

title: Jean-Luc in Blue Jeans: Picard Cosplay Taught Me How Much Patrick Stewart Is Loved
snippet: My husband was assimilated at an Emerald City Comic Con, and even the Borg adored him. Thank you, Patrick Stewart.
fullText:
Star Trek fans never doubted the amount of love the community had for Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday at age 86. But I experienced that love firsthand. Back in 2021, my husband, Rob, dressed as Captain Jean-Luc Picard for Emerald City Comic Con in Seattle, and the adoration he received, simply for cosplaying Stewart’s beloved character, was overwhelming.

Our planning wasn’t complicated. Looking for a costume that would go with his shaved head and being a big fan of the show, it made sense for him to put on a red and black Star Trek uniform shirt, pin on a combadge and four pips to denote the Starfleet rank of captain, and step into some black shoes. Except for his glasses (and mask since this was 2021, the second year of the COVID-19 pandemic), it was an eerily accurate look.

Read more: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86

			

More from CNET

Once we walked into the Seattle Convention Center for the con, it was as if the real Patrick Stewart had shown up. The respect Stewart had built up for Picard transferred seamlessly to his lookalike. Just walking around with Rob made me feel like a celebrity escort. We couldn’t travel more than a few feet without someone noticing and calling out to him, always with glee, always with respect.

“Hey, Captain! Captain!”

“Jean-Luc!”

“Make it so, sir!”

“Engage!”

“Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!”

Rob didn’t even wear costume-authentic black pants. In a hurry to get out the door and not expecting this level of attention, he had just pulled on his jeans. That led to a few of the funnier comments.

“Hey Captain! Was it casual day on the bridge?”

Comic Con attendees go all out. There were eerily realistic characters from Star Wars, Pokemon creatures, groups of friends dressed as The Incredibles, at least five Spider-Men, the Doctor from Doctor Who and exquisite, elaborate characters from anime. Many, many people had put more time, money and sweat equity into their costumes than we did, but few received such a universally awed reception.

Read more: Remember Patrick Stewart by Streaming Star Trek, X-Men and Other Genre-Defining Roles

Other Star Trek characters were also portrayed, for sure. Two separate Will Rikers, Picard’s trusted “Number One,” raced up to us at different times to take photos with their captain. One woman cosplaying as Kathryn Janeway, captain of the USS Voyager from Star Trek: Voyager, also posed with Rob for a two-captain photo.

And then, they saw us. A group of Comic Con attendees dressed as the Borg, the villainous cyborgs who take Picard hostage to assimilate him and temporarily turn him into Locutus of Borg. 

These Borg did not throw their costumes together last-minute. They could have walked off a Hollywood set. They had working lights on their outfits, ocular and cranial “implants,” corpse-like face makeup, arms built into cybernetic tools. Of the Borgs, three were towering men and one was a woman. The woman played the Borg Queen, her bald head covered in white makeup, elegant and terrifying.

The minute the Borg saw Rob’s Picard in the convention center crowd, they came after him. Resistance, as they say in the show, was futile.

Thankfully, they were a jollier sort than the television Borg, and after one joke about his casual-day jeans, they whisked him away to stroll around as a group and snap photos. 

These Borg were so realistic that I felt a bit unnerved the entire time he was gone — and relieved when they returned him unharmed, thanked us, waved and headed on their way. I’m sure there were other serendipitous meetups between cosplayers at the convention, but this one was amazing to see and even more so to be even a small part of.

Rob poses in front of a number of Star Trek posters, including Picard and his famed “Make it so!” command.Gael Fashingbauer Cooper

We’ve been to Emerald City Comic Con other times. Our daughter has cosplayed a variety of characters, and Rob once went as Dr. Stone, a science prodigy with green-tipped white hair (which required a wig). People in the know enjoyed that cosplay, too, and he was similarly asked to pose for photos.

But the sheer love we felt when he dressed as Captain Picard was like nothing I’ve ever felt. Since his death, I’ve seen Stewart called a generation’s space dad, and there’s truth in that. People at the convention were delighted to see their space dad, even if just a doppelganger. It buoyed us along on an unexpected high on that cold December day in 2021.

In the famous Star Trek: Next Generation episode Darmok, Picard is trapped on a planet with the Tamarian captain, Dathon. They can’t understand each other. The entire Tamarian language is constructed out of mythological and historical metaphors, none of which Picard knows

Slowly, Picard begins to comprehend. He figures out that one of the most frequent phrases, “Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!” references Darmok and Jalad, warriors who united on the island of Tanagra and eventually became friends, just like he and Dathon. 

But there’s another phrase I’ve been thinking of lately. “Kiazi’s children, their faces wet.” An online Tamarian dictionary translates it as “downplaying the severity of a perceived injury.” 

There’s no downplaying this loss. We’re all Kiazi’s children today, our faces wet.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Gael Cooper
						

						

											

								

											CNET editor Gael Fashingbauer Cooper, a journalist and pop-culture junkie, is co-author of "Whatever Happened to Pudding Pops? The Lost Toys, Tastes and Trends of the '70s and '80s," as well as "The Totally Sweet '90s." She's been a journalist since 1989, working at Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, Twin Cities Sidewalk, the Minneapolis Star Tribune, and NBC News Digital. She's Gen X in birthdate, word and deed. If Marathon candy bars ever come back, she'll be first in line.

title: Pile-ins, payouts, and pacing pressure: the investors behind the VCs open up
snippet: The money behind the money is thrilled, mostly.
fullText:
The limited partners who provide the capital to venture firms — the “money behind the money” — are feeling great right now. They’re in uncharted territory in many ways, but also potentially exceedingly lucrative territory.

Normally, LPs typically spread their bets across many firms to diversify their own portfolios. They write checks to emerging managers and established ones, to generalist firms and specialists. The goal is a strong return, but also to minimize risk.

That’s the typical playbook. But typical is out the window. OpenAI and Anthropic’s valuations have shot up so quickly that nearly everyone has piled into the same two companies on the way up, often inside the same venture firm, despite the longstanding venture convention of avoiding investments that conflict with one another. No one is complaining, either. The LPs I speak with seem unbothered by this big gamble, given the potential returns; they’re expecting a bonanza.

But they do see danger ahead, even if they describe this as a “yellow light” situation, and they’re uneasy about how quickly VCs are coming back to raise new funds.

I talked about all of it recently with Beezer Clarkson of LGT Capital Partners, a Zurich-based diversified asset manager, and Amit Bhatti of TrueBridge, a Chapel Hill firm that focuses solely on venture. This conversation has been edited for length.

These are strange days — exciting but also scary. How are you feeling about your roles right now, and your place in this startup ecosystem?

Beezer Clarkson: It’s very busy, but I wouldn’t say it’s scary. There’s a lot of change and a lot of variables at play. I love venture, so I find the chaos fun. I’ve been doing this for a couple of decades, so seeing the cycles makes it less scary. You appreciate that these things happen, and that we should enjoy the upside, because sometimes there’s downside, and the up is a lot more fun than the down.

Amit Bhatti: If anything, it’s exciting. Venture is sometimes looked at as a niche, and now that AI is all-consuming, all the attention is on venture. This feels like our moment more than it is like, “Oh gosh, what’s going to happen?” The pace of investing and the valuations may be different, but really meaningful stuff is happening, and all the attention is focused on this corner of private equity.

Your funds all hold the same brands now, OpenAI and Anthropic, multiplied across however many funds you back, and your job is to keep your institutions diversified. How do you think about that? Obviously it’s great right now, but if things turned, it would be less great.

Amit Bhatti: Venture has always been a power law business, so I actually view the concentration as a good thing. If we were getting to the maturity of one of our funds and there were still lots of tiny positions, something’s gone wrong. Our funds that are 10-plus years old are starting to consolidate into a few names. There’s a lot of Databricks, a lot of SpaceX, a lot of Stripe. In this generation of funds, I would hope there’s a lot of Anthropic and a lot of OpenAI. That’s a feature, not a bug. Not every one of these companies is going to work out, but that consolidation is typical. What’s different is how quickly it’s happened. I don’t view it as an immediate panic signal.

Beezer Clarkson: At the early stage, you still see quite a diversity of opportunity sets, and the dollars are smaller. It aggregates up into the same companies, but early-stage funds obviously aren’t doing the big late-stage stuff, so you have more diversity there, if that’s what you’re looking for.

Funds that invested on four-year cycles have shrunk that to three, then two, then 18 months. Is the pacing okay, or is it concerning?

Beezer Clarkson: We’re seeing funds come back on one-year pacing, which is fast. The norm was probably two to two and a half years. Some funds are deploying much faster because they’re taking concentrated, big-check positions. That could be a worrisome sign. It could work out, we don’t know, but it’s typically harder to do a one-year vintage and get it right.

Amit Bhatti: Similar for us. I would have said 24 to 36 months was roughly normal. Now 12 to 18 is not crazy for some of the funds going really quickly. A lot of funds are bumping up their fund sizes mid-cycle, which is definitely unusual. That’s partly because rounds have gotten so large. If Anthropic is raising a giant quantum of capital and you put 20% of the fund into it, you’re obviously going to be ahead of pace. Seed round sizes have gone up almost 2x, too, so if you want to lead, you’re writing 2x the check. It’s definitely a yellow light. It gives us a little bit of heartburn.

But when we look at what these managers actually bought, the numbers are different. The last time we had accelerated pacing, there was a lot of investing in zero-revenue crypto moonshots. Now we’re seeing a lot of companies go from zero to $100 million in revenue, which was totally unheard of before.

If you’ve got a great manager who comes back every year but the returns are still on paper, can you say “call me next time,” or do you lose your seat at the table?

Beezer Clarkson: It’s very hard to leave a manager and then come back. It happens, but it’s more typical to downsize your check. In 2021, a lot of LPs said, “If I was going to give you $10 million, I’ll do $5 million, because $10 million was for two years.” In our portfolios, the pacing gets pulled through, so we think about our pacing as well as yours.

Amit Bhatti: Same here. We’re building out a calendar of when we expect to make commitments, so if someone goes way off that map, we need to make sure the capital is there. You see people downsize or communicate it up front. It’s hard to say you’re sitting it out altogether, because then you’re not reliable capital. That’s also why you’re seeing upsizes; managers don’t want to come back and say they’re raising a whole new fund, so they bump up the old one.

Beezer Clarkson: People also rotate out of venture sometimes because capital calls keep running with no distributions coming back, and they still have to meet operating commitments, whether it’s the endowment, the hospital, or the foundation. That puts a lot of strain on those situations.

LPs like time diversification, yet a lot of funds were raised in recent years, including that backed startups at high valuations during the pandemic. How are those funds doing, and how would you describe 2026 so far?

Beezer Clarkson: The 2021 vintages are still early, five years in, but they argue against doing one-year funds. Some will catch a piece of an AI company and look excellent, but your odds of getting it right in one year are just tougher, and the valuations were extreme.

Amit Bhatti: If I look at the last 15 years of our portfolio, I wouldn’t bet on the COVID vintage being the best one. But a couple of breakouts will come from it. OpenAI was around in that era, and Cursor started pretty far back, so they’re in some of those funds. And liquidity has started flowing. The past two years were definitely slower, but SpaceX is the headline, Cerebras was a big exit this year, there have been a couple of other IPOs, and a lot of M&A. We’re seeing $10 billion-plus M&A exits, a $60 billion one [with Cursor]. Liquidity is going beyond just IPOs.

How are your venture fund managers thinking about secondaries? If I were a VC, I’d have been tempted to take money off the table in OpenAI or Anthropic.

Beezer Clarkson: Secondaries have become much more sophisticated in venture over the last, call it, five years. It’s localized in the top handful of companies, but it’s much more prevalent than before, which I think is good, because the ecosystem needs liquidity options. Venture is predicated on that, and if you wait 20 years for an IPO, that is not what structurally we all thought it could be. They’re also happening at multiple levels now. LPs sell stakes of their GPs, a strip of their portfolio, and the taboo around it is less.

Amit Bhatti: It’s the third leg of liquidity now: IPOs, M&A, secondaries. Private equity has always had a well-developed secondaries market, and venture didn’t. It was kind of a dirty word. You were only selling if you were distressed. Then people were holding the bag in 2021 and thought, “I should have sold.” Now more managers use it as a tool, and more judiciously. If you still believe it’s the power law company, you’re probably not exiting the whole position. But if you can sell 20% of your position and return your fund, you should probably do it.

There’s a lot of founder selling and employee tenders — often very early into the company’s “journey.” How do you feel about that?

Amit Bhatti: We were talking before about the analogy to crypto, where things got very difficult in part because employees were paid in tokens that were liquid immediately. What’s your motivation to stick around when things get hard? So I think it’s great that there are employee tenders, especially for companies that have been around a long time, like Stripe and Databricks, with a very clear financial picture. For them to offer partial liquidity to employees is totally reasonable. But a lot of the enforcement falls on the lead investors. Investors we back have told companies, “We don’t want you to do an employee tender right now.” Those conversations are happening behind the scenes, and people have learned some lessons from last time. It’s all based on leverage, though. If the founder has incredible leverage . . .

Forget it.

Amit Bhatti: Yeah.

When these companies go public and employees get liquid, will they become partners or competitors to your venture managers? These employees have amazing networks. 

Beezer Clarkson: We’ve seen it multiple times: when a company becomes very productive, employees can become LPs or GPs themselves. It’s entirely possible there’ll be a whole new raft of emerging managers backed by people coming out of OpenAI and Anthropic. It happened in the Google days. But being an LP means signing up for many millions of dollars and a multi-decade business. 

Amit Bhatti: The real estate part [given the soaring cost of home prices in San Francisco] is going to be tough. But those people stay in the ecosystem, investing in others, building new companies, starting new firms. That’s why no other place is taking SF’s place anytime soon.

Housing costs here in San Francisco have shot up so fast. Do we price out the next generation of founders, and does the next hub end up in New York or somewhere else?

Beezer Clarkson: History would argue that the density effect in the Bay Area is a great pull. Maybe it moves out of San Francisco and back into the suburbs. Back in the day, YC was in Mountain View. New York obviously has its own very deep tech scene, but there’s such a density here that it’s been really hard to push back against.

A handful of venture funds now lock down most of the committed capital from limited partners. Is there a wedge in for emerging managers?

Beezer Clarkson: There are still first-time and emerging managers, funds one through three, being raised this year, last year, the year before. You still need a differentiated point of view, a reason for being. Fundraising has gotten harder, but we see them being funded, and the fund sizes are just smaller. Fifty percent of the money might go to the big funds, but if your average first fund is $25 million to $50 million, there can still be enough of those to add up to $1 billion.

Amit Bhatti: There are people raising $5 million or $10 million right here in SF, maybe formalizing their angel investing. A lot of really well-known funds started with a $5 million fund. It’s much better for an emerging manager to build the track record, prove out the thesis, your access and your judgment with whatever capital you have, and then fund two will be easier to raise. If you try to raise $50 million or $100 million on day one, you’re creating a giant hill to climb.

Beezer Clarkson: If you’ve only angel invested, that’s a different story from spinning out of a platform where you have an installed base of LPs who know you. Those managers typically raise more.

Can you talk about specific kinds of emerging managers you’ve backed, and what made you write the check?

Amit Bhatti: People define “emerging” very differently. We’ve backed founders who are still running their companies and investing on the side. We’ve backed people leaving a bigger firm for something earlier. And we’ve backed extremely young GPs, 22 and 23 years old, who have really close access to the next generation of AI-native founders. They started an accelerator program at MIT, Harvard, and Stanford, and the first couple of batches had Cursor and Mercor in them. They’re young, but they’re around an incredible density of talent. The VC job is sourcing, picking, winning, and they did a pretty decent job of picking when there was no money involved. Success begets success in venture, so we were happy to give them a shot.

Beezer Clarkson: There’s much more flexibility now. I remember a time when an LP wouldn’t fund somebody who had a job and was also investing, and people are open to that now. I’ve been investing in emerging managers, along with established ones, for 14 years, and they run the whole gamut, from an operator-turned-investor raising $10 million, to a spinout raising a few hundred million [dollars]. It’s interesting when they’re still operating, because it gives them insights. The trick is whether they’re doing what they need to do to win the right to be on the best cap tables.

Amit Bhatti: Especially early stage, there’s no one-size-fits-all. You can be part-time, you can be diversified, you can be concentrated. There are more outs in the deck, if you will, for returning something that’s small and experimental.

What’s the smallest check you’ll write to a fund, and how much of a fund will you take?

Beezer Clarkson: Given our program, it’s hard to do less than $5 million. I’ve generally taken the view that if you’re [representing] too much of a fund, there are challenges for the GP going forward, so I’d want to be no more than 20%. There are situations where I’d consider more.

Amit Bhatti: Three to five million for us, and on occasion smaller in very specific scenarios. We don’t really care about concentration if it’s the right scenario. We’ll do half or all of it. But Beezer’s right that it’s not ideal for the GP, and we tell them up front to diversify their LP base. We’ve done a fund where we were half the capital, and the next fund we were closer to 20%, because they did well.

The limited partners who provide the capital to venture firms — the “money behind the money” — are feeling great right now. They’re in uncharted territory in many ways, but also potentially exceedingly lucrative territory.

Normally, LPs typically spread their bets across many firms to diversify their own portfolios. They write checks to emerging managers and established ones, to generalist firms and specialists. The goal is a strong return, but also to minimize risk.

title: This Is What an iPhone Duo’s Crease Looks Like After 139K Folds
snippet: After a week of nonstop folding, we briefly turn the iPhone Duo’s display off to check out how the crease looks.
fullText:
For foldable phones, it’s typical for a crease to become more noticeable after years of use. And we want to find out exactly how much bending Apple’s new $1,999 iPhone Duo can take. 

CNET has been speeding up those years using our Fold-a-Phone machine. After a week of nearly nonstop folding, our iPhone Duo test unit has surpassed 139,000 folds.

You can see the iPhone Duo’s crease when the display is off.CNET

In this clip from our YouTube channel, you can take a closer look at the crease, which has remained largely unchanged since we began the test. That is to say, you can certainly see the crease as the phone opens and closes, but when the display is on, the crease is quite hard to see. When the display is turned off during a break in folding, the crease is substantially more noticeable, though that’s also the case when you take the Duo out of the box before turning it on.

			

More from CNET

That doesn’t mean the crease isn’t getting wear and tear, but Apple’s nano-texture matte display helps disguise it by reducing reflections. This matte layer is removable, and some people who have peeled it off are discovering that the Duo’s crease is far more visible without it — the same as on other book-style folding phones like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. One clip posted to X by Ice Universe shows this off.

Unbelievable! The iPhone Duo's display has been hiding a shocking secret!

Someone finally dared to peel off the matte film covering the iPhone Duo's display, and what they discovered was astonishing.

With the film removed, the screen underneath looks surprisingly uneven, with… pic.twitter.com/nrij2Iblge

— Ice Universe (@UniverseIce) October 22, 2026

The ability to remove that layer is intentional, and Apple offers a service to replace it: $19 with AppleCare and $49 without the program. 

Our folding tests will continue until the iPhone Duo can no longer fold. You can watch how it’s holding up in our machine every weekday as we livestream on CNET’s YouTube channel.

title: Apple TV has three shows with finales next week, here’s what’s ending
snippet: Apple TV just premiered Nocturne, a new crime thriller that’s earning a lot of praise. But the streamer also has three series all scheduled to wrap up next week. Here’s what’s ending. more…
fullText:
Apple TV just premiered Nocturne, a new crime thriller that’s earning a lot of praise. But the streamer also has three series all scheduled to wrap up next week. Here’s what’s ending.

Brothers, Small Prophets, and Knife Edge all air season finales next week

It’s rare for Apple to cycle out the majority of its weekly lineup in a single week. More often, the streamer’s schedule sees shows ending and starting in more staggered fashion.

But next week is an exception, with three shows all wrapping up within days of each other:

Brothers, the Matthew McConaughey-Woody Harrelson comedy airs its finale November 4

Small Prophets, the very highly acclaimed British comedy also ends November 4

Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars, the food-centric docuseries wraps November 6

The fate of all three shows is currently an open question, though hopefully we get at least one renewal announcement next week.

Small Prophets seems especially likely to continue on. Its perfect 100% Rotten Tomatoes score no doubt helps, with critics saying it may be “the finest show to hit Apple this year.”

Additionally, the BBC production was technically already renewed for season 2 last month—but not by Apple. It’s one of the only Apple TV series that’s licensed from a third party. While it’s assumed that Apple negotiated the rights to future seasons, that hasn’t yet been confirmed.

If you’re looking for new series to watch on Apple, the crime thriller Nocturne sounds like a winner, with Stephen Graham (“Adolescence”) playing a serial killer who evokes Anthony Hopkins’ iconic Hannibal Lecter.

For lighter fare, the heartfelt comedy Stick returns next week starring Owen Wilson and Rhea Seehorn (“Pluribus”).

You can find a full rundown here of everything new Apple TV has coming in November.

title: Gemini Notebook for Android, iOS adds built-in audio recorder
snippet: After introducing Connected App integration last week, Gemini Notebook has rolled out an audio recorder on Android and iOS. more…
fullText:
After introducing Connected App integration last week, Gemini Notebook has rolled out an audio recorder on Android and iOS.

Between the camera and “Create New” floating action button at the bottom, you’ll see a new microphone icon. This lets you “capture lectures and record your thoughts on the go,” with the audio file creating a new notebook if you launch the recorder from the homepage. 

Your notes will live directly alongside your sources, meaning you can chat, cite, and build from them anytime, all while making ongoing edits. 

Recordings will be saved to an existing Notebook if you tap the microphone from the Sources tab.

The recorder interface is very simple with a pause button and checkmark that starts the upload once you’re done. A Gemini Notebook-themed waveform and live count appear above. You can switch to another application or lock your screen and have recordings continue in the background. There’s a 1-hour capture limit.

	

Google first announced the audio recorder in September, and it’s now widely rolling out today on Android and iOS. Force stop the app if it’s not live on your device.

Meanwhile, Google this week made a small tweak wherein tapping the “Create New” FAB immediately starts a new notebook rather than sliding up the “Add a source” panel. 

These updates follow the recent launch of the Live button in the Chat tab that lets you have a real-time conversation with your notebooks.

title: Google says Android Auto video apps are still ‘coming soon’ as deadline nears
snippet: In a brief update at its latest dev conference, Google says that video and browser apps for Android Auto are still “coming soon,” with the company’s self-imposed deadline approaching quickly. more…
fullText:
In a brief update at its latest dev conference, Google says that video and browser apps for Android Auto are still “coming soon,” with the company’s self-imposed deadline approaching quickly.

Back in May 2026, Google announced that video apps on Android Auto would be available this year on select vehicles. This would support using your car’s display for watching content from apps such as YouTube, with Google also confirming that background play would kick in after the vehicle shifts out of park. 

With only two months left until Google’s year-end deadline lands, one might expect a beta release or some news on timing, but the company’s latest update doesn’t really bring much to the table.

At the Android Dev Summit this week, Google says that video and browser apps for Android Auto are still “coming soon.” Video apps are now “open” on Android Automotive (Google built-in) with browser apps in beta, but the phone-projected platform is still waiting. Google is also currently testing an updated version of audio apps using the Cars App Library, as well as new messaging and calling apps.

title: Someone is bringing Android Auto back to your phone’s screen, and it actually works [Gallery]
snippet: When Android Auto first debuted, it didn’t require a fancy display in your car. It just worked on your phone screen and, now, someone is bringing that functionality back after Google killed it. more…
fullText:
When Android Auto first debuted, it didn’t require a fancy display in your car. It just worked on your phone screen and, now, someone is bringing that functionality back after Google killed it.

Back in 2019, four years after Android Auto hit the scene, Google announced that it would be shutting down support for using Android Auto on your phone’s display. Its replacement, Google Assistant’s driving mode, was so unfinished at launch that it required Google to release “Android Auto for Phone Screens” as a stopgap. That later shut down in 2022 as Google made Android Auto “only available for car screens.”

And, in the time since, there haven’t been very many good alternatives to that functionality. You can get in-car displays for cheaper and cheaper – the average prices on Amazon are around $80 or so –  but it’s also just conveinent to get it on the phone screen.

That’s what “PhoneAuto” wants to do. 

	

This new app is in development and soon to debut on the Google Play Store and lets you run Android Auto on your phone screen, just like you used to be able to. Well, almost like you used to. The difference here is in how the app gets Android Auto going, using the “head unit server” developer functionality to run Android Auto on-device. It takes a couple of added clicks but gets the job done, but it does work. You also have to tap the “quit” button in your notifications to stop the head unit server from running after you’re done. “PhoneAuto” can partially automate this if you grant it accessibility permissions.

As for actual performance and functionality, it works about as well as I’d expect from a beta.

On my Galaxy Z Fold 8, the portrait mode setting doesn’t work very well, with plenty of lag in play, but the landscape setting works just fine on both the inner and outer displays. The layout adjusts to your screen, just as it does in a car, and I found that touch is responsive enough. It doesn’t run at a full frame rate as you’ll find in some newer vehicles. 

But it works. It puts Android Auto on your phone’s display, something you haven’t been able to do for years.

The beta is available for sideloading via GitHub – install at your own risk, as always – with an expiration in January. Presumably it’ll be available in the Play Store before that date.

title: Remember Patrick Stewart by Streaming Star Trek, X-Men and Other Genre-Defining Roles
snippet: Celebrate the life of Patrick Stewart through his iconic roles in TV and movies.
fullText:
Patrick Stewart, the legendary actor known to many as Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the Star Trek universe and Professor Charles Xavier from the X-Men movie franchise, died on Wednesday at age 86. An Instagram post announcing the news says Stewart passed after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

When looking back at the slate of work Stewart put out into the world, you’ll find over six decades worth of performances. The actor cut his teeth in the world of Shakespearean stage productions and smaller TV projects, mostly in the UK, before he broke out into mainstream popularity in 1987, leading the crew of the Enterprise in Star Trek: The Next Generation.

Read more: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86

			

More from CNET

Along with Picard, he’s most known for the role of Professor Charles Xavier, the wheelchair-using leader of the X-Men. His final performance as Professor X will be seen in Avengers: Doomsday later this year. 

To remember Stewart, you can tune in to many of his projects on various streaming services. Since I’ve stuck to roles that can be streamed, his memorable performances as Ebenezer Scrooge in 1999’s A Christmas Carol, John Thornton in 1975’s North & South and the ghost of Hamlet’s father in 2009’s Hamlet, for instance, aren’t listed.

Read more: ‘Star Trek: Picard’ Season 3 Review: The ‘Next Generation’ Reunion We’ve Been Waiting For

Star Trek: The Next Generation and Star Trek: Picard (1987-2023)

Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation.

CBS

Stewart made Star Trek an obsession for me growing up, and his performance as Captain Jean-Luc Picard is simply iconic. He starred as Picard in seven seasons of Star Trek: The Next Generation before taking the character to the big screen in four movies in the grander franchise. Stewart reprised his role as Picard in the aptly titled sequel series Star Trek: Picard, which lasted three seasons, with the final one acting as a must-see TNG reunion.

The X-Men franchise (2000-2017)

Patrick Stewart as Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men.Attila Dory/20th Century Fox

After he made a name for himself, boldly going wherever the Enterprise took him, Stewart stepped into an even more legendary role: Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 X-Men movie. He reprised his role as leader of the X-Men in six installments in the franchise, including the stand-alone Wolverine movie, Logan. In December, audiences will see him one final time in the role in Avengers: Doomsday.

Green Room (2015)

Patrick Stewart as Darcy Banker in Green Room.A24

It wasn’t common to see Stewart in a villainous role, so his performance as Darcy Banker in Green Room is a riveting turn for the actor. The movie takes place mostly inside a bar that caters to a white supremacist crowd, and Darcy is not just the bar owner, he’s their soft-spoken, violent leader.

Moby Dick (1998)

American Zoetrope

Stewart starred as Captain Ahab in the 1998 miniseries adaptation of Herman Melville’s epic Moby Dick. The series follows the quintessential story of Ahab’s hunt for the white whale and delves into his backstory and relationships, introducing his wife, Elizabeth. Costarring in the series are Gregory Peck, Piripi Waretini and Henry Thomas.

Dune (1984)

Patrick Stewart as Gurney Halleck in David Lynch’s Dune.Dino De Laurentiis Corporation

David Lynch’s take on Dune may have been a box office failure, but in the years since it hit theaters, the movie has achieved cult status. Stewart takes on the supporting role of Gurney Halleck, who Josh Brolin played in the new Dune franchise.

The Prince of Egypt (1998)

Stewart had a recognizable, resonant voice, and his voice-acting work appeared in a slew of animated films. The Prince of Egypt featured the actor as Pharaoh Seti I, the film’s antagonist. He was joined by a stacked slate of talent, including Val Kilmer, Ralph Fiennes, Steve Martin and Sandra Bullock.

Extras (2004)

Screenshot by Aaron Pruner/CNET

Sometimes, the best Stewart was the one who poked fun at Stewart. In the first season of the Ricky Gervais comedy series Extras, Stewart appeared as a heightened version of himself. He may have just appeared in one episode (Episode 6, to be exact), but he definitely left an impact.

Jeffrey (1995)

Screenshot by Aaron Pruner/CNET

Jeffrey is a comedy that came out at a time when gay-themed movies were few and far between. The movie stars Steven Weber as the titular character, who decides to become celibate out of fear of contracting AIDS. It should be noted that this is a comedy and Stewart and Weber, along with the likes of Michael T. Weiss, Bryan Bratt, Nathan Lane and Sigourney Weaver, deliver on that front.

The Sheep Detectives (2026)

Patrick Stewart voiced the character Sir Ritchfield in The Sheep Detectives.Amazon MGM Studios

One of Stewart’s final roles is that of Sir Ritchfield, the elder sheep featured in The Sheep Detectives, from Amazon MGM Studios. The movie follows a group of sheep who take it upon themselves to investigate the untimely death of their shepherd, George Hardy, played by Hugh Jackman.

“Visual polish” and fix several display bugs on Android

Transfer music between rooms

fullText:
Apple TV has a new crime thriller premiering tonight—Nocturne—and early reviews indicate it could be another hit series for the streamer.

When the desperate search for Jurek’s last missing victim forces Jonah to send his surrogate daughter, FBI Agent Saga Bauer (Zazie Beetz), up against Jurek, how far will Jonah go?

title: I’ve been using Android’s iPad Mini OLED for months, and it’s the better tiny tablet
snippet: Apple has just released a new iPad Mini with an OLED display and it looks great, but I’ve spent the past few months with Android’s equivalent in the Redmagic Astra 2, and it’s well worth your attention. more…
fullText:
Apple has just released a new iPad Mini with an OLED display and it looks great, but I’ve spent the past few months with Android’s equivalent in the Redmagic Astra 2, and it’s well worth your attention.

The new iPad Mini with OLED is a long-overdue upgrade. As 9to5Mac details, this new tablet delivers an 8.5-inch OLED display, a chassis that’s just 5.4mm thick, and weighs just 255g. By all means, it looks great.

Apple unveils all-new iPad mini: OLED, thinner design, more

But over the past few months, I’ve been using what has now turned out to be a close rival to that tablet. The Redmagic Astra 2 may be a gaming-focused Android tablet, but it matches or even beats the new iPad Mini in some crucial ways.

The 9.04-inch OLED display on the RedMagic Astra 2 is a bit bigger than Apple’s (it’s a slightly thicker and heavier tablet, too), but it’s still very much in that same ballpark. And it’s a gorgeous display. For everything from movies to games, it’s been an absolute pleasure to use. Colors are vivid, blacks are as deep as only OLED can do, and it beats Apple’s peak brightness at 1,600 nits too. 

	

The biggest point in Redmagic’s favor is in that display, too. Where Apple is still refusing to give the iPad Mini a 120Hz refresh rate with this latest model – utterly insane in the year two thousand and twenty-six, if I do say so myself – Astra 2 has a 185Hz refresh rate. I’ve not found that inherently better than a standard 120Hz panel, but it’s way better than the 60Hz panel Apple’s latest will still be using. You do miss out on stylus support on the Astra, though (sadly).

As for performance, Redmagic Astra 2 is packing Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and 12GB of RAM in its base model. Over the past couple of months that performance has been absolutely stellar. Not that that’s a surprise, these are the same core specs as you’ll find in something like the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Redmagic’s Android skin isn’t particularly heavy either.

I’ve been hooked on Metalstorm throughout the review period, and it runs brilliantly even on max settings on the Astra 2.

It also never gets warm, probably thanks in part to the liquid cooling loop and fan built into the tablet. While the whine of the fan can be heard in super-quiet rooms (like late at night in bed), it’s typically never a problem. Despite the fan, Astra 2 is still IP54 rated, too. 

Battery life is also great to the point where it’s barely a thought, not surprising for an 8,300 mAh cell. Gaming sessions up to an hour barely make a dent, and the standby time is ridiculous. At one point I didn’t have a chance to use the tablet for over a week and it only drained about 25% in that time. When it came time to charge, any USB-C cable works and you’ve got the choice of two ports, so you can easily top off in the way that’s easiest for you while still being able to use USB peripherals if you want. I just found this convenient for being able to choose between the side-mounted charger on my bedside table or the bottom port when I was still actively holding the tablet.

Astra 2’s hardware, by the way, is an aluminum body that’s 6.9mm thick. It has a little glass window on the back with some RGB accents, but it’s overall subtle enough, and you can turn off the RGB entirely.

The software, as mentioned, isn’t all that heavy. It’s certainly not what you’d expect for something marketed as a gaming tablet. Outside of a gamer font (which you can change), the UI doesn’t feel that far off from a Pixel. It’s not the cleanest, but it’s far from the heavy iOS clones you’ll find elsewhere. There are even nice additions such as lockscreen widgets. A customizable switch up top defaults to a gaming mode (which has a full gamer UI and optimizes performance) can serve whatever function you like, including acting as a mute switch or to active the flashlight. 

Meanwhile, there’s also the conversation around price. Apple’s starting price is lower at $699. That said, while the price on Astra 2 is higher at $749 – and that’s the result of a quiet price hike that landed quite literally within the last few days – that’s for the 12GB/256GB model. On Apple’s side, the equivalent iPad Mini lands at $799. Redmagic’s slate is actually a great deal with that in mind, even more so on the 512GB model at $849 compared to Apple’s $999.

Following the other big interface updates this month, Google is rolling out a small ‘plus’ redesign to Gemini Live on Android that lets you more easily add photos and files.

title: Google’s new Metal Mesh Fitbit Air band is more versatile than you think
snippet: A metal mesh band might not be right for every watch or wearable, but I can’t say I don’t love using it on the Fitbit Air. more…
fullText:
A metal mesh band might not be right for every watch or wearable, but I can’t say I don’t love using it on the Fitbit Air.

The Fitbit Air has suffered from a lack of band options since launch, and it hasn’t improved very much. The Pokémon Sleep band, while a cool collectible, is still a variation of the Performance Loop strap. The Stephen Curry band is a cool choice, but it suffers from the same lack of elasticity that’s sort of expected from a fabric band.

Google’s new Metal Mesh band, though, is a nice little departure from the existing options. It mounts to the Fitbit Air the same way, with a molded cutout for the small tracker to tuck into. One end of the mesh strap is secured to the plastic Firbit Air case, and a metal loop attaches to the other side. Just like the Performance Loop band, the Metal Mesh strap is secured through that loop and doubles over to secure.

I generally look for a couple of things with mesh bands: a fabric-like lay and a solid clasp. The clasp was a little stiff out of the box, and it took a bit of extra effort to loosen and adjust, but it was painless after the first go. The buckle slides up and down the weave of metal links so you can get the perfect fit. Once secured, putting the strap on is quick. I’d almost go so far as to say it’s easier than strapping down the Performance Loop band.

	

The mesh quality is better than I had expected out of the box. If it falls and conforms to something like fabric, that’s generally a good indicator that it’s secure and made well. A bad mesh band will bunch up or put up some resistance to bending. The Fitbit Air Metal Mesh band doesn’t do that.

It comes in two colors: Champagne Gold and Polished Silver. The Champagne version comes in a bundle, but both colors can be bought separately.

I’ve been wearing the Polished Silver, and it’s so easy to pair with whatever I’m wearing. I haven’t really removed it from my Fitbit Air since putting it on. I love a good fabric band for the versatility, but this has been so comfortable, even during workouts, that I’ve simply never found a reason to take it off. It might not be everyone’s preferred style choice, but it can be worn with almost everything.

Now, a $69.99 price tag might be a deterrent for some. And that goes double for what is a sub-$100 fitness tracker. At the very least, I think this is the best Fitbit Air band Google sells for its screenless Fitbit wearable.

But the Metal Mesh band for the Fitbit Air.

title: Oppo Find X10 Ultra is in the works, and I can’t wait to try its upgraded cameras
snippet: Not long after the Oppo Find X10 series launched globally, we’re already hearing details about the company’s Ultra model which is set to pack more impressive cameras – and that’s a pretty tall order. more…
fullText:
Not long after the Oppo Find X10 series launched globally, we’re already hearing details about the company’s Ultra model which is set to pack more impressive cameras – and that’s a pretty tall order.

We just reviewed the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max last week and, long story short, it has fantastic cameras. As it turns out, slapping three 200MP sensors into a single phone puts out some excellent images, and the phone around those cameras is pretty great too.

Now, there’s word that Oppo is still building out a Find X10 Ultra despite the impacts of RAMageddon.

Leaker Digital Chat Station says (via GSMArena) that the Oppo Find X10 Ultra is set to include at least two 200MP sensors of its own, but in another league. The cameras confirmed so far include:

	

200MP 1/1.12-inch main sensor, LOFIC

200MP periscope telephoto with 1/1.3-inch sensor, zoom unknown

50MP 10x periscope telephoto

100MP front-facing square sensor camera

That main sensor sounds pretty similar to last year’s Find X9 Ultra, as does that 10x periscope telephoto lens. The other telephoto shooter may not have a confirmed optical zoom length yet, but it’s likely 3x if Oppo is looking to match the Find X9 Ultra, and the sensor size is pretty much unchanged as well. There’s no word on the ultrawide yet, but that seems like an obvious candidate for a 200MP sensor if Oppo is looking to follow up on the Pro Max. Find X9 Ultra had a 50MP shooter here with a 1/1.95-inch sensor.

LOFIC on the main sensor is a new technology that improves dynamic range. It’s also expected to show up on other 2027 flagships, including Galaxy S27 Ultra.

The biggest upgrade here looks to be the front-facing camera, with the move over to a 100MP sensor, twice that of the prior generation, but also a square (1:1) sensor. That would allow for a more flexible shooter akin to the one Apple has been using in its latest iPhones.

Oppo Find X10 Ultra, if it follows the Find X9 Ultra’s pattern, will probably launch around April 2027. After using last year’s model, I can’t wait.

title: iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is it a Galaxy Fold moment?
snippet: Apple’s first foldable is running into a problem. iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is this a case of a flawed design like Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold, user error, or a bit of both? more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable is running into a problem. iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is this a case of a flawed design like Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold, user error, or a bit of both?

The earliest days of Android foldables were turbulent, to say the least. The original Galaxy Fold ran into major display issues within just 48 hours of reviewers getting their hands on the phone prior to the official release, leading to Samsung ultimately delaying the Galaxy Fold’s release for months. Part of the issue at the time was that curious minds were removing the top-layer screen protector that, as every foldable now makes abundantly clear, was never meant to be removed. The other problem came in the form of debris that would get under the display and kill the panel from underneath.

During the delay, Samsung ended up making some updates to the Galaxy Fold’s design, including making the top layer extend under the bezel, adding caps to the top and bottom of the hinge to prevent dust and debris from getting under the display panel, and reinforcing the display itself to protect it. At the time, Samsung’s CEO admitted that the launch was “pushed… before it was ready,” leading to the “embarassing” delay.

Galaxy Fold display failures from 2019 from The Verge

Now, Apple seems to be running into its own first-gen foldable issues.

	

As our sister site 9to5Mac highlights, there are a growing number of reports of early iPhone Duo units breaking, with the inner display failing in the exact same way across a number of units. The display fails in the middle, with a green line forming across the right side of the panel before further damage develops over time. 

The cause of the failure, it seems is a flaw in Apple’s hinge design. iFixit hypoethsizes that a support bar isn’t dropping far enough to leave room for the display panel, in turn creating a point of stress that could explain the broken iPhone Duo displays.

Similarly, iFixit’s teardown of the original Galaxy Fold in 2019 seemed to reveal the cause of Samsung’s display failures – and ended up being very much on the right track based on Samsung’s later fixes – though iFixit ended up removing the teardown at Samsung’s request. 

Another YouTuber has found a similar point of failure in the iPhone Duo’s hinge that seems to point to why displays are breaking the in same location. Affected users have found that the hinge has resistance before the display cracks, including an “audible crack.” 

In Samsung’s case, the problem was two-fold (pun intended), with some clear flaws in the hinge design and user error in the removal of the top layer. Samsung responded by delaying the release and making adjustments before re-releasing its first-gen foldable.

In Apple’s case, it’s certainly a bit trickier as this problem wasn’t revealed until the iPhone Duo landed in the hands of customers. The company has yet to issue a formal response to the problem, and affected users seem to be getting mixed messages from support channels. It’s still unclear in the chaos of the iPhone Duo’s launch just how widespread the issue is.

Update: Apple has acknowledged the issue in a statement to 9to5Mac.

Apple responds to reports of iPhone Duo’s inner display cracking

What do you think of the iPhone Duo’s display failures? Coincdence, or a bigger problem?

title: Ternus addresses Apple breaking touchscreen Mac taboo: ‘Who knew?’
snippet: In an interview with WIRED, Apple executives including CEO John Ternus, hardware chief Johny Srouji, and marketing chief Greg “Joz” Joswiak discussed the company’s decision to bring touch to the Mac. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In an interview with WIRED, Apple executives including CEO John Ternus, hardware chief Johny Srouji, and marketing chief Greg “Joz” Joswiak discussed the company’s decision to bring touch to the Mac. Here are the details.

Apple execs discuss touch about-face

For years, online commenters countered rumors of touchscreen Macs with quotes from Steve Jobs and other Apple executives, including Phil Schiller, arguing that touchscreens had no place on the Mac.

Shortly after Apple announced the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, journalist Steven Levy published an interview with Apple executives in WIRED discussing the company’s decision to reverse its longstanding stance on touchscreen Macs.

I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.

Ternus beams. “Who knew?”

In the interview, Ternus notes that while indirect input through the trackpad and keyboard remains central to the Mac experience, “there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”

He also stresses that Apple sees touch as an add-on, rather than a feature that should require compromises to the MacBook Pro’s design.

Throughout the interview, much of Apple’s reasoning for finally bringing touch to the Mac revolves around the fact that it reworked and developed several hardware and software components to make touch possible without compromising the Mac experience.

From WIRED:

“We needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”

As for Srouji, he argued that advances in technology over the past decade had finally made it possible for Apple to meet its standards for a touchscreen Mac.

	

That included custom silicon, a redesigned thermal system to keep the display from feeling hot to the touch, and a reworked hinge to minimize screen wobble when users interact with it.

“Ten years is a very, very long time,” says Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer. “Many things have changed, whether it’s the display technology, the custom silicon, et cetera.” Eventually, he told me, the confluence of chips, display tech, and software architecture “met our bar.” “I like my engineers to be gated by physics, not imagination or timelines,” he says.

Joz, in turn, noted that part of Apple’s decision was driven by a new generation of touch-first users who expect to interact directly with their screens:

“Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone,” Joswiak says. “So this is something that they’re natural with. There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.”

He added that professional users, including “engineers, scientists, software developers, and media creators,” had also been asking Apple to bring touch to the Mac.

The full interview also touches on (no pun intended) how Apple adapted macOS for touchscreen interactions, the new gestures for Dynamic Island, and whether touch might eventually make its way to other Macs. You can read it in full here.

title: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 still feels refreshing in all the best ways [Video]
snippet: With the iPhone Duo now a thing, it puts the Z Fold 8 in an even more interesting position. Yes, it’s an attempt by Samsung to get ahead of the curve, but, in truth, it really has worked. more…
fullText:
With the iPhone Duo now a thing, it puts the Z Fold 8 in an even more interesting position. Yes, it’s an attempt by Samsung to get ahead of the curve, but, in truth, it really has worked.

So now that Apple is here, there is no doubt that the Z Fold 8 faces its fiercest competition, but to me, it highlights so much of what Samsung did so well with. I do not think that the Duo renders Samsung’s design obsolete. Apple’s entry into the market only sharpens the contrast between these competing design philosophies. It even underscores precisely why I’ve come to prefer Samsung’s passport-size footprint.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

I’m not even sure it’s Samsung that has pushed the form factor forward too drastically. 

	

I’m not alone in realizing that, for a lot of people, passport size makes the most sense. The outer screen is just enough of a taster without being too big; switch to the inner if you want a little more playroom is immediately obvious from the get-go. Everything feels reachable on the outer screen, while the inner screen is the big canvas for all other content.

Sure, the Z Fold 8’s outer display isn’t perfect. Some UI elements can feel cramped; you will need to adjust how tall your keyboard is, but it isn’t as rigid as what Apple seems to have done on the Duo. That’s a good thing as the flexibility of Android just suits the multi-sized form factor.

The thing is, you’re going to fall into one of two categories. Those of us who want a smaller, tablet-y shape, or a phone that happens to open to run more apps side-by-side.

Objectively, the “traditional” folding phone size and shape will be more useful in basically most scenarios. Subjectively, I don’t really care about those as much. I’m in the privileged position of having a decent selection of handsets on deck at any one time to test-drive, and those satisfy something else entirely.

As I was saying, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has arguably been the most interesting and, now, my most-used phone throughout 2026. Of course, that is alongside the Pixel 10 Pro in early 2026 and now the 11 Pro. It has my backup SIM permanently tucked inside. Backup because I don’t get distracted as much with so many notifications, but that SIM has free roaming, making it my favorite travel companion…and my Balatro on-the-go handheld.

Every week, I’ll download a few movies and TV shows, like a sort of digital “prepper,” so I can be on a flight or a train and just know I have something to watch on a screen that tucks neatly into my side bag or jacket pocket. It is a mini tablet that weighs less than most other phones. You barely notice it. As I keep repeating: It feels so fresh.

One thing I have to appreciate about the slimline design is that I haven’t babied it; I have put a screen protector on the outer display for basic protection. It has handled a couple of days at the beach as an e-reader, and as yet, it’s accrued just one minor ding on the top frame edge, no major damage. That’s a good thing to me, as I haven’t found a Z Fold 8 case I really love yet. It’s super light and razor-thin; I never want to dull that sheen. It’s like the perfect realization of what the Flip ought to have been and likely won’t ever become.

I’ve seen a lot of complaints online about the inner display being both glossy and having a very visible crease. It’s not something I’ve dwelled on too much. They’re not big problems for me, in all honesty. I would like to see some enhancements, but it is what it is. That sounds like me handwaving away those complaints. I’m in agreement that we need to see Samsung make changes, especially now that Apple has a foldable with an almost-invisible crease and, frankly, a beautiful anti-reflective coating. Samsung is the undoubted king of displays, so we need more from the company in the future. That said, I still love the inner screen once I’m zipping around the system.

Against my better judgment, I have recently tried a “matte” screen protector from Amazon. So far, so good, but it’s nowhere near as matte as advertised. It does dull reflections, but I’m still on the lookout for something that might mimic the iPhone Duo display to see what the fuss is about. The screen protector I picked up does make a difference by reducing smears and fingerprints, but you might not want to put something on the inner screen, as Samsung doesn’t entirely recommend it, and it can be a bubbly mess if you get it wrong. It took me a few attempts to get the fit just right.

Back to the software: It helps that One UI is basically the perfect starting base for a foldable, and I think that is what has sealed the deal in a lot of ways. I’m a steadfast Material 3 Expressive fan, and while it’s still my preferred way to experience Android, One UI has continued to evolve in ways that Google likely doesn’t care about. I liked the Pixel 9 Pro Fold and 10 Pro Fold, but they felt less playful than the Fold 8 because I don’t think that Google does quite enough to truly optimize for the non-standard dual UI experience.

Sure, you need to use some of the Home Up and Good Lock plugins, but it opens up the door to vast customization that most other brands can’t really compete with. I like being able to make even minor adjustments to things like the volume UI or icon layout. Don’t get it twisted, I’m not doing insane things on my Z Fold 8, but even the minor adjustability holds weight on a device that acts as both a phone and a tablet, depending on which screen you’re about to use. Even the bottom dock is better placed than what I can glean from how Apple has added a right-sided dock on the iPhone Duo, while the volume buttons are just sensibly placed on the Fold, too.

The “big” apps are all well optimized. Instagram on the inner screen is awesome because you can see the comments and your feed in one instance. It feels like a tablet UI, probably because it is. There’s a little jank when running two apps side-by-side, but nothing that a little resizing can’t fix. I stick to two apps, as adding that third makes things cramped.

To expand on that a little further, I am actually really happy that Apple is about to wade into the foldable waters. For starters, it means we’ll hopefully get even better application support from the biggest developers. 

From launch, the Z Fold 8 has had a few apps tuned to take better advantage of the smaller outer display, and while they’re not quite perfect, at least some work has gone into them. I’m really excited about the prospect of more apps being refined, and with so many big corps effectively relying on AI for faster ports, surely the next few years might prove to be a golden age for foldables. The truth is that most Android apps already scale reasonably well, so no major issues. The odd UI section might feel cramped here and there, but I don’t think I can complain too much.

Now, for a few of the weakest portions of the Z Fold 8 that can’t really be glossed over too much.

Yes, the camera is not quite as good as the best in the business. 

At its worst, it’s purely functional, and ordinarily that would be a complete dealbreaker, but I’m at an age where a sharp, clear photo that does the job is more than good enough. Maybe I’m a glutton for this kind of punishment, as I find myself working around the limitations to get acceptable shots. It’s not ideal, but foldables compromise here more than any other devices, save the affordable options. So in that regard, you are well aware of that going in anyway.

It probably helps that I haven’t given up the Pixel 11 Pro as my mainstay photography phone. Not everyone can do that, so it’s arguably the biggest complaint you can have on the Z Fold 8 in my opinion – save the price, of course.

Battery life is another one of the weakest points. It will withstand most people’s usage patterns, but nobody should spend nearly £2,000 or $2,000 to have the Fold 8 not reach the end of the day. I think we all know by now that folding phones are going to compromise in this one area quite substantially. Luckily, it does manage to do movies and TV shows more than enough justice with longevity. I have watched multiple episodes of Widow’s Bay back-to-back on a couple of flights recently, and it doesn’t sap the battery all that much so long as you put the thing in flight mode.

In fact, I have been impressed when you’re not glued to the screen. It isn’t amazing, but I wouldn’t call the battery bad on the Z Fold 8 by any stretch. I have a super-slim Anker power bank in my bag at all times, so on a long-haul flight I’d just plug it in to be sure I can keep enjoying that lovely inner display. I can charge while watching and then just unplug, ready to go at my destination.

Now for the brief section where I will unashamedly just say some truly out-of-touch things (although this entire post is debatably out of touch): this is the most special phone I have used this year. Not even because it’s the best at any one thing. It could simply be a symptom of so much being “samey” or feeling so incremental in Western markets right now. This is a luxury product, and that instantly marks it down in most people’s eyes.

If Apple, the tastemakers of the non-tech buying public, are ready to give this form factor a real college try, then Samsung has made the right decision. The Z Fold 8 is easily the most elegant Android phone I’ve used in a while. I’m smitten with it. It’s something I want to unfold, fondle, and play with. What’s somewhat annoying is that, because I’ve enjoyed it so much, I’m giving in to a phone addiction I have tried so hard to curb over the past 18 months, since there is something refreshing here that is hard to truly quantify.

I’ll try my best to quantify it, though.

In my mind, there’s a Swiss Army Knife feel about the Z Fold 8 that no other phone has had for me for a long time. A tablet, gaming screen, reading screen, webpage dream all rolled into a passport package that respects my pockets – or the space in my sidebag. 

It’s a really versatile gadget that isn’t just a siloed phone, and that is probably why it’s resonating with so many people – myself very much included.

If you’re bored with your current phone and ready to switch, the Z Fold 8 might be worth taking a look at, provided you can stomach the price.

I’ll drop some of the best deals currently available on the Z Fold 8 down below, but expect to see discounts and sales soon, now that Apple has entered the fray and we’re on the cusp of Black Friday sales in the coming weeks.
