So now that Apple is here, there is no doubt that the Z Fold 8 faces its fiercest competition, but to me, it highlights so much of what Samsung did so well with. I do not think that the Duo renders Samsung’s design obsolete. Apple’s entry into the market only sharpens the contrast between these competing design philosophies. It even underscores precisely why I’ve come to prefer Samsung’s passport-size footprint.

title: Fitbit Edge Review: Too much and too little at the same time
snippet: When Google announced the Fitbit Edge, my assumption was that it would be a great in-between for the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air. In a way, that’s true, but this isn’t the product I thought it was – it’s just a new, slightly better Fitbit that leaves me wanting more. more…
fullText:
When Google announced the Fitbit Edge, my assumption was that it would be a great in-between for the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air. In a way, that’s true, but this isn’t the product I thought it was – it’s just a new, slightly better Fitbit that leaves me wanting more.

At $180, the Fitbit Edge is closer to the lower end of Google’s wearable lineup than it is a proper middle ground. It’s closer to a Fitbit Air with a screen than it is a “Pixel Watch Lite.”

That starts in the software, which has been updated to visually resemble this new era of Google Health. The main “Clock” face brings about a new assortment of options that draw inspiration from the Pixel Watch. There’s a baker’s dozen of these faces available, with the “Modular” series being my personal favorite. 

These support complications just like on Pixel Watch, allowing you to quickly see various data points around fitness tracking, or even pull in weather conditions. It’s not nearly as flexible as Pixel Watch – personal favorite weather data points such as UV index and sunset are missing, for example – but it’s a good glanceable bit of information, something the Air completely lacks.

	

What’s more frustrating than anything about the faces is that it’s all powered through the same basic and clunky interface that Fitbit trackers used for years. It’s incredibly slow and clearly not native to the Health app. It gets the job and works better than I remember it being the last time I used a Fitbit tracker, but it’s still a poor experience compared to the rest of the software.

Using the software on the tracker, you’ve got notifications below the clock and Quick Settings above, with Tiles to either side. It’s very familiar for Pixel Watch owners, and it’s visually a huge upgrade over the Fitbit Charge series. Google’s Material design language is felt throughout and everything is very clean with smooth animations. You can only customize the Tiles via the Google Health app on your phone (through the same clunky UI as faces), with the overwhelming majority being health/fitness-related, with weather and media controls also mixed in. This was the place I found the Edge most useful over the Air. Where tracking a workout on Fitbit Air either required relying on automatic tracking or starting it on your phone, Edge’s display lets you quickly jump into the workout of your choice. The “Quick Start” tile is helpful here, saving your most recent workouts. This was the biggest upgrade I found over the Fitbit Air outside of just, well, having the time shown on the thing on my wrist.

On the note of smartphone notifications, this is where I felt the biggest lacking from Pixel Watch. Inherently, a tiny display like this isn’t going to be as capable or useful as a full smartwatch, but the experience is just not very good. Notification previews can’t scroll through more than the first couple of words from a notification unless you tap “Open,” and incoming notifications also stack in the UI. The side button is used to go “back” in the software, but each notification is treated as its own layer, at least up until a certain point. When several notifications come in at once, this is a dreadful experience. They’re also not working consistently. I couldn’t get notifications working for much of the review period and, after many troubleshooting attempts, they just randomly started working on their own. Jordan Floyd on our video team says he still hasn’t managed to get them up and running. Google tells us that an upcoming Health app update will address notification issues.

Don’t get me wrong, notifications on Fitbit Edge are a huge step forward beyond the Fitbit Charge series, but they’re still not good either.

Apps on Fitbit Edge include the usual Health suite, as well as an alarm clock, Google Maps, a stopwatch, a timer, and a very basic weather app. The Google Maps experience leverages the Edge’s GPS but is really just a mirror of walking directions from your phone. You can’t start navigation on the Edge. The Weather app gets the job done, but it’s incredibly basic and lacks information I’d want outdoors such as UV exposure.

The biggest missing app here is Google Wallet, as the Edge lacks NFC support. Google says hardly anyone used it on the last generation, but I disagree with that logic – the Charge had many other downsides that prevented it from being appealing to those who also wanted Wallet, where the Edge is much closer to a fully usable smartwatch. Lack of mobile payment support is ultimately the biggest dealbreaker for me.

On hardware, Fitbit Edge is very much just an Air with a display.

Compared to a Pixel Watch, wearing the Fitbit Edge feels like wearing nothing. It’s very lightweight and, in turn, comfortable. Google’s bands from Pixel Watch also make the jump here, with the included Active band being just as comfortable as it is on Pixel Watch – though it is a hair magnet, picking up dog hairs far more readily than my Pixel Watch bands ever have. Google also sent over the Magnet Band which, personally, I’m not a fan of. It’s uncomfortable when on and, at least for my wrist, is difficult to put on. The two halves of the band are the same length and, if you sit in between the small and large sizes, it’s hard to get it on since there’s nothing for the band to grip on to until it’s fully connected. I’d rather go for something like the default Fitbit Air band here.

I was disappointed to see a problem from the Charge era make its way to Fitbit Edge. One multiple occasions through the review period, my Edge just fell off my wrist because the band connector failed. This happened once overnight and once as I was just walking through my home. It’s a disconcerting feeling, and was the eventual deal-breaker for me on Fitbit Charge 5 – I nearly lost the tracker while snowboarding, and it was shelved not long after that trip. Fitbit Edge doesn’t seem nearly as prone to this issue, but having it happen twice, with official bands, during my two-week review period is not exactly faith-instilling. A good habit would be to pull on the band to ensure it’s fully seated, but I’d argue this shouldn’t be necessary if you hear it click into place.

The connector here works well for switching bands quickly, but I would have appreciated seeing something new from Google here, especially seeing as it’s not like Fitbit Edge can use bands from the Charge series anyhow.

I reviewed the “Fog” setup with a silver tracker, and I do really appreciate that this splits the difference between a smartwatch and tracker in the looks department. With the right band, this is totally passable in a dressy situation.

Easily my favorite hardware decision here is the physical button on the side of Fitbit Edge. Prior Fitbit tracker toyed with a haptic button that was not at all a true button replacement. Not once was I fooled into thinking I was pressing a button, and the illusion only broke further when trying to turn the device on from an off state. It wasn’t the worst idea in theory, but a physical button is so much more satisfying. Fitbit Edge’s button isn’t the most premium, but it’s very much good enough and a welcome change on Google’s part.

But of course, none of that matters without fitness tracking to back it up.

I wore Fitbit Edge for the better part of two weeks – and only needed to charge once during that time, battery life is great, at least with the always-on display disabled – and used it mainly for tracking treadmill and strength workouts, with stats roughly lining up with the baselines set by Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5. You should never take stats from a fitness tracker as absolute truth, but the Edge is certainly more than capable enough at helping you to establish trends and work towards goals.

That’s all done in conjunction with the Google Health app, which I’ve been using with the Air and Pixel Watch for months at this point. Google Health, like virtually any AI tool, is inherently not perfect, but I’ve certainly come to appreciate it. The app opens to a simple overview of your cardio, steps, and other key data sets before diving into insights from the “Coach” – i.e. Gemini – around your trends. You can speak with “Coach” in natural language to set your goals around fitness, weight loss, strength training, or any number of things.

In that way, this is not the classic Fitbit of years past. This is very much a new experience built on the foundation of the old Fitbit, and one that you’ll either probably come to love, or come to hate. Personally, the experience has really grown on me. The app’s daily notifications summarizing my movement are a good last-minute way to get in some extra movement on quiet days, or a good morale boost when I was particularly active. As a workout novice, it’s also great for helping me figure out strength training workouts that suit my day. If I have more time or want to focus on a specific area, the “Coach” is pretty easy to work with in tailoring your workout. 

It’s not perfect, of course. It still tends to randomly get automatic workouts wrong, but for my needs it has done quite well. As we learned in our Fitbit Air review, though, your results may vary – at the end of the day, this is an AI-powered experience we’re talking about and, as Google itself repeatedly stresses, “AI may make mistakes.”

Of course, you’ll need to pay Google for a monthly subscription to use most of those features. Without Google Health Premium, the Edge is still capable, though, with support for basic step, heart rate, and workout tracking. Health Premium is bundled into the AI Pro plan which also includes Google Home Premium.

As a side note, kudos to Google for continuing on with the ability to use Fitbit Edge in tandem with other Google wearables in the Health app. While I used the Edge almost exclusively over the testing period, there were a couple of short Pixel Watch 5 stints mixed in for specific needs, and the Health app does a great job and syncing everything across not just the app, but each device. That said, it’s a less useful feature on the Edge. Where using a Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch in tandem is a fantastic experience, there’s almost no scenario I can imagine where it makes sense to have a Fitbit Edge alongside either one of those devices.

And therein lies my main takeaway with the Fitbit Edge.

This middle-ground wearable exists in a weird little bubble. It’s not a Pixel Watch, not even close, actually, but it’s also not a Fitbit Air.

I’ve found myself coming to appreciate the Fitbit Air as a way to find some reprieve from a connected lifestyle, with the Pixel Watch then stepping in when I need that connection or the added functionality of apps. The Fitbit Edge gets everything right on the fitness tracking side, but it also doesn’t really feel like it knows what it wants to be. It’s too connected and complex compared to the Air, but also too restricted compared to the Pixel Watch. It’s somehow both too much and too little at the same time.

	

That said, the Fitbit Edge might just need to be thought of in a specific light – it’s just not something new. This is a Fitbit tracker, an updated version of the same Fitbit tracker that millions have known and loved for years. In that light, it’s rather good, it just depends on whether or not you’ve moved beyond that point. I think I have.

Fitbit Edge starts shipping on October 27.

Fitbit Edge at Google Store

Fitbit Edge at Amazon

Fitbit Edge at Best Buy

					

Inherently a good and capable fitness tracker, Google’s new Fitbit Edge sits in a place where it’s somehow managing to bring too much and too little to the table at the same time.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Excellent battery life

											

Much better software than Fitbit Edge

											

Google Health is a good fitness coach

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Limited functionality outside of fitness

											

Clunky clock face selector

											

Paid subscription to unlock most features

title: Shrinking season 4 just got exciting release timing update
snippet: Shrinking just aired season 3 earlier this year, but all signs point to a refreshingly quick return, as one of the show’s stars just confirmed season 4 is officially done filming. more…
fullText:
Shrinking just aired season 3 earlier this year, but all signs point to a refreshingly quick return, as one of the show’s stars just confirmed season 4 is officially done filming.

Shrinking season 4 has finished filming ahead of expected early 2027 premiere

TV’s streaming era has brought a lot of advantages over linear TV, but undoubtedly one drawback is that shows tend to have much longer waits between seasons.

Traditional broadcast television usually schedules shows to premiere in the fall and run through the spring, then return after a short summer break for a new season in the fall.

In streaming, viewers are shocked when a show comes back after only a year.

Apple TV has slowly been getting better at this. Slow Horses is the best example, but another recent one is Your Friends & Neighbors. And we’re seeing signs of other series getting quicker turnarounds between seasons, including Shrinking.

Shrinking aired its season 3 finale this April, and by May we heard that filming on season 4 was about to start.

Now Jessica Williams, the star who plays Gaby, has confirmed that season 4 has officially wrapped production. This means the series will almost certainly return in early 2027.

On a show like Shrinking, post-production is a much quicker process than with series that are heavy on CGI and other special effects. So we could see Shrinking season 4 premiere in late January, exactly one year after season 3 debuted. 

More conservatively, the show returning by spring 2027 seems a safe bet.

You can watch Shrinking seasons 1-3 here on Apple TV.

title: The delightfully messy state of Apple gadgets
snippet: The iPhone has more screens! The MacBook has a touchscreen! The HomeView does CarPlay apps! For the first time in a long time, Apple is in a period of unabashed gadget experimentation, and while the final results aren't always perfect, it's fun to watch the most successful product maker try some new things again. Even when, in this case, "trying" amounts to just slapping a touch panel on a lovely new MacBook Pro - just to see if you might use it. On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate the merits of a touchscreen laptop, Nilay explains why he is absolutely positively going to buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
David Pierce

 

is editor-at-large and Vergecast co-host with over a decade of experience covering consumer tech. Previously, at Protocol, The Wall Street Journal, and Wired.

The iPhone has more screens! The MacBook has a touchscreen! The HomeView does CarPlay apps! For the first time in a long time, Apple is in a period of unabashed gadget experimentation, and while the final results aren’t always perfect, it’s fun to watch the most successful product maker try some new things again. Even when, in this case, “trying” amounts to just slapping a touch panel on a lovely new MacBook Pro — just to see if you might use it.

On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate the merits of a touchscreen laptop, Nilay explains why he is absolutely positively going to buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and David asks, as always, could this have been an iPad?

After that, the hosts discuss Instagram’s foray into long-form content, and Adam Mosseri’s increasingly complicated relationship with AI content. Instagram is at once extraordinarily powerful and under serious threat, and Mosseri’s going to have a hard time making it all work. Finally, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, news about Anthropic’s IPO and Anduril’s laptops, and much more.

title: Moto Tag 2 brings its UWB and Android Find Hub integration back to $20
snippet: After briefly ending the promo earlier this month, Motorola has dropped Moto Tag 2 back to $19.99. more…
fullText:
After briefly ending the promo earlier this month, Motorola has dropped Moto Tag 2 back to $19.99.

Moto Tag 2 is, at the moment, the only Android Find Hub tracker that supports UWB precise finding alongside Bluetooth, and it’s an excellent option for Android users. With upgraded battery life compared to the last generation, compatibility with AirTag accessories, and everything else you’d want in an item tracker, it’s a hard one to say no to. 

That math got a bit more complicated, though, when Motorola stripped away a long-running offer that had raised the price of Moto Tag 2 to its actual retail price of $30. Before that, it had been available for months for just $20. 

Now, Motorola has dropped the price yet again. Moto Tag 2 is available for $19.99 in a 1-pack from both Motorola.com and Amazon, with a 4-pack at $69.99.

	

Moto Tag 2 at Amazon – 1-pack | 4-pack

It’s easily the best deal in an Android Find Hub tracker, at least assuming you don’t need one of the dual-network finders available from the likes of Pebblebee and Chipolo. 

As a reminder, you can only get the orange “Arabesque” color through the purchase of a 4-pack.

Meanwhile, Google is gearing up to launch the Pixel Tag as its first-party Find Hub tracker, complete with UWB support. But that will cost $30 and also lacks the AirTag accessory compatibility that Moto Tag 2 offers.

We’re just weeks away from the launch of Google’s first Android Find Hub tracker, the Pixel Tag, and that’s also going to bring new options to the Find Hub app, as revealed in a new app update.
